abstract: The Long-Integration Magnetar Burst Observatory (LIMBO) is a real-time radio transient detection pipeline designed to search for dispersed fast radio bursts (FRBs) from Galactic magnetars. LIMBO employs a 4.3-m dish with a dual-polarization feed to continuously monitor a <inline-formula><tex-math>$125 \,\mathrm{MHz}$</tex-math></inline-formula> effective band centred at <inline-formula><tex-math>$1460 \,\mathrm{MHz}$</tex-math></inline-formula>. A real-time processing pipeline performs a search for dispersed transients on the summed polarizations, with detections triggering dumps of buffered voltage data to disc. Based on calibrated sensitivity measurements, synthetic signal-injection and recovery tests, and successful detection of pulses from the Crab Pulsar, we determine that LIMBO is sensitive to radio transients with fluences <inline-formula><tex-math>$\gtrsim 43 \,\mathrm{Jy \, ms}$</tex-math></inline-formula>. Between May and August 2023, LIMBO conducted 833 h of follow-up observations of the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154, yielding 12 candidate FRB detections. If these events are true, we measure FRB-like event rates from SGR 1935+2154 of <inline-formula><tex-math>$R(\ge 65 \, \mathrm{Jy \, ms}) = 112.3^{+81.3}_{-54.5} \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$</tex-math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><tex-math>$R(\ge 130 \, \mathrm{Jy \, ms}) = 17.7^{+40.8}_{-15.1} \,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$</tex-math></inline-formula>. Combining these results with previously reported FRBs-like from SGR 1935+2154, we infer a cumulative rate--fluence power-law slope of <inline-formula><tex-math>$\alpha =-0.60^{+0.24}_{-0.28}$</tex-math></inline-formula> in the fluence range between 10 and <inline-formula><tex-math>$10^6\rm \, Jy \, ms$</tex-math></inline-formula>. These observations demonstrate the capability of continuous, real-time monitoring of Galactic magnetars and establish LIMBO as an effective instrument for detecting Galactic FRBs.

abstract: Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are highly energetic radio sources whose duration is of the order of milliseconds. The physical origin of these sources is still unknown. Many models suggest magnetars as possible progenitors of FRBs, and this is supported by the association between FRBs and the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154; other proposed progenitors include binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, that are themselves linked to magnetar formation. In this work we investigate the possible connection between FRBs and BNS mergers, including magnetars that might be produced in such events, by comparing the detection rates inferred from synthetic BNS and associated FRB populations with the rates observed by CHIME. We produce a synthetic catalog of BNS mergers by combining recent theoretically predicted BNS merger rate as a function of redshift and the neutron star mass distribution inferred from measurements of Galactic BNSs. Using this catalog we predict the number of BNS systems ending as magnetars (stable or supramassive neutron star) or black holes (formed promptly or after the collapse of a hypermassive neutron star) for different equations of state. We then simulate for each BNS (and therefore for each magnetar remnant) an associated FRB and estimate how many of them can be potentially detected by CHIME. We find that the rate of BNS mergers and the rate of magnetars produced after BNS represents a non-negligible fraction of the FRBs detected by CHIME, both repeating and non-repeating. Although additional formation channels need to be considered to account for the entire population of FRBs, the existence of a fraction of FRBs that might genuinely be associated to BNS mergers has profound implications in the context of multi- messenger astronomy, supporting the systematic searches of coincident detections of FRBs and GWs from a BNS merger with current and future facilities.

abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are commonly classified into repeating and apparently nonrepeating sources, yet whether this distinction reflects intrinsically different physical populations remains uncertain. Using the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog, we apply an unsupervised machine learning framework combining uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) with density-based clustering to investigate the intrinsic structure of the FRB population in a multi-dimensional parameter space. We find that FRBs are primarily separated into two robust clusters dominated by spectral morphology. One cluster is characterized by narrowband emission and longer durations, while the other exhibits relatively broadband spectra and shorter burst timescales, confirming previous findings based on the first CHIME/FRB catalog. This classification scheme achieves a recall of 0.94 for known repeaters. Within the repeating population, we further identify a stable subclass of atypical repeaters that are broadband, shorter in duration, and more luminous, resembling nonrepeating bursts. Furthermore, broadband nonrepeaters exhibit systematically higher dispersion measures (by approximately 200 pc cm<SUP>-3</SUP>) and isotropic luminosities approximately an order of magnitude larger than those of repeating FRBs. Without invoking catastrophic progenitor scenarios, these differences are naturally explained by instrumental sensitivity limits and distance-dependent selection effects. Our results provide new statistical evidence for a physical connection between repeating and nonrepeating FRBs.

abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are bright flashes of radio emission with millisecond durations. Many fundamental questions remain regarding their origin, in particular the nature of their host galaxies and local environments. In this study, we gather all known repeating and well-localized FRBs with publicly available data that have been observed by the Swift observatory. We perform a systematic X-ray analysis using HEASARC tools to search for both transient and persistent emission from the FRB positions. Our search disfavors the brightest X-ray sources as dominant FRB progenitor candidates and favors FRB progenitors in moderate or low X-ray activity environments, consistent with compact objects such as neutron stars or magnetars. We summarize our results and present the largest homogeneous set of constraints to date on the persistent X-ray luminosities of FRB sources. We discuss prospects for significantly deeper constraints with higher-sensitivity instruments such as Chandra and future observatories including NewAthena, enabling the exploration of faint X-ray counterparts and ULX-like environments.

The formulas for the semi-analytical modeling of the gravitational wave signal from precessing neutron stars by the method of perturbations in the small neutron star ellipticity parameter are deduced.

abstract: We present deep Chandra observations of the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) powered by PSR J0007+7303 in the composite supernova remnant CTA 1. The merged ACIS image shows a ~20″ jet extending south of the pulsar and bending toward the southwest, a faint counterjet to the north, and a compact torus oriented approximately perpendicular to the jet axis. Using an archival observation from 2003, we perform relative astrometry over a ~20 yr baseline and constrain the pulsar's transverse velocity to ≲200 km s<SUP>-1</SUP> at a distance of 1.4 kpc at 95% confidence. This relatively low transverse velocity, along with the morphology of the jet, indicates a possible interaction with the SN reverse shock. Spatially resolved spectroscopy shows hard spectra for the jet and torus (photon indices Γ ≈ 1.2--1.4) and a softer spectrum for the extended nebula (Γ = 1.85 ± 0.11), indicating minimal radiative cooling in the compact regions. Modeling of the torus, associated with the termination shock, as an inclined circle yields a viewing angle ζ ≈ 50°. The outer gap and two-pole caustic pulsar emission models then imply a moderate magnetic inclination (α ~ 20°--70°). Broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling from radio to PeV gamma rays for a one-zone leptonic scenario yields a low magnetic field (B ≈ 1.4--3.2 μG) and a high electron cutoff energy (E<SUB>cut</SUB> ~ 0.2--0.3 PeV), indicating that the magnetic field decreases rapidly outside of the compact nebula. These results establish CTA 1 as a young, low X-ray efficiency PWN with a hard injection spectrum capable of accelerating particles to PeV energies.

abstract: The rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) is widely regarded as the dominant mechanism responsible for the synthesis of heavy elements in the universe, yet its astrophysical sites remain an open question. Recent studies suggest that the high-entropy, rapidly expanding baryonic material ejected by magnetar giant flares may provide favorable conditions for r-process nucleosynthesis, while the late-time gamma-ray emission observed from the magnetar SGR 1806-20 offers direct observational support for this scenario. In this work, we perform nuclear reaction network simulations to investigate the nucleosynthesis yields of magnetar giant flares and to characterize the associated nuclear gamma-ray line emission arising from the radioactive decay of heavy nuclei. The nuclei synthesized in magnetar giant flares are found to be mainly distributed near the first and second r-process abundance peaks. Owing to this nuclide composition, the gamma-ray opacity is found to be strongly energy-dependent, with the opacity in the keV band exceeding that in the MeV band by approximately three orders of magnitude. The nuclear gamma-ray emission is dominated by MeV photons at early times (t ≲ 10<SUP>3</SUP> s) and gradually extends toward the sub-MeV and keV bands as time progresses, thereby offering a diagnostic of heavy element enrichment in the ejecta. The gamma-ray spectrum exhibits a peak near ~ 1 MeV with major contributions from <SUP>88</SUP>Kr and <SUP>92</SUP>Sr, whose radioactive decays produce several bright gamma-ray lines with fluxes exceeding ~ 10<SUP>-8</SUP> erg cm<SUP>-2</SUP> s<SUP>-1</SUP>, making them the most promising lines for detection by MeV gamma-ray detectors. Because magnetar giant flares occur in the Galaxy at a rate roughly three orders of magnitude higher than neutron star mergers and their nuclear gamma-ray lines are accessible to current MeV instruments, they offer new and valuable science opportunities for MeV gamma-ray astronomy.

abstract: The identification of fast radio burst (FRB) host galaxies, and subsequently their redshifts ($z$), has allowed the FRB dispersion measure (DM) to be used to probe the cosmological distribution of ionised gas, and study the properties of the FRB population itself. However, current methods cannot account for FRBs with uncertain host galaxy associations, leading to underutilisation of data, and potential biases towards nearby, bright hosts. In this work, we develop a methodology which can. We do so by combining three ingredients - the zDM code, for modelling the Macquart relation; PATH, for statistical host galaxy identification; and a set of models able to describe the intrinsic FRB host galaxy distribution - into a single formalism. We prove the fidelity of our formalism by using a synthetic set of FRB observations, with simulated hosts sampled from galaxy catalogues, and show that it reproduces intrinsic host galaxy properties even for FRB localisation uncertainties of 30", where a traditional PATH analysis produces no confidant host associations. When applied to a sample of FRBs localised by the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder, we confirm previous results showing that FRBs prefer host galaxies fainter than that predicted by star-formation, consistent with an exponential surface density scaling as $0.41^{+0.13}_{-0.09}$ times the half-light radius. We encourage the application of this formalism to data-sets from other FRB-hunting instruments.

abstract: We present analyses of new and archival Chandra and NuSTAR data on two old millisecond pulsars, a young highly-energetic pulsar, and a young neutron star. PSR J1810-0623 is a recently-discovered 4.55 ms radio pulsar in a binary with a possible carbon-oxygen white dwarf companion. We tentatively detect the pulsar for the first time in X-ray using a new short Chandra HRC-I observation. Its faintness suggests a distance more in accord with the further (≍1kpc) of its dispersion measure-inferred distances. PSR J1933-6211 is a 3.54 ms radio pulsar also with a carbon-oxygen white dwarf companion. Our first-time X-ray detection in an archival HRC-S image indicates its X-ray luminosity is similar to that of the 1.9 ⊙ pulsar PSR J1614-2230. Next, PSR J1813-1749 is a 1-2 kyr pulsar with one of the highest known spin-down luminosities. We measure its spin period of 44.7 ms using 2025 NuSTAR and 2026 Chandra ACIS-S data and update its spin evolution model. We show for the first time the pulse profile of PSR J1813-1749 at 3-79 keV, and we find that the spectra of the pulsar and pulsar wind nebula at these energies did not change significantly between observations in 2018 and 2025. Finally, for the 5-10 kyr neutron star CXOU J182913.1-125113 in the supernova remnant G18.95-1.1, we combine ACIS-I observations from 2009 and 2024 to better measure the neutron star's spectrum.

abstract: Context. PSR J1913+1102 is a highly asymmetric double neutron star (DNS) system, making it an excellent laboratory for testing scalar-tensor gravity theories and a potential progenitor analogue of GW170817 that will merge in 470 Myr. Aims. To maximise the utility of this system for testing gravity theories and to better understand its origin, we carried out timing measurements with the aim of refining the proper motion and post-Keplerian (PK) parameters. Methods. We performed an updated timing analysis of the system by combining 13 years of data, consisting of historical Arecibo observations and the latest FAST measurements. abstract: Since the launch in 2017 June, Insight-HXMT has been in service smoothly in orbit and its scientific productivity has been particularly high since 2024. Among a total number of 425 papers published so far based on Insight-HXMT data, roughly 150 were published from April 2024 to June 2026, accounting for 35% of the total. These studies cover a variety of scientific subjects, including the basic properties of black holes and neutron stars, the outbursts of accreting black hole and neutron star X-ray binaries, thermal nuclear burst probes, quasi-periodical oscillations, cyclotron resonant scattering features, fast radio bursts and gamma-ray bursts, etc. This paper reviews the overall progress with a focus on some potential breakthroughs.

abstract: Recent gravitational wave (GW) events, such as GW190814 and GW230529, have hinted at the existence of compact objects that fall in the transitional regime between the maximum neutron star mass and the minimum black hole mass. The nature of these compact objects is heavily debated. We investigate a potential formation channel of heavy neutron stars that exceed a mass limit of 2.5M<SUB>⊙</SUB>, where fallback accretion induced simultaneous mass growth and spin-up can enable them to remain either temporarily (long enough to emit detectable GW signals) or permanently stable at supramassive levels. An optimistic scenario was modeled using defined initial parameters. Spin evolution and mass growth were calculated by implementing a power-law decay equation and rotational stability criterion based on a spin-dependent maximum mass model. The parameter space included variations in the fallback angular momentum and neutron star mass. Considering both direct fallback and accretion disk formation, we found that fallback can push neutron stars beyond their non-rotating Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff limit and sustain excess mass, but the spin-up is insufficient to delay collapse for the star to persist at such high masses. Findings suggest that a neutron star origin for events such as GW230529 is unlikely under our assumptions.

abstract: We have analyzed a number of features in radio pulsars with surface magnetic fields in the range <inline-formula><tex-math>$10^{9}{-}10^{10}$</tex-math></inline-formula> G. In the distribution of magnetic fields for the pulsars from the ATNF catalog the sample under study corresponds to the minimum between the millisecond and normal pulsars. We provide arguments for the assumption that the central neutron stars in this sample are in binary systems and continue to spin up through the accretion of matter outflowing from the companion. More than <inline-formula><tex-math>$70\%$</tex-math></inline-formula> of the pulsars under study are actually members of binary systems. They must be younger than the millisecond pulsars that have reached their minimum spin period. Indeed, their mean characteristic age is a factor of 2.5 shorter than that of millisecond pulsars, while their kinematic age, which is much closer to the real one, is several million years. In this time, such pulsars could not go far from the Galactic disk, where they were born and evolved. Indeed, they are concentrated near the disk, while their height <inline-formula><tex-math>$z$</tex-math></inline-formula> above the Galactic plane does not exceed several tens of parsecs for most of the pulsars in the sample under study.

abstract: During the past two years, the Gravitational-wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) has developed into a multi-instrument constellation, including GECAM-A/B, GECAM-C, and GECAM-D, for monitoring high-energy transients over a broad energy range from about 10 keV to 5 MeV. GECAM observations have produced important results on gamma-ray bursts, compact binary mergers, magnetar X-ray bursts, high-energy counterparts of fast X-ray transients, and terrestrial high-energy events. This review summarizes highlight of GECAM results published from 2024 to 2026, emphasizing observations of GRB 221009A, GRB 230307A, and the prolific Galactic magnetar SGR J1935+2154. These observations demonstrate the important role of GECAM as a high-time-resolution, all-sky gamma-ray monitor in time-domain multi-messenger astronomy and space science.

abstract: The main types of energy losses experienced by ultrarelativistic electron-positron pulsar plasma in the upper atmosphere of a companion star are considered. These energy-loss mechanisms include ionization losses due to interactions with atoms of the medium, excitation losses associated with the energy transferred to plasma particles, losses resulting from the production of δ electrons, Cherenkov radiation losses, bremsstrahlung losses, synchrotron radiation losses, and inverse Compton losses. It is shown that the fastest component of the pulsar plasma can reach the top of the convection zone of the nearby companion star. The kinetic energy range of the plasma particles reaching the upper boundary of the convection zone corresponds to the energy range of the giant dipole resonance (GDR). As a result of the interaction between the pulsar plasma and the upper atmosphere of the companion star, localized regions of the photosphere and of the photosphere-convection zone boundary at different depths undergo nonuniform (spot-like) heating. This interaction may also produce neutron-rich isotopes, which are subsequently transported into the upper layers of the photosphere.

abstract: We discuss the mechanism for FRB generation as the impact of Small Bodies (SBs) such as asteroids and comets onto a neutron star (NS), which was recently proposed by Geng and Huang (2015) as applied to young NSs, taking into account thermal effects such as sublimation and distant cracking of SBs due to thermal stresses. In such a scenario, the remnants of a planetary system of asteroid-comet origin, after entering the periphery of the planetary system of the newborn NS, return to the star along trajectories close to parabolic in their motion along elongated orbits. In this case, there is no difference in the origin of the infalling objects; they can also be interstellar objects (ISO). We also take into account the fact that, according to Pastor-Marazuela et al. (2025), young neutron stars are very hot objects, and the region where their destruction begins can be located much further from the star than assumed in previous studies. Heating of SBs by the star's radiation causes cracks to appear within these bodies, which then disintegrate into smaller fragments. Taking into account thermal processes, namely the thermal destruction of SBs, leading to their destruction at large distances from the NS, allows us to conclude that the duration of flares in FRB increases even for relatively small objects, ranging in radius from 10 to 50 m. We do not analyze binarity, the matter accretion from the binary component, the infall of large bodies, stellar mergers, or other exotic processes that cause FRBs, nor do we analyze the influence of magnetic fields. Our conclusions are applicable to a specific range of infalling body sizes and energies of about 10e35 ─ 10e41 erg, according to Pham and Hopkins et al. (2024), and cannot be applied to super-energetic flares.

abstract: Sub-millisecond time resolution is essential for unveiling relativistic compact objects and explosive phenomena like Fast Radio Burst (FRBs). While high-cadence observations are standard in radio and high-energy astronomy, progress in the visible band has been slower. However, fast photometers like SiFAP2 are now probing the optical sky at sub-ms scales with impactful results. The recent detection of unexpectedly bright optical pulsations from 3 millisecond pulsars (MSPs) has opened a new window into relativistic particle acceleration and its interaction with accretion disks and intrabinary winds. These discoveries revealed diverse emission mechanisms, with optical efficiencies significantly exceeding predictions from rotation-powered models. Key questions remain regarding the universality of MSP optical pulsations and the processes driving fast variability challenges that require high-time-resolution optical/IR observations. In this talk, we discuss the potential of future facilities for a systematic exploration of the fast-varying sky. We present a pipeline to identify and characterize transients on sub-ms timescales. This tool has already uncovered a large population of fast optical events, demonstrating its versatility in searching for counterparts of FRBs and magnetar bursts, as well as tracking satellites and space debris. A major future challenge will be discerning astrophysical transients from anthropogenic objects, a crucial step for next-generation time-domain surveys.

abstract: The study of accretion columns of X-ray pulsars helps us characterize accretion physics in this extreme regime of strong gravity and strong magnetic fields, while also advancing our understanding of neutron stars themselves. Previous observations of the X-ray pulsar Hercules X-1 revealed the presence of a highly broadened Fe K fluorescence emission line, associated with Doppler motions exceeding 0.1c, suggesting its origin in the accretion column. We recently obtained a high-spectral resolution view of the Fe K energy band of Her X-1 thanks to a 200 ks observation with the XRISM observatory. In this talk I will present new results from the analysis of this high-quality spectral dataset. We confirm the presence of a broad, symmetric line at 6.5 keV with a typical width of 1 keV. Performing a pulse-resolved analysis, we find that the feature is strongly variable with Her X-1 pulse phase. This is consistent with the origin in the accretion column, where strong variability is expected due to the rotation of the magnetosphere and the various projection, Doppler and relativistic effects associated with high infall velocities in the vicinity of the neutron star. Additionally, the variability pattern evolves with the 35-day cycle of Hercules X-1, supporting a scenario according to which the neutron star and its accretion columns undergo free precession, in agreement with recent X-ray polarimetric results from the IXPE observatory. Finally, I will discuss future applications of the modeling of this broad line in X-ray pulsars with physical spectral models, to detect and track neutron star free precession and advance our understanding of neutron star interiors.

abstract: Detection of the cyclotron resonance scattering features (CRSFs or cyclotron lines) in the X-ray spectrum of a neutron star is the most reliable method for measuring its magnetic field. Moreover, it is known that in bright X-ray pulsars positions of cyclotron lines are strongly dependent on an instantaneous accretion rate, making them a valuable diagnostic tool sensitive to the geometry of the X-ray emission region. The situation with CRSFs is quite complicated for a well-known 4U 0115+63 - 3.6s X-ray pulsar in binary system with a Be-star. Despite numerous efforts there is still no unambiguous identification of a fundamental cyclotron absorption line, with number of lines and their positions varying in different works. In our research we trace the evolution of the 22 keV CRSF with accretion luminosity during two giant outbursts using the NuSTAR data. We compare CRSF positions between separate observations, obtained in different parts of outbursts. Also, thanks to the strong mHz quasiperiodic oscillations that are present at the outbursts peak, we are able to probe CRSF centroid energy variability on short timescales, using pulse-intensity resolved spectroscopy. Our analysis shows that, despite source being in supercritical accretion regime, cyclotron line centroid shifts to the higher energies as the luminosity increases, which comes to disagreement with predictions of the current theory of accretion onto magnetized neutron stars. We have also verified that such behavior holds for different continuum models, which makes our method more robust than the usual approach using a tentative fundamental line.

abstract: More than 50 years after the discovery of neutron stars, their interior composition and structure remain unknown. Because the extreme densities and matter asymmetry in neutron star interiors are out of reach for Earth laboratories, the equation of state of bulk nuclear matter is unknown, with important implications for astrophysics and nuclear physics. Thankfully, measurements of neutron star masses and radii are direct probes of the interior of these compact objects. In the past two decades, X-ray observatories such as Chandra, XMM-Newton, and more recently NICER, have provided some measurements of neutron star radii and therefore some constraints on the dense matter equation of state. Each telescope has its unique capabilities to apply a specific method to measure masses and radii from observations of neutron stars. For example, Chandra has the spatial resolution to hunt quiescent low-mass X-ray binaries in the crowded cores of globular clusters to perform spectral analyses at very low-background levels, and uncontaminated by nearby sources. NICER, on the other hand, has a single-pixel 6 arcmin field of view with a fairly high background, but it relies on unprecedented timing resolution to perform pulse profile modelling of pulsars with millisecond spin periods. NewAthena will have sufficient spatial and timing resolution combined to a high collecting area and a low background to apply these various methods to measure masses and radii from observations of neutron stars. In this talk, I will present the future performances of NewAthena to constrain the EoS of dense matter with spectroscopy of quiescent low-mass X-ray binaries or with pulse profile modelling of millisecond pulsars. Preliminary simulations indicate that NewAthena will be able to reduce the uncertainties on the radius from about +/- 1 or 2 km currently to uncertainties of about +/- 200-300 m in a shorter exposure time than needed with current observatories.

abstract: Discoveries of accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars (AMXPs) and transitional millisecond pulsars (tMSPs) have provided observational support for the idea that millisecond pulsars are spun up to millisecond periods by the accretion torques in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs). In this study, we have employed the stellar evolution code MESA to investigate both the binary evolution and the accompanying neutron star evolution of LMXBs that form AMXPs by following three distinct evolutionary tracks. These tracks are defined according to the donor type in the resulting AMXP systems. We adopted a recently developed analytical model for the inner disc radius and the associated torque calculations across different rotational phases of LMXBs to explore the long-term rotational evolution of AMXPs. In this model, the inner disc radius depends on the spin period, the magnetic dipole moment, and the mass inflow rate of the disc. While the morphology of mass-transfer history depends on the magnetic braking index, we find that the initial orbital period is the most influential parameter shaping the binary evolution. For reasonable model parameters, we obtain spin periods and period derivatives consistent with the observed properties of AMXPs along these evolutionary tracks. For selected individual sources along each evolutionary track, we have shown that the model can simultaneously reproduce the NS and binary properties of AMXPs. Finally, we discuss the characteristic timescales and lifetimes of the evolutionary tracks, as well as the conditions under which these systems may be observable at different stages of their long-term evolution.

abstract: In this talk, I will show our recent statistical study of broad-lined Type Ic supernovae (SNe Ic-BL), which includes 69 GRB-unassociated and 11 GRB-associated events. Using a magnetar central engine to model the early-time peak emission and ^56Ni decay for the late-time tail, our model successfully reproduces the multi-band light curves of these SNe. We find that the initial spin period of magnetars in SNe Ic-BL may range from ∼1 to 5ms, with magnetic field strengths between ∼10^15 and 10^16G. Importantly, we did not observe any statistically significant differences between GRB-associated and GRB-unassociated SNe Ic-BL. By fitting the inferred explosion energies and ejecta masses of SNe Ic-BL and comparing them with other superluminous SNe Ic (SLSNe Ic) and fast blue optical transients (FBOTs), we identified a universal relationship, suggesting a common origin. We confirmed this universal relationship using binary star evolution models, supporting the idea that SNe Ic-BL, SLSNe, and FBOTs may originate from a tidal scenario. Additionally, we found that SNe Ic-BL share similar ejecta and ^56Ni production properties with normal SNe Ic, implying that their main difference likely lies in whether their progenitors retain high rotation rates, enabling the formation of rapidly spinning magnetars that influence the explosion energetics. Based on these findings, we propose a unified model for these stripped-envelope supernovae.

abstract: Direct N -body codes such as NBODY6++GPU can solve the dynamical evolution of globular clusters with great accuracy, yet historically uses simple models: spin period, spin-down rate, and magnetic field strength are never updated once a neutron star forms. Earlier works in this series identified this gap, proposed a seven-scenario framework (S1─S7) covering the full range of pulsar evolutionary channels, and demonstrated the absence of pulsar tracking in an existing cluster simulation. Here we bring together three subsequent stages that solve this gap. A pulsar evolution subroutine was first tested in isolation across all seven scenarios, with two independently written codes agreeing to better than 0.1$%$ over more than two thousand compared values, and reproducing accretion-driven spin-up for the first time within this framework. The validated framework was then embedded directly into NBODY6++GPU, and test integrations spanning timescales from under a Megayear up to a Gigayear show that the resulting period-period derivative distribution already resembles the pattern seen in real globular cluster pulsar populations. Finally, an early production test followed ten neutron stars self-consistently through the integrated code over roughly 28 Myr, uncovering that most of them pass through at least one episode of backward evolution, a behaviour that only becomes visible when spin parameters are sampled at every simulation step rather than inferred afterwards. Taken together, these results show that pulsar physics can now evolve as an integral part of cluster dynamics rather than a separate bookkeeping exercise, setting the stage for a full production run at N = 250,000.

abstract: A couple of milliseconds after the merger of a binary system of neutron stars can play a fundamental role in amplifying the comparatively low initial magnetic fields into magnetar strengths. The basic mechanism responsible for this amplification is the Kelvin--Helmholtz instability (KHI), and we here report the first systematic study of the impact of rapid rotation on the KHI-amplification process, exploiting general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations at very high resolutions of 35 m. Concentrating on four different spinning configurations, we find that aligned, antialigned, and mixed (aligned/antialigned) spin configurations lead to markedly different growth rates of the electromagnetic (EM) energy, field topologies, and vortex properties when compared to the irrotational case. These differences arise from intrinsic variations in the system dynamics, such as tidal deformation, collision strength, and contact surface area, with the antialigned configuration producing the largest vorticity and growth in EM energy. Importantly, while different spin configurations lead to significantly different initial growth rates of the poloidal/toroidal components, all systems converge to a specific topological partition where the ratio of the poloidal to toroidal magnetic energy is approximately two.

abstract: Although pulsars exhibit a particularly stable rotation, this stability can be affected by glitches. This phenomenon consists of a sudden increase in the rotation frequency of pulsars. Its cause is not well understood, but it is likely related to the behavior of matter inside neutron stars. Therefore, glitches can provide constraints on the equation of state of neutron stars. With the aim of thoroughly characterizing these glitches, since 2019 we have been conducting a high-cadence monitoring campaign of glitching pulsars from the Argentine Institute of Radio astronomy (IAR). Up to date, we have detected and characterized two giant glitches in the Vela pulsar, one in PSR J0742-2822, one in PSR J1740-3015, and two mini glitches in PSR J1048-5832. We fully describe them in this poster presentation.

abstract: Transitional millisecond pulsars (tMSPs) are a unique class of neutron star binaries that alternate between an accretion-powered low-mass X-ray binary (LMXB) state and a rotation-powered radio millisecond pulsar state, providing a direct link between accretion and pulsar recycling. The prototypical system PSR J1023+0038 is currently in an LMXB state and exhibits rapid switching between distinct high, low, and flaring modes across X-ray and optical wavelengths. Understanding the physical origin of these mode transitions is essential for constraining accretion processes operating at low luminosities. We present a comprehensive multiwavelength study of J1023 based on Kepler K2, XMM-Newton (optical monitor and X-ray), ULTRACAM, and MUSCAT observations spanning multiple epochs. We develop a dedicated analysis framework for optical light curves that removes orbital modulation and reveals intrinsic mode-dependent variability. Using statistical analyses of flux distributions, variability properties, and mode durations, we investigate correlations between emission states across different wavelengths. Particular attention is given to high─low mode transitions, their recurrence timescales, and the anti-correlation between X-ray and optical variability. Our results characterize mode-dependent emission properties and provide new constraints on the physical mechanisms driving rapid state switching in tMSPs. We further compare optical orbital modulation before and after the state transition of J1023, showing that optical emission in the radio MSP state is dominated by the irradiated companion star, while the LMXB state requires an additional accretion-disk component that modifies the orbital variability beyond a simple flux offset. These findings offer new insights into disk─magnetosphere interactions and accretion dynamics in transitional systems, contributing to a broader understanding of neutron-star LMXBs at the boundary between accretion- and rotation-powered regimes.

abstract: Neutron stars (NSs) are compact stellar remnants that provide unique opportunities to study matter and fields under extreme conditions. Standard pulsar searches rely on flux variability, but this approach may be blind to an unexplored population: aligned rotators, NSs whose spin and magnetic axes are aligned and therefore do not exhibit conventional pulsations. I will discuss how we exploited the X-ray polarization to probe various neutron star systems with our software, detecting aligned rotators and placing definitive constraints on their magnetic field geometry. I will also discuss the simulations we conducted to determine the detection limits for various test cases and how they compare with the IXPE observations of various classes of NS systems.

abstract: I will summarize four years of observations of LMXBs with neutron stars using the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE). Roughly speaking, they divide into two classes, those neutron stars with strong magnetic fields (i.e. pulsars) where the emission is primarily from the accretion column, and those with weak fields, where the emission is primarily from the accretion disk and the boundary layer between the disk and the star. In the case of pulsars, the primary tool of use is the rotating vector model (RVM). While the RVM can be fit in many cases to the polarization position angle dependence on phase, the prediction of the polarization degree with pulse phase is not as well modeled specifically with either "pencil" or "fan" beam models. The case of Her X-1 is particularly interesting, where the spin axis was detected to change over two different time scales, giving some indication of the coupling of the core and crust. With low magnetization, the weak polarization appears to result when X-rays from the boundary layer reflect from the disk. However, there are complications with both simple pictures!

abstract: With spin periods shorter than 10 ms, millisecond pulsars are the fastest-spinning pulsars known. Often found in binary systems, millisecond pulsars achieve their high spin frequencies through a Gyr-long recycling phase involving the accretion of matter and angular momentum from a low-mass companion star. This phase ends when mass transfer declines, transforming the pulsar into a radio millisecond pulsar powered by the rotation of its magnetic field. The discovery of the accreting millisecond pulsar SAX J1808.4-3658 confirmed the recycling scenario, showing that mass accretion in a low-mass X-ray binary can spin up a neutron star to millisecond periods. SAX J1808.4-3658 was also the first of this class to show optical/UV pulsations during a bright accretion event. Challenging conventional rotation or accretion-powered scenarios, these pulsations offer key insights into the different emission mechanisms of pulsating neutron stars. I will present optical observations performed with the fast optical photometer TNG/SiFAP2 during the 2022 outburst of SAX J1808, aimed at investigating the nature of the pulsations at these energies. Optical pulsations detected during the 2022 outburst are compared with those observed for the first time in 2019, allowing us to study their evolution across different outbursts. We find an anti-correlation between the X-ray flux and the amplitude of the optical pulsations, with the latter increasing as the X-ray flux decreases. I will also discuss optical observations obtained during the quiescent state of the source, probing the pulse emission mechanism over a large range of mass accretion rates.

abstract: We report the first detection of X-ray polarization with the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) from the X-ray pulsar (XRP) 4U 1954+319. The source belongs to an extremely rare class of systems in which a slowly rotating neutron star accretes from the dense wind of a red supergiant companion. Coherent pulsations are detected at P_ spin=5.49±0.05 h, which is one of the longest spin periods known among XRPs. While the phase-averaged analysis shows no significant polarization, with a 99% confidence minimum detectable polarization (MDP_99) of 4.9% in the 2─8 keV band, the phase-resolved analysis shows one interval at pulse maximum in which the polarization degree (PD) exceeds its MDP_99, giving PD=10.2_-3.0^+3.1%. The polarization angle (PA) exhibits a smooth ≍150^∘ rotation over the pulse, and a joint evaluation of all phase bins yields an overall detection significance of 3.3σ. Using the rotating vector model, we identify a geometric solution that reproduces the observed PA variation and measure a phase-independent PD of 6.1±1.1% in the 2─8 keV band, corresponding to a 5.5σ detection.

abstract: Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are among the most enigmatic transients in the time-domain sky, and their interpretation increasingly relies on coordinated multiwavelength and multimessenger observations. A detailed characterization of their local environments and persistent radio counterparts represents one of the most promising avenues to constrain progenitor models and their physical conditions. Recent discoveries of compact persistent radio sources associated with 4 FRBs provide compelling evidence for nebular synchrotron emission powered by a long-lived central engine. These findings favour magnetars as the primary progenitors, while leaving open alternative channels such as hyperaccreting X-ray binaries or compact-object mergers in specific environments. In the next decade, new wide-field radio facilities (e.g. SKA, DSA-2000, ngVLA precursors) are expected to deliver dozens of arcsecond-localized FRBs per year, dramatically improving host-galaxy statistics and enabling systematic searches for persistent continuum counterparts. The scientific return will depend critically on rapid alert dissemination, coordinated follow-up across radio, optical, X-ray and gamma-ray facilities, and efficient data exploitation frameworks within the multimessenger ecosystem. This contribution reviews the current observational status of persistent radio emission associated with FRBs and discusses future prospects in the context of multimessenger synergies, highlighting the role of next-generation radio observatories in bridging transient discovery, host characterization, and cross-facility coordination.

abstract: Transitional millisecond pulsars (tMSP) represent a dynamic category of celestial sources that establish a crucial connection between low-mass X-ray binaries and millisecond radio pulsars. These systems exhibit transitions from rotation-powered to accretion-powered states and vice versa, highlighting the tight evolutionary link expected by the so-called recycling scenario. In their active phase, these sources manifest two distinct emission modes named high and low, occasionally punctuated by sporadic flares. In this talk, I will present high time-resolution optical spectroscopic observations of the prototypical tMSP J1023+0038 in its sub-luminous disc state. The dataset allows us to probe the system on minute timescales, revealing pronounced variability in the colour and in the properties of the main emission lines, including changes in line strength and profile. I will discuss how this short-timescale variability provides new insight into the structure and dynamics of the accretion flow and its interaction with the neutron star during its disc state.

abstract: Low-mass X-ray binaries are interacting systems in which a compact object accretes matter from a low-mass companion star, releasing most of its energy in the X-ray band. When the compact object is a neutron star, these systems provide unique laboratories to investigate accretion physics under extreme conditions of gravity, density, and magnetic field strength. Among them, accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars represent a particularly informative subclass. These systems host rapidly rotating, weakly magnetised neutron stars that channel the accretion flow onto their magnetic poles, producing coherent X-ray pulsations at millisecond periods. Their rich phenomenology includes transient outbursts, thermonuclear X-ray bursts, quasi-periodic oscillations, and strong variability across a wide range of timescales. The combination of fast timing and spectral diagnostics enables us to probe the interaction between the accretion disc and the neutron-star magnetosphere, study surface emission and thermonuclear burning, and trace the spin evolution of neutron stars. In this talk, I will present an observational overview of accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars, highlighting recent results from the outbursts of sources such as MAXI J1957+032 and IGR J17511−3057. These case studies illustrate how coordinated spectral and timing analyses provide new insights into accretion geometry, variability mechanisms, and the physical conditions near the neutron-star surface.

abstract: We present high-cadence 10 minute rotation-measure (RM) monitoring of PSR J0814+7429 using the LOw-Frequency ARray, aiming to probe ionospheric variability along the pulsar line of sight (LoS). By separating the ionospheric contribution from the observed RM, we quantitatively reconstruct the diurnal variation of the ionospheric electron density along the pulsar LoS based on the World Magnetic Model. The derived variations exhibit clear solar-driven modulation, including the ionospheric noontime bite-out phenomenon, and show good agreement with the LoS total electron content reconstructed from independent global vertical total electron content maps. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using pulsars as probes of temporal variations in the electron density of the Earth's ionosphere.

abstract: X-ray polarimetry has recently opened a new window on accreting neutron stars, providing direct access to their emission geometry and radiation processes in extreme magnetic fields. The first polarimetric measurements of X-ray pulsars obtained with IXPE have already revealed unexpectedly low polarization degrees and complex phase-dependent polarization behavior, highlighting both the diagnostic power of polarimetry and the limitations imposed by current sensitivity and energy coverage. In this talk, I will discuss how the enhanced capabilities of the eXTP mission will transform polarimetric studies of accreting neutron stars with strong magnetic field. The large effective area will enable detailed energy- and phase-resolved studies of X-ray pulsars over a wide range of luminosity regimes. This will allow stringent tests of emission models, magnetospheric geometry, and radiative transfer in ultra-strong magnetic fields. eXTP will thus provide a decisive step toward a comprehensive physical understanding of polarized X-ray emission from accreting highly magnetised neutron stars.

abstract: The discovery of optical pulsations from millisecond pulsars has marked a turning point in high-time-resolution astronomy. While millisecond pulsars have traditionally been investigated at radio and high-energy wavelengths, the optical band has only recently become accessible thanks to the development of ultra-fast photometers capable of resolving variability on sub-millisecond timescales. I will present a review of optical pulsations from millisecond pulsars, highlighting detections in systems spanning different physical regimes: an accretion-powered millisecond pulsar during outburst, a rotation-powered one, and a transitional system swinging between these traditional states. The presence of coherent optical pulsations in such diverse systems challenges long-standing emission paradigms. By comparing optical, X-ray, and UV pulsations, I will discuss what these observations reveal about the coupling between the pulsar magnetosphere and inflowing matter. I will outline ongoing and future efforts to systematically search for optical millisecond pulsations, emphasizing the role of advanced timing techniques in exploiting the high photon statistics of ultra-fast optical photometry to uncover weak, previously inaccessible signals.

abstract: The frozen surface dipole magnetic field of a millisecond pulsar formed at the end of LMXB evolution results from ohmic diffusion through the neutron star crust in initial stages of accretion. The magnitude of this surface magnetic field is correlated with the accretion rate. The expected correlation together with the dependence of the equilibrium rotation period on the surface dipole magnetic field and the accretion rate leads to a simple explanation for the minimum rotation period of millisecond pulsars.

abstract: Low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) are the best sources to study the interaction of the neutron stars (NSs) with the geometrically thin optically thick accretion disks. Significant developments in the theory of accretion disks helped us understand the physical mechanisms that can account for most of their observed characteristics. While it is commonly accepted that millisecond pulsars are spun up to millisecond periods by the accretion torques in these systems, as supported by the discoveries of accreting millisecond pulsars (AMXPs) and the transitional millisecond pulsars, there are still long-lasting problems of LMXBs which cannot be explained by the conventional models: (1) ongoing accretion at low X-ray luminosities, L_x, and transitions to the propeller phase at L_x levels much below those required for the spin-up/spin-down transitions, (2) torque reversals without significant changes in L_x and torque magnitudes on the two sides of the torque reversals, and (3) the lack of X-ray pulsations from most of LMXBs. We have developed an analytical model to calculate the inner disk radius, r_in, the torques acting on the neutron star (NS) in different rotational phases, and the critical conditions for the transitions between these phases in LMXBs. We have shown that the model can account for the three problems listed above. The difference between the predictions of our model and the conventional models is basically due to the difference in the r_in calculation. Conventionally, r_in is estimated to be close to Alfven radius, r_A. In our model, r_in depends on spin period as well as mass inflow rate of the disk and the magnetic dipole moment of the NS, and is found to be much smaller than r_A in both the strong propeller and the spin-up phases. We summarize the results of our model calculations and applications.

abstract: In 2019, Fujimoto, Fukushima, and Weise proposed a new color-superconductive state, the 2-flavor color superconducting (2SC)+<inline-formula><tex-math>$\mathinner {\langle {dd}\rangle }$</tex-math></inline-formula> phase, which can be smoothly connected to the low-density baryon superfluidity in contrast to the 2SC phase. In this scenario, the neutron <inline-formula><tex-math>${}^3P_2$</tex-math></inline-formula> superfluidity on the low-density side of the phase transition is inherited by unpaired d-quarks in the 2SC phase on the high-density side. Since this could be realized in hybrid stars (neutron stars containing hadronic and quark matter), the 2SC+<inline-formula><tex-math>$\mathinner {\langle {dd}\rangle }$</tex-math></inline-formula> phase may change the properties of neutron stars compared to the traditional 2SC phase. In this work, we study the thermal evolution of hybrid stars with the 2SC+<inline-formula><tex-math>$\mathinner {\langle {dd}\rangle }$</tex-math></inline-formula> phase for the first time. We find that neutron stars with the 2SC+<inline-formula><tex-math>$\mathinner {\langle {dd}\rangle }$</tex-math></inline-formula> phase become hotter than those with the 2SC phase, and are close to the color flavor-locked phase. The <inline-formula><tex-math>${}^{3}P_2$</tex-math></inline-formula> superfluidity plays an important role in cooling curves with not the 2SC but 2SC+<inline-formula><tex-math>$\mathinner {\langle {dd}\rangle }$</tex-math></inline-formula> phases due to the suppression of quark <inline-formula><tex-math>$\beta$</tex-math></inline-formula>-decay. We therefore point out that, if the scenario of the 2SC+<inline-formula><tex-math>$\mathinner {\langle {dd}\rangle }$</tex-math></inline-formula> phase is true, it could be specified through low-temperature observations such as those of Vela, 3C58, Vela Jr., and Vela-like pulsar.

abstract: Most X-ray pulsars in high-mass X-ray binary (HMXB) systems exhibit both global and local trends of spin acceleration (spin-up) and deceleration (spin-down). Moreover, decades-long monitored objects display even more general spin-up trends in their spin evolution and simultaneously demonstrate a decrease in the orbital period, so-called orbital decay. Although obvious, those general behavior leaves the open question on the energy source and the mechanism of angular momentum transfer that ensures the neutron star's spin acceleration. We hypothesize that the observed spin acceleration of X-ray pulsars in HMXB (RLO and sgXRB) systems results from orbital angular momentum transfer via tidal interactions with their massive companions. To study these phenomena, we sample five well-studied objects with the longest observational history of their spin periods from the population of known Galactic persistent X-ray pulsars in HMXB systems. We obtain the spin frequency change from the observational data and estimate energy loses for orbital decay and pulsars's spin acceleration. We propose a new term of super-global spin-up trends, and show that their observable values do not exceed theoretical upper limits predicted within the scenario of orbital decay due to the tidal interaction between the neutron star and its massive companion [Kim V. and Aimuratov Y., 2025, ApJ, Vol. 991, id.42].

abstract: Transitional millisecond pulsars (tMSPs) bridge the gap between accreting neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries and millisecond radio pulsars, offering a unique laboratory to study the interplay between accretion and pulsar activity. These systems exhibit a subluminous X-ray state characterized by alternating high, low and flaring emission modes. Multi-wavelength campaigns on the prototype tMSP, PSR J1023+0038, have helped establish a solid understanding of how tMSPs are powered. A complex interplay between a compact jet, discrete ejecta, accreting matter and the pulsar wind seem to be regulating the behaviour of this puzzling source. Recently, using polarimetric data from the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE), the Very Large Telescope (VLT), and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA), we conducted the first multiwavelength polarimetric study of PSR J1023+0038. A linear polarization of (12±3)% in the 2─6 keV band was observed during the high mode. The polarization angle aligns with the optical polarization observed by the VLT, suggesting a shared physical mechanism. During the low mode, the significance was insufficient for detailed analysis, resulting in an upper limit of 26% (90% confidence) on the polarization degree. The results strongly indicate that both optical and X-ray polarization originate from synchrotron radiation at the boundary between the pulsar wind and the inner accretion disc. Finally, simultaneous radio, optical, and X-ray observations obtained as part of this campaign have shed light on the poorly understood flaring mode emission, emphasizing the critical role of outflows in tMSPs.

abstract: Millisecond pulsars are spun up during their accretion phase in a binary system. The exchange of angular momentum between the accretion disk and the star tends to align the spin and orbital angular momenta on a very short time scale compared to the accretion stage. This alignment can also be seen as the equality between two angles : the orbital inclination angle i, corresponding to the angle between the line-of-sight of an observer and the orbital angular momentum ; and the viewing angle ζ, corresponding to the angle between the line-of-sight and the rotation axis. In this work, we studied a subset of gamma-ray millisecond pulsars in binaries for which the orbital inclination angle i has been accurately constrained thanks to the Shapiro delay measurements. Our goal is to constrain the observer viewing angle ζ and to check whether it agrees with the orbital inclination angle i, in other words if ζ is approximately equal to i. We use a Bayesian inference technique to fit the millisecond pulsars gamma-ray light curves based on the third gamma-ray pulsar catalogue (3PC). The emission model relies on the striped wind model deduced from force-free neutron star magnetosphere simulations. We found good agreement between the two angles i and ζ for a significant fraction of our sample, about four fifth, confirming the spin-orbit alignment scenario during the accretion stage. However about one fifth of our sample deviates significantly from this alignment. The reasons are manifold: either the gamma-ray fit is not reliable or some precession and external torque avoid an almost perfect alignment.

abstract: Context. Fast radio bursts often exhibit strong linear polarization together with pronounced spectral structure. Yet in coherent curvature radiation, spectral decoherence and depolarization are not necessarily simultaneous. Aims. We investigate spectral and polarization coherence in curvature radiation from extended ultrarelativistic sources. Methods. Using the coherency matrix formalism together with an asymptotic phase expansion for a uniformly emitting extended source, we derived the spectral and polarization coherence properties of curvature radiation. Results. We show that spectral decoherence and depolarization are governed by distinct physical conditions and therefore develop on separate scales. Retardation phase variations suppress spectral coherence, whereas polarization remains largely preserved across the relativistic beaming cone, naturally producing a broad polarized but spectrally decoherent regime whose relative extent increases toward higher frequencies and larger Lorentz factors. Conclusions. Spectral decoherence without strong depolarization naturally arises in ultrarelativistic curvature radiation and may explain highly polarized fast radio bursts with strong spectral modulation or narrowband structure.

abstract: Most neutron star (NS) low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not show coherent X-ray pulsations. We have investigated whether X-ray pulsations are quenched due to the inner disc extending down to the NS surface, preventing magnetically channelled mass accretion on to the poles. We estimate the inner-disc radius, r_ in, using the analytical model developed to account for torque reversals in LMXBs, where r_ in depends not only on the magnetic dipole moment, μ, and the mass inflow rate of the disc, Ṁ_ in, but also on the spin period, P. The r_ in values estimated in this model are much smaller than those in the conventional models in both the spin-up and the strong propeller phases. Our results indicate that the inner disc in most NS LMXBs could reach the NS surface with their estimated μ and Ṁ_ in ranges and thereby quench the pulsed X-ray emission. The model is also consistent with the presence of X-ray pulsations from the accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars (AMXPs).

abstract: SAX J1808.4-3658 is the prototype of accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars and the first of this class to show optical and UV pulsations during an accretion outburst. These pulsations challenge standard rotation- or accretion-powered scenarios and provide a unique window into the emission mechanisms of pulsating neutron stars. Before returning to quiescence at the end of its outbursts, this source shows several reflares of particular interest to provide insights into the physics of the accretion disk at low accretion rates. I will present the first simultaneous X-ray and UV timing and spectral study of XMM-Newton and Hubble Space Telescope observations of the source during the final stage of its 2022 outburst. Using XMM-Newton data collected during the reflaring stage of the outburst, we find shifts in the pulse phase and amplitude, with a distinct phase jump of approximately 0.4 cycles. These are among the most intriguing ever observed from this source and tightly correlate with the X-ray flux. We interpret such a correlation in terms of hot-spot drift on the neutron star surface, driven by an increase in the inner-disk radius when the mass accretion rate decreased. Simultaneous HST observations confirmed the presence of significant UV pulsations, with a luminosity exceeding the predictions of standard emission models, as further confirmed by the shape of the pulsed spectral energy distribution.

abstract: Many compact object binary systems that power gravitational waves have likely passed through a "common envelope" phase, where a neutron star is engulfed in the envelope of a red giant. However, the physics of this critical evolutionary phase is not well understood. Whether the binary can survive and become a gravitational wave progenitor depends on the drag forces and torques that exchange energy and angular momentum between the neutron star and the envelope. Because common envelope evolution spans extreme spatial and temporal scales, we adopt a local "wind-tunnel" approximation, where the stellar envelope is modeled as a stratified, magnetized flow past the neutron star. Although existing works have studied common envelope evolution using this approach, they have done so mainly with hydrodynamics, using a sink to model the neutron star. However, realistic neutron stars have strong magnetic fields and rapid rotation, making it necessary to include magnetic fields and general relativity. We perform the first high-resolution, long-duration 3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations of magnetized neutron star accretion in a wind tunnel using the GPU-accelerated code H-AMR. We explore how the neutron star dipole strength, field orientation, and wind magnetization modify the drag force, accretion rate, and the power of neutron star-driven outflows. Our results elucidate the microphysics of magnetized wind accretion and will provide improved sub-grid prescriptions for CE population synthesis. Future work will include more realistic stellar envelope stratification and additional microphysics to better connect with observations of compact object binaries relevant to upgraded LIGO─Virgo─KAGRA and the upcoming LISA mission.

abstract: Current neutron star equation-of-state inferences assume that a common equation of state describes all neutron stars. However, {poorly understood dense-matter physics may give rise to distinct long-lived stellar subpopulations following different mass--tidal-deformability relations, invalidating this assumption. In this Letter, we demonstrate that next-generation gravitational-wave observatories enable neutron star equation-of-state universality to be transformed from an assumption into a testable hypothesis. By combining hierarchical Bayesian inference with a piecewise-polytropic parametrization of the neutron star equation of state, we establish a framework for testing equation-of-state universality with next-generation gravitational-wave observatories. We find that about 30 (50) loud binary neutron star mergers with network SNRs above 100 are sufficient to provide compelling evidence for departures from equation-of-state universality, even if only 20% (10%) of the population exhibits one of the representative non-universality parametrizations considered here.

abstract: Accreting neutron stars in X-ray binaries have broadly similar behaviors to black holes, including the launching of jets. Many aspects of jets are yet to be well understood, such as their formation and launching mechanisms presumably by magnetic fields in the vicinity of the accretor. But just how similar are black hole and neutron star jets, and what does this indicate about jet formation? In this talk I will review the radio behaviors of neutron star jets and how they compare to the jets of black holes in X-ray binaries. Starting with long timescale evolution and correlation with spectral state and mass accretion rate, then moving to rapid variability down to minutes timescales, observations indicate that neutron star jets are remarkably similar to those of black holes, though typically at much fainter radio luminosities. Finally, I will show examples of neutron star radio jet variability in observations and of how studying radio jets may help to further understand accretion processes and overall X-ray binary behaviors, including potentially neutron-star-only phenomena.

abstract: Oscillation frequencies excited in neutron stars are crucial for extracting their interior properties. In addition to the fundamental and pressure modes, the gravity (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-)modes can be excited even in zero-temperature stellar models due to the composition gradient. In this study, we systematically study the <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-mode frequencies, focusing on the nucleonic equation of state. Then, we derive an empirical relation for the first <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-mode frequencies as a function of the stellar compactness and the combination of the nuclear saturation parameters, <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>η</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo>≡</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>, where <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> denote the incompressibility of symmetric nuclear matter and the density dependence of the nuclear symmetry energy, respectively. If an observed first <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>g</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-mode frequency significantly deviates from our empirical relation, it may indicate the emergence of additional degrees of freedom or new compositions inside the star.

abstract: Following the evolution of understanding of Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) in the last 50 years, we evidence the existence of three kinds of GRB sources: 1) GRBs originating from binary neutron star (BNS) mergers resulting in short GRBs (see, e.g., Rueda, Ruffini, Wang, JHEAP Vol. 50, 100464, 2026). There, in the source GRB 090510 at z=0.9, a gravitational wave during the coalescence phase of the 1.2+1.2 M☉ BNS is observed, evaluated following the Taylor-Kramer approach, and consistent with energy and angular-momentum conservation. After the merger, a 2.4 M☉ magnetized Kerr black hole (BH) surrounded by a disk is observed. The extraction of BH rotational energy accounts for the observed GeV afterglow emission, and the accretion of the disk onto the BH accounts for the recorded X-ray afterglow emission. 2) GRBs originating from a massive CO-core of 10 M☉ with a binary NS companion, originating, through its collapse a hypernova of type Ic with the nickel decay emission from its core and the formation of a BH by the SN accretion on the NS companion (see e.g. Y. Aimuratov et al 2023 ApJ 955 93 with references and examples), namely, Binary Driven Hypernovae (BDHNe). 3) We are exploring the possibility of a third family of more energetic GRBs originating from a highly magnetized CO-core in fast rotation driven by a binary NS companion: its gravitaional collapse leads to a Pair SN (BDPairSN), creating, by accretion on the NS companion, a newly formed BH, originating a GeV afterglow, as well as a very young millisecond newNS with a powerful optical afterglow, overshining the nickel decay process and originating a pulsar emission. Also in this case, the X-ray afterglow is observed (Ruffini et al., GRB 240825A, submitted). The remarkable observations and their theoretical understanding confirm first the occurrence of gravitational-wave emission at extragalactic distances, as well as the electrodynamical process of extracting the rotational energy of a BH of mass above the observed upper limit to the NS critical mass. We are proceeding to probe the extension of our results to more energetic systems.

abstract: Modeling the thermal evolution of accreting neutron stars is a powerful tool to study the neutron star interior. Of particular interest are transient sources whose cooling after an accretion outburst can be observed in details revealing the details of the stellar crust temperature. We here describe the evolution of several such systems with a particular emphasis on the effects of nuclear energy release in the outer crust from the burning of the accreted matter to the presence of catastrophic events as superbursts and hyperbursts.

abstract: The Einstein Telescope (ET) is set to revolutionize stellar-mass compact object astronomy by detecting mergers at unprecedented cosmological distances. This will offer transformative opportunities for multi-messenger astrophysics. We investigate the multi-messenger emission properties of binary neutron star (NSNS) and black hole-neutron star (BHNS) mergers detectable by ET to provide projections in terms of detection rates jointly with the electromagnetic emissions, either gamma-ray burst (GRB) and/or kilonova (KN). Using a synthetic population of compact binary mergers, we model the GW signal-to-noise ratio and sky localization uncertainty for each source. We simulate multi-wavelength electromagnetic (EM) signatures, including KN light curves in optical and near-infrared bands, as well as GRB prompt emission and afterglows across the radio, optical, X-ray, and very high energy (VHE) bands. Our analysis compares ET as a standalone observatory (under two possible configurations) against its performance within a global network of next-generation detectors. Our findings show that while ET will detect over 10^4 NSNS mergers annually, thus enabling the observation of hundreds of EM counterparts, BHNS mergers present more challenges, despite a projected tenfold increase in joint GW-EM detection rates over current instruments. We also quantify how uncertainties in the neutron star equation of state (EoS) and mass distributions impact these rates. Finally, we highlight that while standalone ET detection rates are high, sky localization remains a critical bottleneck. These results underscore the necessity of integrated global networks of ground based facilities and optimized space-based EM satellites to fully realize the multi-messenger potential of the ET.

abstract: A comprehensive investigation of nonradial oscillations in neutron star (NS) admixed with gravitationally bounded dark matter (DM) is carried out within the framework of full general relativity. The relativistic mean field (RMF) formalism is employed to illustrate the hadronic equation of state (EOS), while a physically motivated, gravitationally captured, non-uniform fermionic Higgs-portal DM component is incorporated to model DM-admixed NS. The DM distribution is characterized by two free parameters: αM<SUB>χ</SUB>, an effective control parameter that combines the DM concentration and the DM candidate mass, and β, a steepness parameter controlling the DM density distribution. The quasi normal mode (QNM) characteristics such as fundamental (f) mode frequency and its corresponding gravitational-wave (GW) damping time (τ) is calculated for DM-admixed NS by solving the general relativistic perturbed equations involving axial as well as polar modes. The study demonstrates how the inclusion of DM distribution modifies the f-mode frequency and enhances the damping rate, reflecting a stronger coupling between matter and spacetime perturbations. Considering DM effects, the correlation analysis among DM model parameters, NS observables and QNM characteristics also carried out. Analytic fits for the <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math> and <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mstyle><mml:mi>Λ</mml:mi></mml:mstyle><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math> relations are constructed and calibrated for DM-admixed NS models. Building upon asteroseismic universal relations (URs), multimessenger constraint from the GW170817 event is employed by mapping the tidal deformability Λ<SUB>1.4</SUB> into the (f<SUB>1.4</SUB>, τ<SUB>1.4</SUB>) space, thereby providing observational bounds on the oscillation properties of canonical DM-admixed NS model.

abstract: Neutron stars are born in the aftermath of supernova stellar explosions. They enclose the mass of one or two suns within only ten kilometres, so that their gravity is so high that general relativistic effects become important in their proximity, affecting the space time and light propagation near their surface. Due to their compactness, their interior reaches densities unattainable on earth. Their matters can be superfluid, superconductor and in their core even free quarks may appear. When they are in orbit with a companion star, they can capture the outer layers of the latter. This new matter can burn unstably on the surface of the neutron stars and explode in bright X-ray flashes called the type I bursts. In this talk I will show how modelling the burning during the type I bursts gives us a window on the physics of the neutron stars, such as their interior composition or their magnetic fields, of nuclear reactions and of the binary systems in which the bursts occur, such as accretion processes.

abstract: Type I X-ray bursts are powered by unstable thermonuclear burning on the surface of accreting neutron stars in close binary systems. These brief X-ray flashes, with light curves featuring rise times of 1--10 s, durations of 10--100 s, and recurrence periods of hours to days, represent the most frequent stellar explosions in our Galaxy. With typical energies of ~10<SUP>39</SUP>--10<SUP>40</SUP> erg, they rank among the most powerful astrophysical transients after supernovae and classical novae. To date, roughly 120 bursting X-ray binaries have been identified in the Milky Way. Several studies have been conducted to characterize the dynamics of these events, with emphasis on reproducing the observed recurrence periods and light-curve shapes. In this paper we show, for the first time, that rotation is a key factor shaping the properties of Type I X-ray bursts in rapidly spinning systems. The inclusion of centrifugal forces, together with a suite of rotationally induced mixing mechanisms, such as meridional circulation and shear-induced turbulent diffusion, reduce surface gravity, shortening the recurrence times and lowering burst energies. Rotation also modifies the extent of the nuclear activity during these events and affects the morphology of their light curves, which are distinctly broader for rapidly rotating neutron stars.

abstract: Massive stars commonly form binaries that can evolve into compact systems via common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical but poorly understood phase -- especially when the companion is a neutron star. Understanding the force exerted on a neutron star by the surrounding envelope during CEE is a key to the quantitative evaluation of orbital decay, merger time-scale, and compactness of the resultant binary. In this paper, we conduct general-relativistic hydrodynamical simulations under a novel strategy of multilayer domain-decomposition to treat the vast disparity of <inline-formula><tex-math>$10^4$</tex-math></inline-formula>--<inline-formula><tex-math>$10^7$</tex-math></inline-formula> between the neutron star radius and the accretion radius. Our 10-model survey spans diverse physical conditions that the neutron star may encounter in the envelope of a massive star. We find that nested bow shocks with alternating orientations commonly form. This configuration is qualitatively different from those in the conventional picture and results in an enhancement of the force by one to two orders of magnitude relative to the Bondi--Hoyle--Lyttleton momentum-accretion estimate. Moreover, some of our models that correspond to the inner region of the massive-star envelope produce positive net projected forces, i.e. thrust rather than drag expected in the standard picture. Although the sign reversal in the net projected force should be regarded as still tentative, these results will serve as a basis for improvements of the force prescription in CEE modelling and have implications for binary evolution theory.

abstract: Collimated, relativistic jets can be launched from accreting neutron stars. However, these jets are poorly understood compared to those launched from accreting black holes. This is probably due to a number of factors, including the faintness of neutron star jets and their apparently more complex behaviour. Here, we present optical-infrared photometric, spectral, timing and polarimetric observations of the neutron star LMXBs SAX J1808.4-3658, MAXI J1807+132 and IGR J00291+5934. There is a prominent infrared-excess (above the accretion disc emission) in the optical-IR spectral energy distributions in all three sources, which also show radio jet emission. We show that the origin of this excess is most likely the relativistic jet, and we find that the spectrum, as well as the fast timing and polarimetric properties are similar to the jets of black hole LMXBs, with some interesting differences. The fast variations from the jets are generally of lower amplitude (lower fractional rms) than black hole jets, and there is flickering and unusual swings in polarization, which could be caused by changes in the magnetic field geometry near the jet base, or changing of the origin of polarimetric components.
