abstract: The First LHAASO Catalog (Cao et al. 2024) has revealed a rich population of gamma‑ray emitters, including numerous sources detected with the Kilometer Squared Array (KM2A) above 10 TeV. A key open question is which classes of astrophysical objects can power such extreme emission. Notably, Cao et al. reported that all KM2A sources with identified counterparts are associated with isolated pulsars, consistent with inverse‑Compton emission from ultra‑relativistic electrons. This raises the issue of whether the many KM2A sources still classified as "unidentified" may also be pulsar‑powered. In this work, we develop a refined strategy to assess pulsar associations and identify the pulsar properties required to sustain detectable >10 TeV emission. We examine both KM2A sources lacking known pulsars and, conversely, pulsars that should produce a KM2A‑detectable nebula but do not. We show how the associations constrain key physical parameters, including pulsar‑wind magnetisation and synchrotron‑loss effects, and how the angular separations between pulsars and KM2A sources can be used to limit particle‑diffusion coefficients in the surrounding medium. To support our analysis, we also generate synthetic pulsar populations.

abstract: Transient neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries provide key insights into the physics of accretion discs, outflows, and dense matter in neutron stars. In this talk, I will review our current understanding of outburst triggering and evolution, the diversity of outburst cycles, the role of jets and disc winds, and what can be learned from the quiescent emission. I will highlight recent observational advances, and discuss how ongoing and future X-ray missions will enable to address important open questions by studying transient neutron star LMXBs across their full accretion cycle.

abstract: In the first three years of the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) mission, we learned that weakly magnetized neutron stars can be polarized significantly higher than any theoretical predictions. Both analytical and numerical simulations for polarimetric properties of the emission of various accretion flow components fail to reproduce the high values of polarization degree we observed in many sources. In our search for an explanation, we came to the necessity to break the symmetry of the system as much as possible (and physically justifiable). As several previous observations hinted towards a misalignment between the rotational axes of the NS and the binary system, we worked on the model of polarized emission coming from the tilted neutron star. With this new model, we were able to obtain higher polarization, interpret some observational results and make predictions for the upcoming observations.

abstract: Observations of linear structure connecting pulsars to gamma-ray halos reveal injection of TeV electrons into the interstellar medium (ISM). In some cases, this could be attributed to nearly scattering-free electron transport along large scale magnetic fields connected to pulsar winds with very slow diffusion across the field lines. In this work we model this process with a magnetic flux tube emerging from the pulsar and attached to the ISM magnetic field. We show that particles in this case have an anisotropic distribution of magnetic pitch angle, such that the overall emission is highly beamed. We apply this model to pulsar tails and filaments, including the extended X-ray and TeV emission associated with PSR J1740+1000 and the misaligned X-ray jet in the Guitar Nebula, to constrain their particle population and magnetic fields.

abstract: We present the spatial part of the point-source detection strategy for the upcoming Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio-transient Detector (CHORD) galaxy survey. CHORD, the Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio-transient Detector, is an under-construction drift-scanning compact interferometric radio telescope. CHORD comprises 512 total 6 meter dishes and observes in the 300--1500 MHz frequency range. One of its science goals is detecting galaxies by their neutral hydrogen (HI) 21 cm spin-flip emission line. CHORD's galaxy search will use a matched filter on visibility data. We present the search strategy, along with an analytic prediction tool that can efficiently estimate the output of the matched filter, without producing simulated visibility data. We use this to make quantitative predictions of the effects of spatial aliasing on the galaxy search and how these effects can be reduced by dithering the telescope.

abstract: Pulsar Timing Array experiments are rapidly approaching the era of gravitational wave background anisotropy detection. The timing residuals of each pulsar are an integrated measure of the gravitational-wave power across all angular scales. However, due to the limited number of monitored pulsars, current analyses are only able to reconstruct the angular structure of the background at large scales. We show analytically that this mismatch between the integrated all-sky signal and the truncated reconstruction introduces a previously unaccounted source of systematic bias in the anisotropic background angular power spectrum. The source of this systematic error, that we call ``small-scale leakage'', is the intrinsic presence of unaccounted gravitational wave power at scales smaller than the reconstructed scales. This unmodeled power leaks into large-scale modes, artificially increasing the recovered value of the inferred angular power spectrum by at least one order of magnitude in a wide range of scales. Importantly, this effect is fundamentally independent of the geometry of the pulsar configuration, the anisotropy reconstruction method, the use of different regularization schemes, and the presence of pulsar noise. As the quality of pulsar timing array experiments improves, a robust understanding of small-scale leakage will become paramount for reliable detection and characterization of the gravitational wave background. Thus, the theoretical formalism developed here will be essential to estimate the magnitude of this systematic uncertainty in anisotropy searches.

abstract: We present evidence that the X-ray source 47 Tuc W41, long considered to be an X-ray source powered by coronal activity, is actually a redback pulsar binary. The source continually shows L<SUB>X</SUB> 3 × 10<SUP>31</SUP> erg s<SUP>-1</SUP> (0.5-10 keV), which is well in excess of the coronal saturation limit for active binaries in quiescence, but is consistent with the intrabinary shock observed in redback pulsars, as is its photon index of Γ = 1.4±0.1. In addition, using deep data from the Australia Telescope Compact Array, we show that W41 is a faint (9.8±1.4 μJy at 5.5 GHz) steep spectrum (α = -1.8±0.4) radio continuum source, as expected for a pulsar. Light curve modelling of Hubble Space Telescope photometry shows evidence for ellipsoidal modulation with mild irradiation of a ∼0.5M<SUB>☉</SUB> secondary around an invisible companion, also consistent with the redback interpretation. The precise position of W41, along with its well-measured 10.4-h orbital period, should enable it to be matched to a newly-discovered radio pulsar in future data. Our result shows that close pulsar binaries are still hiding, misclassified among active binaries, even in well-studied clusters like 47 Tuc.

abstract: Accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars (AMXPs) are transient low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) in which neutron stars (NSs) are spun up via mass transfer from their low-mass companions. AMXPs are thought to be evolving in the final evolutionary phases of LMXBs. These sources provide a rich laboratory to study the disk-field interaction and the resultant spin evolution of NSs. In this work, we have used an analytical model developed to explain some typical torque-luminosity behaviors and torque reversals of LMXBs to investigate the torques acting on AMXPs during their outburst and quiescent phases. We have compared the model predictions with the observations of five AMXPs with known rotational properties and X-ray luminosities. Our results obtained from the model calculations are consistent with the observed outburst and quiescent properties, yielding an average spin-down, which is also in aggrement with the observed long-term spin-down trend of these sources. To put in other words, the disk, accretion, and magnetic dipole torques are sufficient to account for the observed long-term spin-down of these AMXPs without invoking additional spin-down torques. Nevertheless, our results are not sufficient to rule out the spin-down contribution of the gravitational radiation torques due to significant timing noise and uncertainties about the bolometric corrections for X-ray luminosity during the outbursts of some sources.

abstract: The internal composition of neutron stars, one of the densest astronomical objects in the universe, is still unknown. Although in the last decade, with the onset of multi-messenger gravitational wave astronomy, several astrophysical observations placed strong constraints on these compact objects, there is still a lack of understanding of the dense matter equation of state. In this work, we model neutron stars as hybrid stars -composed of an inner core of quark matter and a mantle of hadronic matter-, considering an abrupt and slow first-order hadron-quark phase transition in their core. We model the hadronic phase with a piecewise polytropic fit, and the inner quark core through a Color Flavor Locked superconducting equation of state, with corrections due to the strong coupling constant, within the framework of the MIT Bag model. In the framework of this abrupt and slow scenario, it is possible to obtain an extended branch of stable stellar configurations. It has been shown that the appearance of such branches could resolve the existing tension between current astrophysical observations. We analyze the behavior of this extended stability branch by quantifying and systematically studying, for the first time, its length, relating this quantity to fundamental properties of the hybrid equation of state. This study allows not only a deeper understanding of the extended stability scenario with slow hadron-quark conversions but could help reveal the mystery of the composition of neutron stars and, consequently, clarify the uncertainty about the equation of state of dense matter.

abstract: PSR J1023+0038 is a transitional millisecond pulsar (tMSP), the only one where coherent pulsations were discovered in both the Optical and X-ray energy bands to date. We present a detailed timing analysis of new Aqueye+ optical data taken from 2021 through 2023, obtaining an updated timing solution for the pulsar. We perform a new measurement of the phase lag between optical and X-ray pulsations and investigate the recent evolution of the binary system, monitoring the variation of the time of passage at the ascending node. We measured a phase lag between the optical and X-ray pulses of 112.3 ± 30.7 μs, confirming a common origin. After 2017, the evolution of the passage at the ascending node follows a well-defined parabolic increasing trend, suggesting a corresponding increment in the orbital period and orbital separation of the system. This evolution is consistent with a scenario in which the binary system is evolving through non-conservative Roche lobe overflow and the donor is interacting with the pulsar wind, losing mass at a rate much higher than the inferred accretion rate. Finally, we offer a glimpse of the results from observations of PSR J1023+0038 obtained with Iqueye recently installed at Gemini South, which achieved unprecedented photon statistics and time resolution.

abstract: An increasing number of pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe) are being identified in the TeV band by ground-based Imaging Air Cherenkov Telescopes such that they constitute the dominant source class of Galactic TeV emitters. However, MeV-GeV PWN counterparts are still largely lacking. To date, only a dozen PWNe are identified by the Fermi─Large Area Telescope (LAT) in the MeV-GeV band. Most PWNe are located along the Galactic plane embedded within the prominent, diffuse Galactic γ-ray emission, which makes these sources difficult to disentangle from the bright diffuse background. We present a systematic search for γ-ray counterparts to known PWNe in the 300 MeV - 2 TeV energy band using the Fermi-LAT. We target the locations of previously identified PWNe that lack detected Fermi─LAT pulsars to minimize associated pulsar contamination. The sample includes six previously identified Fermi PWNe and eight Fermi─LAT sources associated with PWNe. We report the analysis of 58 regions of interest and classify Fermi─LAT detected sources as either a likely PWN or a candidate PWN counterpart based on their morphological and spectral characteristics across the broadband spectrum. There are nine unidentified Fermi─LAT sources that we consider as likely PWN counterparts, which, if confirmed to be PWNe, would greatly increase the PWN population detected by the Fermi─LAT from 12 to 21. The remaining Fermi─LAT detected sources are considered weaker PWN candidates. A second approach in the systematic search for γ-ray emitting PWNe will involve studying the off-pulse phases of Fermi─LAT detected pulsars for the presence of an obscured PWN and will be reported in a subsequent paper.

abstract: Pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe) evolving inside their host supernova remnants (SNRs) have recently emerged as promising PeVatron candidates that may be capable of accelerating particles to PeV energies during specific evolutionary stages. I will present an overview of these stages, from the PWN's early expansion into unshocked supernova ejecta to its late-phase interaction with the SNR reverse shock, and discuss how multi-wavelength signatures of the PWN/SNR interaction reveal key information about the explosion properties and particle acceleration processes.

abstract: This study focuses on utilizing observations of gamma - ray bursts (GRBs) to investigate the cosmic evolution of the merger rate of double neutron stars. Specifically, we employ samples of Type-I GRB observations from high - energy detectors to study the progenitor stars, which include double neutron stars and heavy-star black holes, and explore how their merger rates vary with cosmic redshift. The main research methods involve using simulated data and the responses of real - world detectors to correct the detector selection effects. To address the issue of an incomplete sample of GRBs with measured redshifts, we apply empirical formulas and hierarchical Bayesian analysis. By doing so, combined with gravitational - wave observations, we can place constraints on the mergers of neutron - star - containing compact stars. These constraints further enable us to infer the cosmic birth history of r - process elements. This research provides valuable insights into the cosmic evolution processes related to compact - star mergers and element synthesis.

abstract: With GW170817 we had the first confirmation that binary neutron star (BNS) merger can power a short gamma-ray burst (sGRB). However, it is not clear whether the updated estimates of BNS local rates are high enough to account for the full population of observed short GRBs. We address this question by analyzing 64 BNS population synthesis models against 16 years of Fermi-GBM data. By simulating synthetic sGRB catalogs under the assumption of various jet geometries, we assess the compatibility of each BNS population imposing a simultaneous agreement with sGRB data and with constrains of BNS local rate from GW observations. Our results demonstrate that population models predicting low local merger rates RBNS(0) ≲ 50 Gpc−3 yr−1 fail to reproduce the observed sGRB population unless we admit large jet opening angles (θc ≥ 15◦) that contradict the narrow cores (θc ≲ 10 deg) inferred from afterglow observations. We find that only models with local rates RBNS(0) ≍ 100 Gpc−3 yr−1 successfully reconcile sGRB observations with realistic jet physics. Finally, we show what is the possible contribution of neutron star - black hole mergers for those populations whose local rate is incompatible with sGRB.

abstract: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE), launched on December 9, 2021, has, within its first four years of operation, successfully measured X-ray polarization in the 2─8 keV energy band for at least six Pulsar Wind Nebulae (PWNe): the Crab, Vela, MSH 15─52, B0540─69, 3C 58, and G21.5─0.9. Leveraging its imaging polarimetric capabilities, IXPE has enabled the first spatially resolved maps of X-ray polarization in PWNe, providing new constraints on the global magnetic-field structure and the level of turbulence within these systems. Owing to their strong synchrotron emission, PWNe have emerged as one of the most highly polarized classes of sources observed by IXPE to date, with polarization degrees in some cases approaching the theoretical maximum for synchrotron radiation. This indicates particle acceleration occurring in highly ordered magnetic fields. By isolating the nebular contribution, significant phase-resolved polarization from the embedded pulsars has also been detected in several cases. Although there is a general trend toward aligned polarization in young PWNe exhibiting jet─torus X-ray morphologies, the full population displays a wide range of polarization properties, suggesting underlying physical differences that are not yet fully understood. In this contribution, I will review the main results from IXPE observations of PWNe, highlighting both common patterns and key differences, and discussing their implications for particle acceleration and magnetic-field structure in these systems.

abstract: Formation rate (FR) history of sources provide crucial information on how the universe emerged from the dark ages to its current stage. Best observed FR is that of stars (SFR) that rises from high redshifts to redshift of 3 and declines to today. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) show a similar trend but with different parameters. Transient sources like gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), and to some degree fast radio bursts (FRBs), by virtue of their large redshifts are good candidates for determining this history and its relation to SFR. Methods: Achievement of this task requires determination of the "Luminosity Function" (LF) and the cosmological evolution of luminosity and FRs. This is often done by a forward fitting of the data to some assumed parametric forms for the LF and evolution, with many parameters, and often ignoring luminosity evolution. However, recent works use the non-parametric methods developed by Lynden-Bell and Efron and Petrosian (EP), which determines the luminosity evolution directly from "truncated" data. In this talk I will review past and more recent estimates of LFs and FR evolution, using theses methods, of GRBs and if time permits FRBs. Data: A critical issue here is to have samples with measured "fluxes" and redshifts (z) with well defined truncation determined by observational selection effects, which we call "complete samples". The main source for GRBs has been the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory with some data from Konus-Wind and Fermi-GBM. The main source for FRBs has been the CHIME radio telescope. A main uncertainty is the selection effects that redshift measurements introduce. As I will discuss use of Machine Learning (ML) to estimates redshifts can help in this regard. Theory: An important issue for the transient sources, which are often poorly localized is their progenitors. GRBs are divided into two groups; Long-soft and Short-hard. So-called collapsars are assumed to be the progenitors of GRBs, while SGRBs progenitors are believed to be neutron star(NS)-NS or NS-black hole mergers, which are also sources of gravitational waves (GWs) and Kilonovae. FRBs also come in two variety "repeaters" and "non-repeaters" with magnetars as likely progenitors. Results: GRBs consistently shown (1) presence of strong luminosity evolution,a broken power-law LF and varied formation rate evolution. Collapsars, being short lived stars are expected to follow the SFR. We find that LGRBs seem to follow the SFR at high-z's but deviate significantly from it, as a low low-z component that increase with decreasing-z. SGRBs show a increasing FR up to lowest z's similar to delayed SFR expected from compact object mergers, similar to the low-z component of LGRB. These finding raise doubt about the standard separation by duration of GRBs and affects the expected frequency of GWs and Kilonovae. FRBs also show luminosity evolution and a delayed FR supporting the magnetar origin. This work is carried out with extensive collaboration with Maria Dainotti and several graduate and undergraduate students.
author: Petrosian, Vahe
title: Cosmological Distributions and Evolution of Gamma-ray Bursts and their relation to Star Formation Rate and Gravitational Waves

abstract: With the discovery of gravitational waves and fast radio bursts, wave optics has become increasingly relevant in astrophysics. This paper studies the behaviour of random gravitational and plasma lenses, presenting the refractive and diffractive expansions, with higher-order terms that allow error estimates and embody the counterintuitive resurgence phenomenon. Specifically, we show that the diffractive expansion converges for a broad class of bounded lens models and provides an efficient description of interference patterns across frequency regimes. Next, building on Picard-Lefschetz techniques, we derive the full refractive expansion, organising it into a transseries. Near caustics, the standard transseries is supplemented with uniform asymptotics. We study this transseries, with both Borel and hyperasymptotic resummation yielding systematic approximations to lensing integrals at all frequencies. Our results give a framework for modelling wave optics lensing near caustics and beyond the geometric optics approximation and thereby illustrate how tools from resurgence and asymptotic analysis can be applied to practical problems in astrophysics. Near caustic singularities, the post-refractive corrections diverge, while the uniform asymptotic expansion becomes accurate. We use the leading uniform approximation to bridge the singular caustic regime. For the Lorenzian lens, the leading-order diffractive-refractive-uniform expansions mosaic the full parameter space, providing quantitative switching criteria.

abstract: We use cyclic spectroscopy to infer the scintillation parameter C<SUB>1</SUB> for the millisecond pulsar B1937+21. This marks the first time this parameter has been measured for any pulsar without assuming a pulse broadening function shape prior to deconvolution from the intrinsic pulse profile, removing significant potential biases in scattering delay estimation and letting us consider a wider range of line-of-sight geometries. At 428 MHz, we find a weighted mean and standard deviation across multiple epochs and independent scintillation fluctuations of C<SUB>1</SUB> = 1.21 ± 0.01, which, along with the consistent presence of diffuse scintillation arcs, favors a thick-screen geometry spanning just over 10% of the Earth--pulsar distance. The resulting precision in our weighted average allows us to rule out various thin-screen geometries, as well as thick-screen geometries comprising more than 30% of the Earth--pulsar distance, with greater than 5σ certainty at this observing frequency. We also use our measured C<SUB>1</SUB> values to determine diffraction scales, which we find to be roughly 11 × 10<SUP>3</SUP> km between 418 and 438 MHz, suggesting an inner scale on the order of 10<SUP>3</SUP> km. Future implementations of our method to other lines of sight through the Galaxy may substantially improve efforts to understand structures that contribute to the majority of pulsar emission scattering in the interstellar medium. As flagship instruments like the Green Bank Telescope begin offering the use of cyclic spectroscopy backends, and other instruments begin exploration and commissioning of similar systems, demonstrations like these will be crucial for the widespread adoption of cyclic spectroscopy.

abstract: EP251023a is an extragalactic fast X-ray transient (eFXT) that was only detected by the Einstein Probe (EP) and that lacks a gamma-ray counterpart. The prompt emission consisted of a main emission with a duration T<SUB>90</SUB> = 292 ± 19 s, followed by a long-lasting tail emission that persisted until the observation ended at T<SUB>0</SUB> + 1571 s. With the upper limit of Konus--Wind, we derived a conservative upper limit on the isotropic gamma-ray energy E<SUB>γ,iso</SUB> of 5.7 × 10<SUP>52</SUP> erg for the main emission phase. We identified a redshift of z = 2.232 ± 0.001 based on the strong absorption features in the Keck spectrum, which also indicate a relatively low host-galaxy HI column density. Based on the broadband spectral energy distribution, the late-time light curves show an achromatic plateau, followed by an extremely steep decay with a slope of 3.99 after a break at about 49 ks. This is consistent with a rapidly spinning millisecond magnetar engine. Under the isotropic wind scenario, we obtained an initial period P<SUB>0</SUB> < 2.27 ms and a magnetic field strength B<SUB>p</SUB> < 8.33 × 10<SUP>14</SUP> G for the magnetar. If a jet collimation with a typical opening angle of 0.1 rad is considered, these constraints are relaxed to P<SUB>0</SUB> < 32.15 ms and B<SUB>p</SUB> < 1.18 × 10<SUP>16</SUP> G. Together with GRB 070707, EP251023a might represent a rare class of optical magnetar-powered internal plateaus with little external-shock contamination. This is different from previous examples that were primarily detected in X-rays. Future discoveries of similar events will help us to clarify the relation between magnetar-powered internal emission observed in the optical band and the emission that is only detected in X-rays.

abstract: The nature of the central engine powering short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs) in binary neutron star (BNS) mergers remains a key open question in the era of multi-messenger astronomy. The ergostar hypothesis, that a rapidly rotating star with an ergoregion can act as a powerful energy source, offers an alternative explanation to the black hole-accretion disk paradigm. In this work, however, we examine this hypothesis using a phenomenological EOS of strangeon matter, i.e., condensed matter with nucleon-like units for three flavors of quarks. By constructing a large suite of uniformly rotating equilibrium models, we systematically investigate the parameter space of the stable ergostars and calculate their maximum extractable energy. We demonstrate that strangeon matter supports a vast and robust parameter space for dynamically stable ergostars, even without requiring differential rotation. We find that the extractable rotational energy from these configurations can be on the order of 0.01 M <SUB>⊙</SUB>, representing a massive energy reservoir, even when accounting for baryonic mass variations (e.g., mass ejection and particle capture during the Penrose process). Our results suggest that BNS merger remnants composed of exotic matter could play a crucial, previously underestimated role in high-energy astrophysics.

abstract: XMM-Newton observations of NGC 5907 ULX-1 offer a unique opportunity to investigate the spectral evolution of a pulsating ultraluminous X-ray source over a long period with X-ray luminosities varying by up to one order of magnitude. NGC 5907 ULX-1 is the most luminous ultraluminous X-ray pulsar known to date and one of the ULX pulsars that exhibits spin-down during its low flux states. Benefiting from the long-term monitoring of the source between 2003-2024, we present the results of a systematic search for the best physically motivated model to fit the continuum of the X-ray spectrum with the help of different emission models and modeling procedures. Such an approach also serves to resolve degeneracies between thermal and non-thermal emission at low and high energies. As a natural outcome of our analysis, we study the correlation between the thermal and non-thermal model parameters such as the inner disk temperature, the photon index, and the electron temperature for Comptonization with respect to the spin observability and the X-ray luminosity of NGC 5907 ULX-1.

abstract: Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are the quickest-spinning neutron stars (NSs) known. The X-ray pulsations produced by hot spots on their surface encode precious information on the mass and size of these compact objects; in this frame, accreting MSPs (AMSPs) are among the best targets because during X-ray outbursts they become relatively bright X-ray sources. Yet, breaking the degeneracy between the many parameters shaping their pulse profiles was not possible because of the limited effective area of X-ray instruments flown so far. X-ray polarimetry is a potential game-changer that provides an independent measure of the geometry of the hot spots. IXPE observed the outburst of SRGA J144459.2-604207 that occurred in February 2024 during a 10-day-long campaign also involving NICER, XMM-Newton, and NuSTAR. This observation provided the first detection of polarization in X-rays for an AMSP. The polarized signal showed a significantly energy-dependent polarization, and, thanks to an accurate pulse-timing solution, a phase-resolved polarimetric analysis was performed. Although the spin-phase variability of the normalized Stokes parameters is not highly significant, applying the relativistic rotating vector model, the hot spots' geometry was determined. The result indicates a moderately fan-beam emission from two point-like hot spots at a small magnetic obliquity. IXPE also detected 52 type-I X-ray bursts, which allowed for obtaining an upper limit on the polarization degree. In 2025, SAX J1808.4-3658 went into outburst, and IXPE observed it; preliminary analyses show a significant polarization also for this AMSP and the presence of a very bright type I X-ray burst in the light In this talk, the results obtained for the only two AMSP observed by IXPE so far are reported.

abstract: Next-generation gravitational-wave (GW) observatories, such as the Einstein Telescope (ET) and Cosmic Explorer, will observe binary neutron star (BNS) mergers across cosmic history, providing precise parameter estimates for the closest events. Innovative wide-field facilities, such as the Vera Rubin Observatory, will rapidly survey large portions of the sky with unprecedented sensitivity to faint transients. Starting from BNS merger populations spanning different neutron star (NS) mass distributions and equations of state (EOSs), we model the GW and kilonova (KN) signals based on source properties. The KN ejecta are described using numerical-relativity-informed fits, including the effects of prompt collapse to a black hole and updated prescriptions for more massive systems such as GW190425. We also include optical afterglow emission from relativistic jets consistent with observed short gamma-ray bursts. In this talk, I will first discuss detection prospects and parameter estimation for different ET configurations, both as a standalone detector and in networks with current or next-generation GW observatories. I will then present target-of-opportunity strategies for Rubin follow-up and assess the joint detection capabilities, showing that ET alone could enable the discovery of tens to hundreds of KNe per year, increasing by about an order of magnitude in network configurations. Finally, I will highlight how rate uncertainties are dominated by the poorly constrained local BNS merger rate, with a weaker dependence on the neutron star mass distribution and EOS.

abstract: In this solicited talk I will review the X-ray spectral-timing phenomenology of neutron star low mass X-ray binaries, including the broadband noise variability, low and high frequency quasi periodic oscillations, including kHz QPO pairs, burst oscillations, and coherent pulsations. I will highlight frequency correlations and rms energy dependences that track changes in the inner disc radius, boundary layer, and magnetosphere. I will discuss the physical coupling between the different components in the accretion flow and compare them with black hole systems. I conclude with open problems and prospects for next generation timing missions.

abstract: 4U 1626─67 is a benchmark system for understanding complex accretion physics in ultracompact low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs). A defining characteristic of this LMXB hosting an accreting neutron star is the presence of a stable ∼48 mHz Quasi-Periodic Oscillation (QPO), exhibited exclusively during the spin-down torque state of the pulsar. We present a comprehensive QPO-phase-resolved study of the source using archival XMM-Newton observations to probe its accretion dynamics. We employed Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) to isolate the QPO signal and extract its instantaneous phase. By resolving the 0.5─10 keV pulse profile morphology over the QPO cycle, we observe a significant evolution in the beaming pattern. This timing analysis is integrated with phase-resolved spectroscopy using simultaneous EPIC-PN and RGS data. We find that the spectral parameters exhibit strong variability with the QPO phase, pointing towards a dynamic X-ray reprocessing scenario. We discuss these findings from the perspective of the neutron star beaming geometry and inner accretion disk structure in 4U 1626─67.

abstract: Neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (NS-LMXBs) with short orbital periods (on the order of hours) undergo recurrent transitions between outburst and quiescence, making them important laboratories for studying transient accretion. These episodes are generally interpreted within the framework of the thermal─viscous instability operating in the accretion disc. Nonetheless, a small number of transient systems exhibit exceptionally long outbursts that are challenging to explain with the standard model. A prominent case is EXO 0748─676, which remained persistently active for at least 23 years, entered quiescence, and later reactivated after a 16-year interval. In this study, we explore whether such prolonged activity can arise from the conventional disc instability mechanism or whether additional physical processes must be invoked. We carry out a systematic comparison between NS LMXBs with long and short outbursts, limiting our analysis to systems with short orbital periods. By examining long-term X-ray light curves, we measure outburst durations, estimate mass accretion rates, and infer accretion disc masses. Our results show that long-outburst systems are clearly distinct from short-outburst sources in parameter spaces defined by accretion rate, disc mass, and outburst duration. This separation suggests that the thermal─viscous instability successfully explains short outbursts but fails to reproduce the extended events. We discuss the limitations of both disc-based and donor-star-driven scenarios in accounting for long outbursts and outline the implications for accretion processes in transient neutron star and black hole X-ray binaries. abstract: We present the first X-ray polarimetric measurement of the eclipsing neutron star low-mass X-ray binary system AX J1745.6-2901 obtained with the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE). This transient source lies within ∼1.5' of the Galactic center and was observed serendipitously during a 150 ks IXPE pointing at MAXI J1744-294. The crowded and highly absorbed Galactic center environment makes polarization measurements particularly challenging, requiring a careful assessment of contamination from the primary target and the surrounding diffuse emission. We detect a polarization degree of PD = 14.7% ± 4.0% and a polarization angle of PA = 122^∘ ± 8^∘. Phase-resolved analysis reveals a significant increase in polarization during the eclipse and dip phase, reaching PD = 34.2% ± 8.7%. The enhanced polarization when the central X-ray source is obscured indicates that scattering processes dominate the polarized emission, likely originating in an equatorial disk wind or extended reprocessing structure. These results provide new constraints on the geometry of high-inclination accreting neutron star systems and demonstrate the diagnostic power of X-ray polarimetry for probing accretion physics in complex Galactic center environments.

abstract: Intermittent unstable thermonuclear burning of accreted matter on neutron stars gives rise to thermonuclear (type-I) X-ray bursts. Such bursts provide a testbed to study nuclear fusion processes in intense radiation, gravity, and magnetic fields. The strongest ones among such bursts temporarily push the photosphere away from the stellar surface, and are known as photospheric radius-expansion bursts. Although several thousand bursts have been detected over the past decades, here we report the first observation of a single burst with two consecutive photospheric radius-expansion events. This burst was found from the AstroSat observation of the accretion-powered millisecond X-ray pulsar IGR J17591-2342. Our basic spectral model for the burst includes an absorbed blackbody to describe the burst emission and an absorbed power law to represent the non-burst emission. The blackbody normalisation shows two consecutive humps aligned with blackbody temperature dips during the burst. Such an unusual behaviour could imply two consecutive photospheric radius-expansion events during the same burst or a systematic metallicity evolution in the neutron star atmosphere. However, our spectral analysis suggests the latter option is less likely to be happening for IGR J17591-2342. This result challenges current theoretical understanding. [A A, 701, A54 (2025)].

abstract: Accretion flow around a black hole (BH) or a neutron star (NS) emits high energy radiations with varying spectral and temporal properties. Observed temporal variations (Mauche et al. 2002, ApJ, 580, 423) point to the existence of a mechanism, dictated by the flow dynamics and not by the stellar surface or magnetic fields, that is common in both types of compact objects. Furthermore, ultra-relativistic jets are emitted from both of these accreting compact objects, strongly implying that there should be at least a common mechanism of jet launching (Fender et al., 2004, Nature, 427, 222). Previously, it was shown that for an advective flow with nominal viscosity and angular momentum, the solution allows two shocks in the flow: 1. outer one forms due to a strong centrifugal barrier, called CENtrifugal pressure dominated Boundary Layer (CENBOL), which is a common feature for both NSs and BHs; 2. inner shock or Normal Boundary Layer (NBOL) forms very close to the surface of an NS, due to the physical boundary. The origin of Quasi Periodic Oscillations (QPOs) in accreting NS, especially the observational features found in HMXBs like Cir X-1, were successfully explained through the oscillations of NBOL and CENBOL (Bhattacharjee, A., and Chakrabarti, S. K. 2019, ApJ, 873, 119). Here, we performed Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations of accreting matter around weakly magnetized neutron stars and black holes, in presence of cooling and viscosity. We vary the accretion rate, the cooling rate, the viscosity, among other things, and explore the effect on both the accreted and ejected matter. We find shock mediated jets in both sources, with an additional NBOL mediated jet for the neutron star. Both types of jet launching mechanisms show coupling with the accretion flow and QPOs, through vertical and horizontal oscillations. Furthermore, with an increase in viscosity, both types of sources show a gradual decrease in outflowing matter. Additional to finding a common accretion-ejection connection, we find that the behavior of the inner accretion disk for NS is more complex than BH, due to the inner boundary condition. We see that the advective flow is more important in NS, as it can pile up on NS surface and provide efficient cooling of further incoming matter, even without a standard disk component. Our results are able to provide possible explanations for multiple observational features: 1. the radio/X-Ray luminosity correlations of both BH and NS; 2. the lower radio fluxes observed in NS jet, as compared to BH jets; 3. the non-suppression of jet activity in steady soft states of NS, unlike BH sources. We also explore the more general cases to compare those results with observation of sources like Cir X-1, Sco X-1 and 4U 1820-30.

title: What is the Origin of Jets in Accreting Neutron Stars? A Unified Accretion-Ejection Mechanism for Compact Objects

abstract: Binary stars are very important in Astronomy. In some cases, it is possible to access, with good precision, the fundamental parameter that determines the evolution of an isolated star: its mass. In close binary systems, if close enough to each other, the evolution of the components changes completely compared to what each of them would have had in isolation, because mass loss may occur by Roche lobe overflow. Examples of objects due to binary evolution are low-mass helium white dwarfs, type Ia supernova progenitors, cataclysmic variables, black widows and redbacks families, blue and yellow stragglers. In addition to the two stellar components, there is another fundamental actor: the accretion disk. Accretion disks have been studied for decades. However, the complexity of the physical processes that occur in it means that we still have a lot to explore. In this poster, we will make a brief description of the evolution of close binary systems composed of a low-mass normal star and a neutron star, using models obtained from our binary evolution code. We show the method we use to search for a possible progenitor of PSR J1622-0315, a redback whose characteristic parameters have been recently determined. Subsequently, we describe the thin disk treatment (``alpha disk''), where it is possible to decouple the vertical from the radial treatment (where temporal evolution is found). We present our first results and discuss the steps to follow to study the effect of neutron star irradiation on the accretion disk.

abstract: A theory of the puzzling spectral "zebra" pattern of the Crab pulsar's high-frequency interpulse (HFIP) is developed. Thus, it solves a nearly 20-year-old mystery of the Crab pulsar radio emission. The observed emission bands are the high-contrast interference maxima, resulting from the combined effects of gravitational lensing and plasma de-lensing, and produced by multiple ray propagating through the pulsar magnetosphere. The model enables space-resolved tomography (like a CT scan) of the pulsar magnetosphere, yielding a plasma profile of n_e∝ 1/r^3, which agrees with theoretical insights. The model essentially resolves a 10-100-km scale at a distance of 2kpc — nearly million times better than EHT, which observed a galactic black hole. We predict the zebra pattern trend to change at a higher frequency when the ray separation becomes smaller than the pulsar size. This frequency is predicted to be in the range between 42 GHz and 650 GHz, which is within the reach of existing facilities like ALMA and SMA. These observations would advance our understanding of the magnetosphere and potentially explore gravity in the strong field regime near the star's surface. — The author acknowledges support by the National Science Foundation (NSF) under grant PHY-2409249. This research was supported in part by grant NSF PHY-2309135 to the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics (KITP).

abstract: Gravitational waves detected from the inspiral stage of a binary neutron star merger give information about the nature of the initial components such as their masses, spins, radii and tidal deformabilities. Similarly, observations of the post-merger stage would give hints on the characteristics and the evolution of the remnant of these coalescences. Since post-merger observations by earth-based detectors are not available yet, only numerical simulations are used to study this stage. Therefore, we will review the main characteristics of this kind of mergers, as well as the results given by the numerical simulations in order to better understand the different outcomes that are produced in these systems and how the final fate is related to the initial components.

abstract: We present the first systematic investigation of the continuous orbital evolution of the Gigahertz-Peaked Spectum turnover frequency ($ν_{peak}$) in the binary millisecond pulsar, PSR J2144$-$5237. Using approximately 50 hours of densely sampled observations spanning the $\sim10$-day orbit with the Parkes Ultra-Wideband Low frequency receiver, we obtained continuous frequency coverage from 704 MHz to 4 GHz, enabling robust measurements of the spectral evolution throughout the binary orbit. We detect a clear and systematic modulation of the turnover frequency with orbital phase for both the $1^{st}$ pulse and $2^{nd}$ pulse components, with both emission components exhibiting remarkably similar evolutionary trends despite originating from distinct emission regions within the pulsar magnetosphere. The correlated evolution of the two pulse components strongly suggests that the observed spectral variability is governed by propagation through the intra-binary environment. The large orbital modulation of turnover frequency can be explained by cyclotron resonance absorption in magnetized plasma associated with the companion, while alternative absorption mechanisms are unable to reproduce the observed behaviour. Modelling the orbital evolution of the turnover frequency within the cyclotron absorption framework, can constrain the electron density distribution in the pulsar wind, estimate the magnetic field strength of the companion, and place limits on the geometry of the absorbing plasma and the binary system. This study establish orbital evolution of the Gigahertz Peaked Spectum as a powerful new diagnostic of the magnetized intra-binary medium and provide a hitherto unexplored probe of pulsar wind-companion interactions in eclipsing millisecond pulsar binaries.

abstract: At the beginning of X-ray astronomy, it was predicted that polarimetry would play a major diagnostic role in this field. Early polarimetry experiments followed the first advances of X-ray astronomy by only a few years. However, when Riccardo Giacconi revolutionized the field with focusing X-ray optics, polarimetry, whose sensitivity was far inferior, was set aside for many decades. The situation changed dramatically with the invention of detectors based on the photoelectric effect in gas. The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer, based on this technique, has extended to polarimetry the breakthrough in sensitivity achieved in imaging X-ray astronomy with the Einstein Observatory. Launched on 9 December 2021, IXPE has so far observed more than 100 sources across all major source classes and detected significant polarization in nearly 80% of them. In many cases, IXPE results have challenged several established views in relativistic astrophysics, expanding our understanding of how the Universe works. The mission has shed light on particle acceleration in pulsar wind nebulae, supernova remnants, and blazars; on scattering processes in molecular clouds around the Galactic Center, in black-hole binaries, radio-quiet active galactic nuclei, and in weakly magnetized neutron-star binaries; on strong-gravity effects also in black-hole binaries; and on the transport of radiation in highly magnetized plasma at the poles of neutron stars, as well as in the extreme magnetospheres of magnetars. In this talk I will review the main scientific results obtained so far with IXPE and discuss possible paths to extend these achievements through future X-ray polarimetry missions in upcoming opportunities.

abstract: Stellar abundances reveal nonmonotonic [Y/Eu] and [Sr/Eu] evolution, a systematic decline with increasing [Eu/H] at low metallicity, a minimum at [Eu/H] ~ -0.3, and then a rise at high metallicity. This behavior requires at least three distinct neutron-capture sources operating on different timescales. We develop a one-zone chemical-evolution model constraining their typical delay times, rates, and yield ratios. Reproducing the observed [Y/Eu] and [Sr/Eu] sequences requires a delayed r-process channel (most likely binary neutron-star (BNS) mergers) dominating Eu production (≳95% of total Eu). A prompt channel preferentially produces first-peak elements with minimal Eu, explaining the increasing [Y/Eu] at decreasing [Eu/H] below [Eu/H] ≲ -2.5, and delayed asymptotic giant branch s-process enrichment with delays greater than t<SUB>min</SUB> = 0.3--0.6 Gyr reproduce the late-time upturn in Y (Sr). Our model quantitatively reproduces all constraints, including the large ∆[Y/Eu] ≈ 0.6 dex variation between the late-time rise [Eu/H] and the minimum value, the location of the minimum at [Eu/H] ~ -0.3, and late-time rise. The first- to second-peak yield ratios correspond to [Y/Eu] ≈ -0.3 (prompt) and ≈-0.8 (BNS mergers). The observed ∆[Y/Eu] amplitude establishes a model-independent lower limit on the first- to second-peak yield ratio of ≳3.4 between the prompt and delayed channels, ruling out models with similar prompt and delayed yield ratios. These results demonstrate that explaining the observed heavy-element abundance patterns requires multiple channels with distinct nucleosynthetic signatures and operational timescales, providing constraints on the relative rates, delay times, and yield patterns of candidate production sites.

abstract: The presence of disks and shells around magnetars is predicted to limit the propagation of high-energy electrons and positrons, which influence observations of galactic cosmic rays in the inner heliosphere. On the other hand, both the presence of precessing disks and precessing magnetars have been invoked to explain the modulation of X-rays by several magnetars. Magnetar ellipticities are key parameters that could distinguish the role of these precessing compact objects from that of precessing disks. The lack of observations of gravitational waves from magnetars, such as pulsars, is another important piece of the puzzle. Inferences on magnetar parameters in the literature will be compared, and a coherent scenario will be presented at the conference.
author: Grimani, Catia
title: Consequences of the presence of extended disks and shells around magnetars

abstract: Context. Multiregion constructions of the neutron star equation of state (EoS) introduce freedom in matching low and intermediate density descriptions. This freedom can generate families of formally admissible stellar models whose physical viability must be assessed against astrophysical observations. Aims. We investigated whether current neutron star constraints are sensitive not only to the high density continuation of the EoS, but also to the low density matching procedure itself. To this end, we compared two baseline constructions propagated through a common high density extension. Methods. In branch 𝒜, the sub-n<SUB>1</SUB> EoS was obtained by smoothly matching a low density β-equilibrated input EoS to a β-stable chiral effective field theory (χEFT) branch. In branch ℬ, the low density branch was continued directly up to n<SUB>1</SUB> = 0.32 fm<SUP>-3</SUP> and served as a control construction. Above n<SUB>1</SUB>, both branches were extended using the same parameterized continuation and were confronted with direct NICER mass--radius posteriors, a hard lower bound on the maximum mass, and an effective constraint on Λ<SUB>1.4</SUB>. This common continuation was used to isolate the role of the low density matching sector. Results. The posterior-favored predictions of branches 𝒜 and ℬ remain strongly overlapping at the observable level. The inferred stellar properties differ only slightly, and the two branches yield very similar continuation parameters, especially n<SUB>2</SUB> and Γ<SUB>1</SUB>. Nevertheless, the NICER-informed posterior induces a nontrivial constraint on the matching parameters of branch 𝒜, favoring n<SUB>m</SUB> ≃ 0.18 fm<SUP>-3</SUP> and ∆<SUB>m</SUB> ≃ 0.021 fm<SUP>-3</SUP>. Conclusions. Current astrophysical data constrain the shared continuation above n<SUB>1</SUB>, while indirectly restricting the low density matching sector. The matching is not arbitrary: even nearly degenerate mass--radius predictions can lead the posterior to favor matching regions. This highlights the need to constrain modular EoS frameworks observationally, where density regimes admit multiple valid connections.
author: Nola, Federico
title: NICER constraints on low density matching and high density continuation in neutron star equations of state

abstract: The Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) detects on average 240 gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) per year, providing the most comprehensive all-sky view of the transient gamma-ray sky. GBM detected the first—and so far only—short-GRB counterpart to a binary neutron star merger observed via gravitational waves (GWs), a discovery that connected relativistic jets, nucleosynthesis, and multi-messenger astrophysics, and helped define the science landscape for future missions. Following the completion of the fourth observing run (O4) of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration (LVK), no additional joint GRB─GW detections have yet been confirmed. Throughout O4, the Fermi-GBM team conducted real-time searches for coincident gamma-ray emission from all public GW events using on-board triggers as well as two complementary sub-threshold pipelines: the Targeted and Untargeted Searches. These analyses allow GBM to place stringent upper limits on prompt gamma-ray emission and produce joint upper-limit skymaps. With its large field of view and continuous monitoring, GBM remains a cornerstone instrument in the era of data-intensive time-domain astronomy, capable of detecting counterparts—or setting meaningful limits—for a wide range of transient phenomena. I will present our follow-up efforts and highlight key GBM results, from fast radio bursts to long-duration gamma-ray counterparts from compact mergers.
author: Veres, Peter
title: The role of the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor in the era of big-data astronomy

abstract: Numerical and analytical calculations are powerful tools for studying the accretion dynamics of X-ray pulsars (XRPs), yet translating their results into quantitative spectral predictions remains difficult. Consequently, dedicated radiative transfer simulations are essential for probing the physics near the neutron star surface and interpreting observational data. In this work, we present a fully relativistic Monte Carlo radiative transfer code developed to investigate the origin of Cyclotron Resonant Scattering Features (CRSFs). To model the accretion environment, we adopted the analytical plasma-density and velocity profiles of Mushtukov et al. (2015), which account for the effects of radiation pressure on the flow. To ensure accuracy in regions of rapid density variation, we implemented an adaptive step-size algorithm. Particular care was given to the boundary treatment at the base of the scattering region (the hot spot). We examined two scenarios for photon-surface interactions: (1) Geometric Reflection, where photons are reflected elastically, preserving their energy; and (2) Thermalization, where photons are instantaneously absorbed and re-emitted, with their energies resampled from the blackbody distribution and directions randomized. We generate angle-resolved spectra across a range of X-ray luminosities to examine the impact of luminosity and viewing angle θ (with respect to the magnetic field). Our results successfully reproduce the observed correlations between the luminosity and the CRSF centroid energy E_CRSF and line width σ_CRSF: both quantities correlate positively with luminosity. Furthermore, they exhibit strong variability over the pulse phase, with E_CRSF scaling negatively with cosθ and σ_CRSF positively. Finally, we validate our framework against the XRP GX 304-1. Our model successfully reproduces the observed spectral variability over an order of magnitude in luminosity, consistent with an edge-on viewing geometry. Looking ahead, extending this framework to include polarization-dependent scattering will yield testable predictions for the new generation of X-ray polarimetry missions.

abstract: Quadratic $f(R)$ gravity carries a massive scalar degree of freedom, the scalaron, whose finite range $λ$ screens its influence on the geometry outside a compact object. We show that this screening severs the exterior of a black hole from that of a neutron star of the same mass. The correction to the Schwarzschild metric is Yukawa-suppressed, falling as $e^{-r/λ}$ instead of polynomially in the coupling, and is thus invisible to any expansion in powers of that coupling; also, the exterior is intrinsically isotropic, so that inverting the temporal potential alone, as in single-potential solutions, fails to solve ]field equations. Applying the Gauss-Bonnet theorem to this geometry, we find the leading deflection angle to be exactly the general-relativistic $4GM/b$, the scalaron contributions cancelling identically in the combination that bends light. The first correction carries the unfamiliar signature $λ^{-1/2}b^{-3/2}e^{-b/λ}$, screened beyond the scalaron range and confirmed against direct quadrature to around 20% at $b=4λ$, improving to 7% at $b=12λ$. What survives is not a difference of degree but of kind. The three ingredients that deliver it, non-analyticity in the coupling, the intrinsically isotropic gauge and the pressure-weighted scalar charge, are here obtained within a single, self-consistent derivation for the first time. A static black hole carries no scalar hair, and lenses precisely as GR requires; a neutron star acquires a scalar charge weighted by the pressure supporting it against collapse, and does not. Weak lensing hence closes as a discriminant of the theory, whilst the horizon, as against a material surface, remains one in principle. The observational advantage lies not in bending angles at large $b$ but in the strong-field imaging of the photon sphere, and in the stellar interior, where the scalar charge is fixed by EoS.

abstract: GW170817 is the first binary neutron star merger with observations of gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation. It is a compelling target for long-term monitoring as its broadband emission (from radio to X-rays) is predicted to rise and remain detectable for over a decade after the merger. The timescale and luminosity of the late-time emission depend on the ejecta mass and velocity, and the density of the interstellar medium (ISM), making late-time observations a diagnostic tool for both the energetics of the ejecta and the merger environment. I will present the latest Chandra observations of GW170817, detected in X-rays for over 8 years after the merger, and discuss the prospects for observing late-time X-ray emission from NS mergers with NewAthena.

abstract: The interior of neutron stars (NS) contains matter with densities several times higher than nuclear atomic density. Obtaining an accurate equation of state (EoS) to describe NS is crucial for enhancing our understanding of matter in such extreme environments. To achieve this, we built ten EoS by considering three diferent crusts which are added to the core of these compact objects using a new thermodynamically consistent formalism. Essentially, for an isolated and cold NS, we assume a linear relationship for pressure and energy density in a small region between the core and the crust. This establishes an interpolation function in the pressure/baryonic-chemical-potential plane. We compared this new way of "gluing" EoS with the classical method that neglects causal and thermodynamic consistency. Then, we solved the TOV equations, which describe a non-rotating, spherically symetric and static object, to obtain the mass-radius relationship and compared it with the existing observational constraints of NS. In addition, we explored changes that the new matching formalism can cause in the oscillation modes. With alternative matching formalisms, even for two or three interpolations of the same crust, the p1 mode exhibited differences in oscillation frequencies and damping times for low-mass NS. In contrast, no visible effects can be appreciated for the f mode, neither in the three models of the crust nor in the interpolations considered. We conclude that independently of the model used for the EoS, the method of construction will impact in NS observables such as the radius, frequencies and damping times of non-radial oscillations.

abstract: Neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries, in particular those in quiescence, were intensively used, over the past 15 years to determine the neutron star masses and radii by spectroscopy of the NS surface thermal emission. However, over time, a series of potential sources of systematic biases on these measurements were put forth in the literature. This is because the spectroscopic method required making assumptions. Among the most critical ones are the assumptions of a non-rotating neutron star, and of a neutron star surface emitting uniformly. It was shown that these can cause biases on the radius by as much as ∼ 40%. Consequently, these M-R measurements from low-mass X-ray binaries were supplanted by those from the pulse profile modelling of millisecond pulsars (e.g., with NICER data). However, I will show that the aforementioned assumptions are no longer necessary. Thanks to new tools permitting realistic modelling., we can now control the related systematics, ensuring an unbiased measurement of the radius from low-mass X-ray binaries. I will present the first results that will bring back quiescence low-mass X-ray binaries to the forefront of mass-radius measurements and constraints on the dense matter equation of state.

abstract: Her X-1 is an intermediate (or low) mass X-ray binary pulsar that exhibits a ∼35-day super-orbital modulation whose origin-disc precession or neutron-star free precession-remains debated. Earlier work reported stochastic variations without a clear long-term trend. Using ∼50 years of data from CGRO/BATSE, RXTE/ASM, SWIFT/BAT, FERMI/GBM, and MAXI/GSC supplemented with archival measurements, we studied the long-term evolution of this modulation. Three methods are applied: epoch-folding searches for constant periods, χ^2 maximisation in the period─period-derivative space, and timing of main-on peaks via an O-C analysis. All approaches consistently show a long term decrease in the super-orbital period at a rate of ∼ -10^-5 s s^-1, with additional short-timescale variabilities superposed on this trend. The possible mechanisms for the observed decay of the super-orbital period will be discussed.

abstract: Cyclotron Resonant Scattering Features (CRSFs) in the spectra of accreting X-ray pulsars (XRPs) are the only direct diagnostic of the magnetic-field strength near the neutron-star surface, and thus, they are essential for probing the physics of these extreme environments. However, their interpretation remains a challenging task as observations have shown that in many cases the line features depend strongly on the X-ray luminosity L and the pulse phase. Of particular interest is the positive correlation observed in low-luminosity XRPs between L and both centroid energy of the CRSF (E_CRSF) and line width (σ_CRSF). In this work, we examine the physical mechanisms driving these trends, specifically the roles of resonant scattering and relativistic plasma motion within the accretion funnel. We adopt the analytical plasma-density and velocity profiles proposed by Mushtukov et al. (2015) to account for the effects of radiation pressure on the flow. To test whether this framework can explain the observed CRSF variability in subcritical XRPs, we developed a relativistic Monte Carlo radiative transfer code featuring an adaptive step-size algorithm. We performed detailed calculations to obtain angle-resolved spectra, varying the accretion luminosity to explore the resulting evolution of the CRSF properties. Our simulations reveal that the emergent spectra exhibit prominent, asymmetric CRSFs accompanied by a broad blue wing. The simulated lines are systematically redshifted relative to the classical cyclotron energy, with the magnitude of this redshift decreasing at higher luminosities and larger viewing angles with respect to the magnetic field. We successfully reproduce the observed positive correlation of E_CRSF and σ_CRSF with luminosity. Crucially, we find that the absolute values of these quantities are sensitive to the viewing angle θ, with E_CRSF and σ_CRSF exhibiting negative and positive correlations with cosθ, respectively. Therefore, we predict that future phase-resolved observations will reveal an anti-correlation between E_CRSF and σ_CRSF. To validate the model, we performed a consistency check using observational data of the XRP GX 304-1, adopting physical parameters appropriate for this system. The model successfully reproduces the observed CRSF variability over nearly an order of magnitude in luminosity for geometries in which the accretion funnel is predominantly viewed edge-on.

abstract: Accreting, weakly magnetized Neutron Stars in Low-mass X-ray binaries (NS-LMXBs) are a fundamental laboratory to study radiation processes in the strong gravity regime. Among the brightest X-ray sources, Z-sources are NS-LMXBs characterized by a wide Z-like three branches track in the hard color-soft color diagram (CCD), typically accreting close to the Eddington limit. In this talk, we discuss the spectropolarimetric results obtained by IXPE and in coordination with other facilities on Z-type NS-LMXBs. Most of the known Z-sources were observed by IXPE during its two-year baseline phase and the first two GO cycles, being among the most polarized NS-LMXBs in the full 2-8 keV band and with a strong correlation between the observed polarization and the position along the Z-track. We will also provide an in-depth interpretation of these results, including the first detailed branch-resolved spectropolarimetric analysis and numerical simulations.

title: X-ray polarization of Z-type neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries

abstract: Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are the oldest but fastest pulsars known to date, the first one, PSR B1937+21 was discovered in 1982. To explain how these pulsars could be formed, a new hypothesis was formulated: the recycling of pulsars, i.e the fact that a pulsar could accrete matter from a companion and be spun up. In this work, we developed a population synthesis algorithm for pulsars which belong to a binary, in order to check whether most of the observed recycled pulsars were formed via an accretion mechanism and derive statistics about their properties, that are difficult to obtain through observations. We also make predictions for future surveys. Toward the presented objectives, we use the code Stellar EVolution for N-body (SEVN) to take into account all the binary processes and our own code to evolve each pulsar self-consistently by taking into account the secular evolution of a force-free magnetosphere, the magnetic field decay, gravitational braking and spatial evolution. Each pulsar is born in binary with a main sequence companion, and evolve to present time. The radio and gamma-ray emission locations were modeled by the polar cap geometry and striped wind model, respectively. Our simulations seem to reproduce well the population of radio and gamma-ray pulsars observed in the selected surveys (FAST GPPS, PMPS, Fermi). We also found that there should be less than 220 unidentified pulsars in the Fourth Fermi-LAT catalogue of gamma-ray sources (4FGL). High values of the viewing angle seem to be needed to be able to observe the recycled pulsars, and it also seems difficult to observe recycled pulsars with an aligned rotation axis and magnetic axis. We find that only a small fraction, approximately 8.10 ^-3 % of oxygen-neon white dwarfs (ONeWDs) in binary systems appear to contribute to the population of mildly recycled pulsars through accretion-induced collapse.

abstract: We discuss the X-ray spectro-polarimetric properties of Neutron Stars in Low-mass X-ray binaries (NS-LMXBs) through recent IXPE observations. These objects are among the brightest X-ray sources and represent perfect targets to constrain the geometry of their innermost accretion flows and helping to break long-standing spectroscopic degeneracies. Z-sources are NS-LMXBs characterized by a wide Z-like three branches track in the hard color-soft color diagram (CCD) and accretes close to the Eddington limit. Most of the known Z-sources were observed by IXPE during its two-year baseline phase and the first two GO cycles, and show polarization properties that vary along their spectral branches, indicating state-dependent changes in emission geometry. Moreover, the polarization is often higher than expected for a standard accretion disk plus boundary-layer scenario, pointing to more complex geometries and a substantial role for scattering. We discuss possible physical interpretations based on spectropolarimetric modeling, and outline how future observations and improved theoretical models may further constrain the geometry of NS-LMXBs.

title: Spectropolarimetric properties of Z-type neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries with IXPE

abstract: In the 4FGL-DR4 point-source catalog of the Large Area Telescope (LAT) onboard NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Observatory (Fermi-LAT), around a third of the sources are still unidentified (unIDs). In this work, we perform a detailed study of one of them, namely 4FGL J2112.5-3043. Only gamma-ray emission has been detected from this unidentified source, with no counterpart observed at any other wavelength as of today. Together with its high detection significance, this makes 4FGL J2112.5-3043 a particularly compelling target for further investigation. The results of our spectral and spatial analyses show that the source photon spectrum is better described with a subexponential cutoff power-law spectral model, with no significant flux variability over time, and a morphology consistent with being a point-like source. We investigate and discuss the characterized emission within the context of both conventional and exotic astrophysics, namely a pulsar origin or potential dark matter (DM) annihilations in a nearby Galactic subhalo. abstract: Non-pulsating weakly magnetized neutron stars in X-ray binaries exhibit a challenging phenomenology that has been studied for decades via spectrometry and timing, revealing the presence of contributions difficult to disentangle: the accretion disk, boundary/spreading layer, reflection, disk wind, and the extended accretion disk corona. Nowadays, X-ray polarimetry provides the potential to improve our understanding of the nature and geometry of the emitting regions in these systems. The most intriguing result emerging is a polarization variation, depending on both time and flux; in particular, the polarization angle is observed to vary in some of these sources, but not in others, such as the stellar-mass black holes. In this talk, I will discuss this variability and possible explanations for these effects based on more recent observations performed in August and September 2025 in the two systems that showed the most prominent variations: GX 13+1 and Cir X-1.

abstract: XL-Calibur is a balloon-borne hard-X-ray polarimeter sensitive in the ∼15-80 keV energy range. The focusing telescope determines polarization by using the angular asymmetry of Compton events, scattering from a passive beryllium rod into a circumjacent CZT detector. In the summer of 2024, XL-Calibur was successfully launched from the Esrange Space Center, Sweden. Conducting measurements from ∼40 km altitude, the payload landed safely near Kugluktuk, northern Canada, approximately five days later. Both the Crab system (pulsar and nebula) and Cygnus X-1 (X-ray binary) were successfully observed, providing the most precise constraints for their hard X-ray emission (∼19-64 keV) to date, complementary to the soft-X-ray range of IXPE (2-8 keV). Data has been shared with the community through HEASARC. Here, we give an overview of the XL-Calibur 2024 flight results, including in-depth follow-up analyses. Upcoming plans are also discussed, as the payload is now being prepared for an Antarctic flight, scheduled for December 2027. Such a flight can last several weeks and give access to southern-hemisphere sources. Targets will be selected for observation based on contemporaneous monitoring with Swift BAT or MAXI and include accreting neutron stars, X-ray binaries and blazars.

abstract: Vela X-1 is an archetypal high-mass X-ray binary pulsar in which strong X-ray irradiation from the neutron star significantly affects the companion's stellar wind. A smooth, isotropic wind cannot explain the observed variability in the system, especially the orbital variation in the absorption column density along the sight line, suggesting the presence of additional structures such as photoionisation or accretion wakes. Furthermore, the source intensity exhibits strong variability from orbit to orbit. India's first dedicated X-ray polarimetry mission, XPoSat, was launched on 1 January 2024 aboard PSLV-C58. The mission carries two payloads: the primary Polarimeter Instrument in X-rays (POLIX), operating in the 8.0-30.0 keV band to measure X-ray polarization, and the secondary X-ray Spectroscopy and Timing (XSPECT) instrument, covering the 0.8-15.0 keV energy range. XSPECT has so far observed Vela X-1 during two epochs, comprising five consecutive out-of-eclipse observations and one full orbital cycle. Using these data, we perform a detailed timing and spectroscopic study of Vela X-1 on orbital-period timescales. We find that the variability observed over the orbital period is driven by a comparable contribution from clumpy stellar winds, intrinsic source variability, and accretion/photoionization wake structures. Furthermore, our results confirm that the wake structure has variability at shorter time scales.

abstract: The recycling scenario, proposed decades ago to explain the formation of millisecond pulsars through a Gyr-long accretion phase, was observationally confirmed by the discovery of the first accreting millisecond pulsar. The link between accretion-powered and rotation-powered pulsars was further highlighted by the identification of transitional millisecond pulsars, which can swing between these two regimes on remarkably short timescales. Despite this progress, our understanding of the physical mechanisms governing these systems remains incomplete. In this talk, I will discuss recent observational results that explore the boundary between accreting and transitional systems, focusing on the detection of coherent X-ray pulsations at low luminosities during the late stages of accretion outbursts. While only one system has so far been observed to clearly switch between rotation-powered and accretion-powered states, these findings provide valuable clues on how accretion may persist or be intermittently halted as systems approach quiescence. I will place these results in the broader context of multi-band observations, which are revealing a more complex picture, partially confirming theoretical expectations while challenging others, including the notion of a sharp boundary between accretion and propeller regimes.
author: Illiano, Giulia
title: An ever-thinning thread between accreting and transitional millisecond pulsars

abstract: The landmark multi-messenger observations of the binary neutron star (BNS) merger GW170817 provided firm evidence that such mergers can produce short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs). However, the scarcity of BNS detections in recent gravitational-wave (GW) observing runs raises a critical question: are intrinsic BNS merger rates high enough to account for the full population of observed sGRBs? We address this question by analyzing 64 BNS population synthesis models against 16 years of Fermi-GBM data. By simulating synthetic sGRB catalogs under various jet scenarios, including GW170817-calibrated structured jets and non-universal geometries, we constrain physically viable BNS properties. Our results demonstrate that population models predicting low local merger rates R_BNS(0) ≲ 50 Gpc^-3 yr^-1 fail to reproduce the observed sGRB population unless they large jet opening angles (θ_c ≥ 15^∘) that contradict the narrow cores (θ_c ≍ 6^∘) inferred from afterglow observations. We find that only models with local rates R_BNS(0) ≍ 100 Gpc^-3 yr^-1 successfully reconcile sGRB observations with realistic jet physics. This analysis effectively disfavors low-rate models as sole progenitors and highlights the growing tension between current GW rate estimates and available sGRB catalogues. Finally, we discuss the broader utility of this framework, highlighting how end-to-end predictions that connect physical assumptions about progenitors directly to scientific outputs are essential for interpreting the next generation of multi-messenger discoveries.

title: Constraining Binary Neutron Star Population Synthesis Models using Short Gamma-Ray Burst Data

abstract: This work is based on 2026 May observation of Be-high mass X-ray binary pulsar XTE J1859+083. NuSTAR observed the source during the initial decay phase of the outburst and no significant flux variation was detected throughout the observation. Coherent pulsations were detected in the 3-60 keV energy band, yielding a neutron-star spin period of 9.795566(2) s at MJD 61176. The pulse profile had a complex energy-dependent morphology, characterized by two peaks, a narrow one ~ 0.2 and a broad peak ~ 0.6 pulse phase. The relative amplitude of the first peak increased up to about 32 keV and subsequently decreased at higher energies. A weak intermediate peak was detected near pulse phase ~ 0.9, appearing most prominently in 7-45 keV energy band. A modest energy dependence was observed in the pulsed fraction, which increased from approximately 36% in the 3-10 keV range to >= 40% at energies above 15 keV. The phase-averaged spectrum was well described by an absorbed power-law continuum with a high-energy cutoff and a Gaussian component accounting for the Fe-K<SUB>α</SUB> emission line. Phase-resolved spectroscopy revealed no systematic pulse-phase dependence of the spectral parameters. Comparison with the 2015 NuSTAR observation shows no statistically significant differences in the timing or spectral properties. The similarity of the pulse profiles and broadband spectra at comparable flux levels suggests that the source was observed in a similar accretion configuration during the two epochs separated by approximately a decade.
