abstract: Observations of accreting X-ray pulsars (XRPs) carried out by the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) have provided completely new insight into these fascinating objects, thanks to the indispensable information embedded in their linear X-ray polarization. X-ray polarimetry enables us to measure the polarization angle (PA) and degree (PD) as a function of pulse phase for XRPs, which allows for the system geometry to be determined. Additionally, the radiation from XRPs was expected to be highly polarized, with estimates for a PD of up to 80% for favorable orientations. About a dozen XRPs have been observed by IXPE so far, and pulsar geometries have largely been determined by successful modeling of the pulse phase dependence of the PA with the Rotating Vector Model (RVM). Interestingly, IXPE observations of XRPs have unveiled surprisingly low polarization degrees consistently across the board, significantly lower than theoretical expectations. Several individual XRPs have demonstrated particularly peculiar polarization properties, which adds to the pool of new questions raised as a result of the polarimetric information. Overall, the XRPs observed with IXPE show little energy-dependence of their polarization properties. However, a couple of XRPs display clear energy dependence of their polarization, with unique swings in the PA between low and high energies, and complex energy dependencies over pulse phase as well. Some XRPs require additional polarized components in order to explain their energy-dependent polarization properties, with possible origins outside the adiabatic radius. I will discuss the energy dependent polarization properties of these sources, which vary in complexity and require different approaches in order to properly explain their behavior. I will also address unresolved questions and discuss the proposed solutions.

abstract: The Galactic Center (GC) hosts a rich population of compact objects and extreme environments that are central to multimessenger astrophysics. An unresolved gamma-ray excess detected by Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope has been suggested to originate from a population of millisecond pulsars (MSPs), although alternative interpretations—including dark matter annihilation—remain viable. Identifying and characterizing a GC MSP population would therefore directly connect gamma-ray, radio, and X-ray observations, and clarify the origin of high-energy emission from the inner Galaxy. We present prospects and latest results from a deep radio search for MSPs in the central parsecs of the Galaxy using a uniquely capable large-aperture radio facility optimized for high-frequency pulsar observations. Observing at such high radio frequencies mitigates extreme scattering and dispersion along the GC line of sight, enabling sensitivity to fast-spinning pulsars that have eluded previous surveys. Our effort complements earlier X-ray searches conducted with Chandra X-ray Observatory and directly tests whether a centrally concentrated MSP population can account for the gamma-ray excess. This program illustrates how coordinated exploitation of gamma-ray, X-ray, and radio facilities can constrain compact object populations in dense environments. We discuss implications for multimessenger strategies in the coming decade, including alert-driven follow-up, cross-band data sharing, and synergies with next-generation radio and high-energy observatories aimed at time-domain studies of compact objects in the Galactic nucleus.

abstract: Context: Gamma-ray binaries are a rare subclass of high-mass stellar systems composed of a compact object (neutron star or black hole) orbiting an O- or B-type companion and produce broadband, predominantly non-thermal emission from radio to TeV gamma-rays. Only nine such systems are currently confirmed, and the nature of the compact object has been definitively established in only three, leaving their physical and emission mechanisms incompletely understood. As interacting massive binaries containing compact remnants, gamma-ray binaries provide a crucial link between massive stellar multiplicity, high-energy binary interactions, and the formation of double-compact systems that may ultimately become gravitational-wave sources. Objectives: This project develops a systematic, multi-wavelength framework to constrain the emission processes in gamma-ray binaries and to indirectly diagnose the nature of their compact objects. The study combines phase-resolved radio observations from MeerKAT and archival ATCA data with X-ray monitoring from Swift-XRT and GeV measurements from Fermi-LAT. By coupling detailed radio characterisation with multi-wavelength cross-correlation analyses, the project probes the spatial and temporal relationship between particle acceleration sites and emission regions. Results thus far: As a foundation for this broader program, phase-resolved MeerKAT monitoring data of 1FGL J1018.6−5856 and LMC P3 have been analysed. Both systems appear as compact radio sources displaying orbital modulation and non-thermal spectra consistent with synchrotron emission. The radio/X-ray cross-correlation analysis reveals clear coherence between these wavebands. In both systems, the inferred delays show a clear trend: high-energy emission precedes the radio, consistent with synchrotron emission cooling. Together, the spectral and timing behaviour favours a colliding-wind pulsar interpretation for both binaries. These initial results demonstrate how coordinated monitoring can constrain the preferred emission mechanisms and geometry, paving the way to extend the approach to a population study and to link gamma-ray binaries to the evolutionary pathway toward double-compact, gravitational-wave-emitting systems.

abstract: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) provides unique comprehension about polarized x-ray emissions from many astrophysical sources such as radio quiet and radio loud AGNs, galactic black hole binaries and neutron stars. Polarization maps in X-rays of pulsar wind nebulae and supernova remnants have been probed. IXPE has demonstrated the scientific potential of the techniques but revealed some limitations such as, due to the deposition of ions onto the dielectric of Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) leads towards the decrease in the gas gain. Also, it has a relatively narrow energy band coupled with rapidly declining efficiency. Another limitation of IXPE GPDs was the large dead time (1.1ms), which is incompatible with the brightest sources. Literature showed that 1-cm drift with an 800-mbar dimethyl-ether gas mixture provides the best polarimetric sensitivity. Further optimization of these parameters depends on the mirror's effective area and the energy of x ray source, but no major improvement is expected with current detector design. So, to overcome all these limitations and better performance, we are developing a next generation 3-D photoelectron track polarimeter based on Gridpix detector with multipurpose ASICs from the Medipix collaboration, Timepix3 and TimePix4. Gridpix structure in principle prevents the buildup of charge on the metallic mesh, offering a small diffusion with respect to GEM. Also, with the Timepix3 we can record Time-of-Arrival (ToA) and Time-over-Threshold (ToT) simultaneously in each pixel. They would also solve the issue of dead time for any planned high- throughput optics. In this work Gridpix detector experimentally characterized at the INAF-IAPS laboratory using a novel gas mixture of argon (Ar) and dimethyl ether (DME) (80:20). Combining the argon with the low diffusion and precise tracking capability of DME improves the detector performance. To extract key parameters such as energy spectra, energy resolution, and calibration from raw experimental data demonstrate a good detector response. For the validation of experimental data, a detailed Geant4 simulation is performed. We present the tuning of the simulation to achieve agreement with experimental measurements obtained using a GridPix prototype, highlighting the importance of accurately modeling both the detector response and the reconstruction methods. These results demonstrate the strong potential of the GridPix detector with an Ar:DME gas mixture as a promising candidate for future high-precision X-ray polarimetry missions.

abstract: TIGERISS, the Trans-Iron Galactic Element Recorder for the International Space Station, is an Ultra-Heavy Galactic Cosmic Ray (UHGCR) detector that will launch to the ISS in August 2027 on SpX-37 with an assignment to Columbus SOX. TIGERISS builds on the TIGER and SuperTIGER mission heritage and will measure the elemental abundances from _5B to _82Pb for 400 MeV/nucleon to 10 GeV/nucleon. With a geometry factor of 1.06 m^2 sr, TIGERISS, in one year of operation, will match the statistics seen by the first SuperTIGER balloon flight without the need for atmospheric corrections. TIGERISS will achieve single-element resolution measurements across this wide range of charge, allowing us to test cosmic-ray origins, including their source environments and acceleration mechanisms. Previous work from SuperTIGER showed that GCR measurements up to _40Zr support a source acceleration model where supernovae in OB associations preferentially accelerate refractory elements that are more readily embedded in interstellar dust grains than volatiles. This injection of the GCR into the ISM appears to follow a charge dependence consistent with their grain sputtering cross sections. However, for Z>40, SuperTIGER saw an enhancement of volatile and dominantly r-process elements which suggests that there may be an additional GCR source or a change in the acceleration model. TIGERISS's measurements will allow us to check SuperTIGER's results and see if that enhancement continues beyond _56Ba, which would allow us to potentially determine if it is from an additional r-process source, a new feature in the acceleration mechanism, or both. With TIGERISS's results covering nearly the entirety of the s-process, r-process, and rp-processes of nucleosynthesis, we will add to the wider multi-messenger effort to determine the relative contributions of supernovae (SN), Neutron Star Merger (NSM) events, and magnetar flares.

abstract: Here, the evolution of the structural features and physical properties of the massive compact stars in the framework of f(R,T) gravity under Tolman-Kuchowicz spacetime has been investigated. The presence of anisotropic interacting quark matter at the core of these stars has been considered. Further, we have also investigated the impact of matter-geometry coupling on the mass-radius relationship of the compact stars. The significant role of anisotropy and charge parameter on the spherically stable compact structure under hydrostatic equilibrium has been depicted. These stars have got a more massive structure in f(R,T) gravity compared to the general relativistic approach. The key role of f(R,T) gravity on the stability of these massive stars becomes very significant under the accelerating expansion of the universe. The obtained results lie in the physically adopted regime which reflects the physical validity of the current model in the context of various astrophysical observations.

abstract: The Trans-Iron Galactic Element Recorder for the International Space Station (TIGERISS) is a Galactic Cosmic Ray (GCR) NASA Astrophysics Pioneers mission in implementation for an August 2027 launch on SpX-37 to the ISS Columbus External Payload Facility Starboard Overhead X-Direction (SOX). TIGERISS will be the first instrument to measure the GCR elemental abundances from _5B to _82Pb with single element resolution, covering the energy range from ∼400 MeV/nucleon to ∼10 GeV/nucleon using the proven combination of ionization (dE/dx) detectors with acrylic and silica aerogel Cherenkov-light-radiator (∝β) detectors demonstrated by the TIGER and SuperTIGER stratospheric balloon-borne experiments flown from Antarctica. It improves on the predecessor instruments by using silicon strip detectors (SSDs) in place of both scintillating fiber hodoscopes for track reconstruction and large area scintillator detectors for dE/dx measurement and the instrument trigger, providing superior charge resolution (σ_Z < 0.25) and signal linearity over the full dynamic range of the TIGERISS SSDs, which has been demonstrated in CERN beam tests. TIGERISS also improves on the heritage instruments by using silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) instead of photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) to avoid the need for high voltage (HV) and for the more compact Cherenkov detector readout allowing the maximum instrument geometry within the payload envelope. The detector is comprised of top and bottom pairs of crossed 9x9 SSD layers with aerogel and acrylic Cherenkov detectors between, yielding an instrument geometry factor of 1.06 m^2sr that will allow TIGERISS in one year to observe GCR statistics comparable to those measured in the first 55-day SuperTIGER flight over their common charge range without the systematics associated with atmospheric propagation corrections. With the possibility of extended observations through the end of the ISS, TIGERISS will test models of GCR origins, including their source environments and acceleration mechanisms, and in measuring nearly the entirety of the neutron capture process nucleosynthesis it will contribute to the wider multi-messenger effort to determine the relative contributions of supernovae (SNe), Neutron Star Merger (NSM), and Magnetar Giant Flare (MGF) events.

abstract: The main objective of the present work is to examine the existence of compact stellar structures characterizing anisotropic charged matter distributions with dual density profiles based on minimum geometric deformation (MGD) within the framework of general relativity. In order to solve the decoupled gravitational field equations, the seed source of the system is taken to be a Gaussian-type density profile, while the new source of the same system is considered to be a Bose-Einstein-Condensate (BEC) dark matter (DM) density profile. The solution of the decoupled systems is obtained separately through the Karmarkar condition and deformation function. We explore the physical characteristics of quantities like effective density, radial pressure, tangential pressure and anisotropy factor with regard to variation in the decoupling constant and DM parameters. The stability of the present compact structure is confirmed through analysis of Herrera's cracking criteria and revised adiabatic condition for anisotropic stellar structures. Analysis of mass-radius curves and moment of inertia-total mass curves provides predicted radii as well as moment of inertia for the observed masses for stars like GW170817-2, PSR J0437-4715, PSR J1903+0327, PSR J074 +6620 and PSR J2215+5135. In the present study, we found the radius of PSR J0740+6620 to be in the range {14.67 km, 15.14 km}, which is in concurrence with the NICER observations.

abstract: Be X-ray binaries, which constitute the largest subclass of high-mass X-ray binary systems, consist of a neutron star in an eccentric orbit around a Be star companion, accompanied by a geometrically thin Keplerian disc. These systems are strong candidates for being progenitors of gravitational waves, as their evolutionary process can ultimately lead to the formation of a binary system containing two compact objects (either two neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole). The interaction between the neutron star and the Be disc results in the accretion of matter, which leads to X-ray outbursts. These X-ray outbursts occur in two varieties: Type I (normal outbursts, with luminosities less than 10^37 erg/s) and Type II (giant outbursts, with luminosities greater than 10^37 erg/s). The variability of the disc can be traced through the changes in the Balmer emission lines in the optical spectra, with the Hα emission line being the strongest and best-studied. In this presentation, I will share the optical and X-ray analysis of several individual outbursting systems that have been monitored with the Southern African Large Telescope (SALT), OGLE, MeerKAT and X-ray missions (Swift and MAXI). The aim is to study the impact of the neutron star on the Be disc under various orbital configurations and environments. I will discuss the unusual long-term behavior of the Balmer lines over multiple orbits of the neutron star and draw conclusions about the structure of the Be disc. Additionally, I will highlight the differences in behavior among the systems and how variations in the orbital parameters affect the evolution of the Be disc and the accretion process, leading to enhanced X-ray emission.

abstract: CU Vir, a magnetic hot star, is the first discovered main-sequence radio pulse emitter (MRP) characterized by its ability to produce periodic radio pulses via electron cyclotron maser emission. Although significant advancements have been made in understanding MRPs, their temporal properties remain mostly unexplored. To overcome this limitation, we conducted a pilot study with the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) in which we observed pulses from CU Vir at 36 epochs over 1--3 GHz. In this frequency range, CU Vir produces two ≈100% circularly polarized pulses, called leading and trailing pulses per rotation period. We find significant differences in the variability indices exhibited by the two pulses as a function of frequencies, with the leading pulse showing higher variability throughout our observing band. This result could be explained in the scenario of centrifugal breakout (CBO) events in the magnetosphere of an oblique rotator causing correlated fluctuations across frequencies, along with intrinsic instabilities associated with coherent emission. In addition, we discover jittering in the arrival phases of pulses that must be considered in future monitoring campaigns. The pulses also exhibit a systematic shift to later arrival times during the course of our observing campaign, allowing us to refine the rotation period to 0.5206882 days. Finally, we estimate that ~30 pulses will be needed to extract global pulse properties for the leading or trailing pulses. This relatively small number strongly motivates more extensive monitoring campaigns of MRPs, both to validate our results and also to pinpoint the origin of the observed temporal variations.

abstract: The spectral and timing behaviour of neutron star high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) offers a unique opportunity to investigate accretion onto compact objects and the wind structures of massive stars. In particular, understanding the X-ray emission from neutron stars is a critical topic of research for current and future astrophysical studies, as highlighted by its prominence in the science cases of the upcoming NewAthena mission. In this talk, we will focus on observations of key persistent and transient sources seen by SVOM and complemented by XMM-Newton, NuSTAR and XRISM. We investigate their temporal and spectral behaviours with targeted observations taken during type I and type II outbursts, the clumpy structure of the material being accreted by the neutron star, and provide valuable data for cross-calibration studies among modern and widely used X-ray telescopes.

In particular, understanding the X-ray emission from neutron stars is a critical topic of research for current and future astrophysical studies, as highlighted by its prominence in the science cases of the upcoming NewAthena mission. In this talk, we will review the current state of the art in stellar wind accretion in HMXBs. In particular, we will focus on observations of key sources on the broad X-ray range using simultaneous XRISM, XMM-Newton and NuSTAR data. We investigate the clumpy structure of the material being accreted by the neutron star with an in-depth view into the accretion and photoionisation wakes, and provide valuable data for cross-calibration studies among modern and widely used X-ray telescopes. We will also present updated X-ray data analysis tools used during these studies, including the jaxspec spectral-fitting library, which enables approaches not possible with classical frameworks.

abstract: Jets are powerful, highly collimated streams of matter and energy that are encountered in a variety of astrophysical systems, ranging from newly formed stars to supermassive black holes in the centers of Galaxies. These jets play a fundamental role in many processes, including the evolution of stars and galaxies, and the formation of large-scale structures in the Universe. Despite that jets are so important and are found everywhere, we do not understand exactly how jets are formed. In this talk, I'll show how thermonuclear explosions occurring on the surface of neutron stars offer powerful means to understand how neutron stars launch and power jets.

abstract: The joint detection of the first gravitational wave signal from a binary neutron star merger and a gamma-ray burst (GW170817/GRB 170817A) unambiguously established a direct connection between short-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and their progenitor systems, confirming that neutron star mergers are key astrophysical sites of r-process nucleosynthesis. Studying the environments and distance scales of short GRBs provides a direct means to probe the different possible formation and evolutionary channels of binary systems, as well as their role in the chemical enrichment of the Universe across cosmic time. We present the peculiar case of short GRB 230906A, which was localized in X-rays with the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and for which very deep near-infrared observations with the Hubble Space Telescope revealed a possible association with a very faint galaxy in a galaxy group at z ≍ 0.453. Deep optical imaging from the Very Large Telescope shows clear signs of interactions and mergers among group members. The unusual location of both the GRB and the putative host galaxy along tidal debris suggests that an enhanced burst of star formation triggered by the galaxy merger may have formed the progenitor compact binary system less than 700 Myr ago. This system subsequently evolved into a neutron star merger that produced GRB 230906A and enriched the surrounding circumgalactic medium with r-process material. We will present the main observational results for this peculiar event and discuss its possible implications.
author: Dichiara, Simone
title: Mergers within mergers: The peculiar environment of the short GRB 230906A and the role galactic tidal interactions in the formation of compact binary mergers

abstract: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) has opened a new window in high-energy astrophysics, demonstrating the unique diagnostic power of spatially resolved X-ray spectro-polarimetry. However, its pioneering observations have also highlighted the need for broader energy coverage and faster response times to fully exploit this observational technique. We present the Enhanced X-ray Polarimetry Observatory (EXPO), a mission concept proposed for the ESA M8 launch opportunity. EXPO is designed to extend the window of spatially resolved X-ray polarimetry into the 2─35 keV energy band with twice better angular resolution and three times effective area in the IXPE energy band, and with three times better angular resolution in NuStar energy band up to 35 keV. . By employing a combination of Low Energy Polarimeters (LEP) and Medium Energy Polarimeters (MEP) based on gas pixel detector technology , EXPO will probe higher energy phenomena inaccessible to current missions, such as cyclotron lines in accreting pulsars, hard X-ray tails in magnetars, the non-thermal emission in young supernova remnants, and expanding sensitively polarimetry of reflection phenomena in molecular clouds, black-hole and neutron star binaries, and radio-quiet AGNs.. A key operational advancement of EXPO is its "Swift-like" agility: unlike IXPE, EXPO features quick slewing and repointing capabilities and flexibility essential for capturing transient phenomena. This allows for the polarimetric study of highly variable sources, including the prompt and afterglow phases of Gamma-Ray Bursts, intermediate bursts of magnetars, and flaring states in blazars and X-ray binaries. To boost the polarimetric science far beyond IXPE and add this time-domain and broad-band science, the payload hosts optics of larger collecting area and better angular resolution and includes a Wide Field Camera for an independent transient detection and spectral imaging capability provided by an on-board Spectroscopic Imaging Camera (SIC). This suite of instruments ensures EXPO can autonomously detect, localize, and characterize the X-ray polarization properties of transient events and in a broad energy band, for a deeper understanding of the most extreme environments in the Universe.

title: Towards fast and broad band X-ray polarimetry: the EXPO mission

abstract: Circinus X-1 (Cir X-1) is a non-pulsating neutron star X-ray binary with an eccentric 16.6-day orbit, whose X-ray luminosity and spectral shape evolve strongly with orbital phase, likely reflecting large variations in the mass-accretion rate near periastron. Throughout its observational history, the source has exhibited both atoll and Z source phenomenology, indicating that its accretion flow can transition among multiple regimes. Cir X-1 is also one of the few neutron stars in X-ray binaries where radio and X-ray jets have been spatially resolved, providing a geometric reference direction in the sky. X-ray polarimetry provides a direct view of the structure of the accreting regions; past observations with the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) reported a rotation of the polarization angle (PA) across different phases of the orbit, with PA never aligned with the radio and X-ray jets' position angle. Moreover, the available PA measurements along the orbital phase were not straightforward to reproduce with a simple precession scenario. Here, the new multi-wavelength observational campaign of Cir X-1 conducted in September 2025 will be presented; these new observations allow monitoring the source along the orbit, including its dipping phase, and correlating the PA variations with the accretion ratio, aiming to resolve the puzzle of the observed PA variation. These observations highlight IXPE's unique capability to track the accretion geometry on orbital timescales. Possible interpretations of these results will be discussed, which may indicate a misalignment between the neutron star axis and the orbital angular momentum.

title: Characterizing the accretion geometry in the X-Ray Binary Circinus X-1 with X-ray polarimetric observations

abstract: Neutron stars are the densest objects found in nature. Extreme matter in the interior of a neutron star remains in an exotic form that is radically different from other astronomical objects. X-ray and gravitational wave observations have been extremely successful in providing several key insights into these extreme objects. Co-ordinated X-ray and gravitational wave observations can provide us with a unique opportunity to decipher their interiors. Although we have observed several transient GW signals from binary mergers, we have not yet detected any persistent/continuous GW signal. In this talk, I will briefly discuss the challenges and opportunities to detect continuous GW signals from accreting binary systems with the view to enrich our understanding of these extreme objects. I will also highlight how some of the X-ray observations can play a critical role in facilitating a potential breakthrough discovery of CW signals.

abstract: Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are extragalactic, non-nuclear objects with luminosities beyond 10^39 erg/s. Proposed accretors apart from the intermediate mass black holes include neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes undergoing supercritical accretion in X-ray binaries. Their extreme apparent luminosities relate to the geometric beaming produced by powerful radiation-driven outflows in the super-Eddington regime. We investigate the properties of the compact accretor through numerical simulations performed with a radiative general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) code. We show that moderately magnetized neutron stars with accretion rates above 20 Eddington units can appear as ULXs. We further find that ultra-compact stars yield higher radiative efficiency and launch more powerful outflows, resulting in greater apparent luminosities; they are brighter than black holes with the same mass.

abstract: Results from the past decade have shown that observations in the hard X-ray/soft gamma-ray energy range are critical for understanding multi-messenger sources, particularly gravitational waves from merging binary neutron star systems (and potentially merging binary neutron star-black hole systems) and their electromagnetic counterparts, short gamma-ray bursts. While LIGO and Virgo are expected to have significant sensitivity upgrades for the 2030's, no hard X-ray/soft gamma-ray missions are approved for the decade. To fill this void, we proposed GRINTA as part of the ESA F3 call for a launch in ∼2034. The mission will be comprised of two complementary instruments that together span 5 keV ─ 10 MeV to detect and localize sources of gamma-ray bursts and other high energy transients, while also performing surveys with sub-arcmin imaging resolution.

abstract: Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) are a ubiquitous feature of accreting compact objects, observed in black hole and neutron star X-ray binaries (XRBs) as variability on characteristic time-scales and their harmonics. These signals are commonly attributed to precession of a warped inner accretion flow. While relativistic frame dragging (Lense─Thirring precession) is often invoked as the driving mechanism, particularly around black holes, magnetic torques from a misaligned field provide a compelling alternative — especially in neutron star systems. In this talk, I will present observational and theoretical evidence that magnetically driven disc warping can generate QPOs across a broad range of accreting binaries, from white dwarfs to ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs). We have discovered several accreting white dwarf systems exhibiting strong optical QPOs with characteristic frequencies and harmonic structure analogous to those seen in XRBs. Because white dwarfs are firmly in the classical regime, relativistic frame dragging cannot operate, demonstrating that magnetic torques alone can drive disc precession and produce XRB-like QPO phenomenology. These systems also provide a new method to estimate magnetic field strengths in weak-field accretors. Extending this framework to pulsating ULXs, we show that magnetically driven precession of the inner accretion flow can simultaneously reproduce observed neutron star spin frequencies and mHz QPOs for accretion rates of 10^-7─10^-5 M_⊙yr^-1 and magnetic fields ≥10^12 G. This unified picture offers a self-consistent explanation for QPOs without requiring relativistic frame dragging, suggesting that magnetic torques may play a fundamental and previously underappreciated role in shaping variability across accreting systems.

abstract: While there are about 100 Galactic sources detected at TeV energies, fewer than ten are associated with binary systems which show regular, persistent, orbitally modulated gamma-ray emission. These sources, known as gamma-ray binaries, consist of a compact object in orbit around an O or Be type star. The non-thermal emission is most likely produced in a shock which forms between the wind from a young pulsar interacting with the stellar wind. The gamma-ray binaries, PSR B1259-63, HESS J0632+057, and LS I +61 303, contain a Be-type star, and the interaction between the pulsar and the Be star's circumstellar disc appears to play a very important role in interpreting the variation in the non-thermal emission produced by these systems. We present our recent results investigating the multi-wavelength behaviour of these Be-gamma-ray binaries.

abstract: A diverse array of Galactic sources has been suggested to be able to accelerate particles up to the cosmic-ray knee at a few PeV. Popular examples include supernova remnants, compact young star clusters, pulsar wind nebulae, and microquasars. While gamma-ray observations directly trace the maximum energies of the accelerated particles, X-ray synchrotron emission is produced by leptonic populations, and provides a valuable tracer of magnetic field strength, constraining the conditions in the region of acceleration. In this talk, I will give a review of observations of Galactic nonthermal sources with the eROSITA telescope. eROSITA is a soft X-ray telescope which has conducted the most sensitive all-sky survey to date, enabling in particular the study of highly extended emission on the sky. This allows us to investigate, for instance, the interaction of gamma-ray bright SNRs with circumstellar clouds, the magnetic-field properties in pulsar wind nebulae and extended pulsar halos, or the particle population accelerated in young stellar clusters.

abstract: Presentation of timing analyses of the neutron star low‑mass X‑ray binary 4U 1820‑30 using data from the Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER), covering observations from its launch to the end of 2022. Using visual inspection, Lomb─Scargle periodograms, and Fourier transforms of the light curves, temporal variations in the flux of the source have been investigated. The primary aim was to search for mHz quasi‑periodic oscillations (QPOs) associated with marginally stable nuclear burning, although searches for kHz QPOs and burst oscillations were also performed. The analysis led to the detection of a mHz QPO with a significance of 6.5σ in one observation where the X-ray source was in its upper island state. The frequency of the feature was measured to be 3.82 ± 0.14 mHz. In this state, features around ∼4 mHz can be seen weakly (<3σ) in several observations. But the features are too weak, and significant evidence of them leading to a burst has not been seen. With the available data, it could therefore not be concluded that the features are connected to marginally stable nuclear burning. Previously, kHz oscillations have been detected from this source in other energy bands (Smale et al. 1997), but the analyses performed using NICER data showed that these features can not be detected with that instrument.

abstract: The spectral and timing behaviour of neutron star high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) offers a unique opportunity to investigate accretion onto compact objects and the wind structures of massive stars. In particular, understanding the X-ray emission from neutron stars is a critical topic of research for current and future astrophysical studies. This is a prominent science case of the NewAthena mission and will be discussed in the upcoming NewAthena Special Issue. Recently, XRISM made it possible to resolve, for the first time in an HMXB, the Fe Kα doublet and to obtain precise measurements of wind velocities via Doppler shifts thanks to its microcalorimeter Resolve. These results demonstrated how high-resolution microcalorimeter spectroscopy can transform our view of (i) the wind geometry, (ii) the ionisation structure and chemical composition, and (iii) line-of-sight dynamics. With NewAthena, we will perform time-resolved spectroscopy for the first time on timescales down to hundreds of sec to track rapid absorption changes as the compact object orbits its donor star. In this talk, we will discuss our recent simulations and results in the context of the NewAthena Special Issue with reliable statistical approaches, using state-of-the-art frameworks for X-ray spectral analysis based on Bayesian inference (e.g. jaxspec).

abstract: On September 7, 2023, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency launched the X-ray spectroscopic imaging satellite (XRISM) equipped with the microcalorimeter Resolve, achieving an energy resolution of 4.5 eV at 6 keV. In this study, we analyze two XRISM observations of the neutron-star X-ray binary Cir X-1, together with simultaneous observations by other satellites, and present results based on detailed broadband X-ray spectroscopy. Cir X-1 is an extremely young neutron-star binary with an age of about 4,600 years and an orbital period of 16.6 days. The orbital phase is defined such that ϕ= 0 corresponds to the companion star being in front of the neutron star along the line of sight. It is known that strong spectral variability occurs during the dip phase (ϕ = 0.8 - 1.0), while the spectrum is relatively stable during ϕ = 0.0 - 0.8. XRISM observed Cir X-1 at ϕ = 0.93 - 0.97 in February 2024 (dip phase) and at ϕ = 1.00 - 1.11 in February 2025 (stable phase). The first observation was simultaneous with NICER, and the second with both NICER and NinjaSat, enabling broadband spectral analysis over 0.38 - 13.0 keV and 0.38 - 50.0 keV, respectively. To interpret the data, we performed photoionization plasma simulations using the radiative transfer code Cloudy and constructed a unified spectral model for both epochs. During the first observation, the X-ray flux above 4 keV varied by about an order of magnitude over ∼ 18 hours, and complex emission and absorption lines from ions with different ionization states were detected. The spectrum can be explained by blackbody emission from the neutron star and accretion disk, inverse Compton scattering by high-temperature plasma in the central region, double partial covering absorbers surrounding the disk, and emission and absorption from a two-layer plasma cloud driven outward by a disk wind. The strong temporal variability is attributed to changes in the covering fraction of the partial absorber, which likely consists of dense clumps originating from inhomogeneities at the impact point where the accretion stream from the companion collides with the disk. In the second observation, the source was about 100 times brighter across the entire energy band and showed only modest variability over two days. No prominent emission lines were detected, while strong absorption lines were present. This spectrum is well reproduced by the same model as in the first observation, but without the partial absorber. Because the blackbody luminosity dominates over line emission from the plasma clouds, only absorption features are apparent. These results can be interpreted by a simple geometric scenario in which the partial absorber is localized along a limited region of the orbit: the first observation probes a line of sight intersecting the absorber, whereas the second does not, and the intrinsic luminosity during the second observation is about 100 times higher. In both observations, two plasma components are required: one highly ionized with a large outflow velocity, and another with lower ionization and a smaller velocity, with no significant changes in their parameters over one year. This study thus provides a unified model that consistently explains the broadband X-ray spectra of Cir X-1, including their temporal variability.

abstract: In the past fifteen years, our understanding of compact stars has significantly advanced through key observations, such as the pulsars PSR J0348+0432 and PSR J0740+6620, whose radius has recently been estimated using NICER and XMM-Newton data, along with the analysis of gravitational waves (GW) events, as GW170817. In this work, we consider polar perturbations, and we calculate the frequency and damping time of the quadrupolar fundamental f-mode of compact objects, constructed using a wide range of model independent hybrid equations of state that include quark matter. We give special attention to the impact of the hadron-quark conversion speed that, in the slow case, gives rise to a branch of slow stable hybrid stars. Moreover, we study the validity of universal relationships proposed in the literature and find out that none of them remains valid when slow stable hybrid stars are taken into account, as has also been shown for the wI-modes and f-modes in blueRaneaSandoval:2022bou, PhysRevD.107.123028 respectively. This fact could constrain the applicability of asteroseismology methods with fundamental modes designed to estimate the properties of pulsating compact objects. We hope that this result could be tested with the start up of the third generation gravitational wave observatories, which might shed some light on the f-mode emission from compact objects.

abstract: We explore the properties of the neutrino-dominated accretion flow (NDAF) around the rotating black hole (BH). Accretion flow of this kind involves a hyper-accretion rate (Ṁ∼ 0.001-10 M_⊙ s^-1) and because of this, the disk becomes geometrically and optically thick, making it difficult for photons to escape. However, the neutrinos are able to move out of the disk easily, resulting in the cooling of the flow via radiative emissions and annihilation processes. Considering all these, we self-consistently solve the governing equations to obtain global transonic shocked accretion solutions for NDAFs. Using these solutions, we calculate the neutrino luminosity (L_ν) and the neutrino annihilation luminosity (L_νν̅) for shocked flows around both non-rotating (a_ k=0) and rapidly rotating (a_ k=0.99) black holes. Furthermore, using our model, we estimate the mass and spin of the central black hole in short GRB sources by considering the predicted range of post-merger disk masses obtained from numerical simulations of binary neutron star and black hole─neutron star mergers. Our results show that shocked NDAFs can naturally reproduce the observed diversity in GRB luminosities, with short GRB luminosities achievable either from low-mass, slowly spinning black holes or from more massive black holes with higher spins. We also identify a robust correlation between M_ disk and a_ k such that M_ disk decreases as a_ k increases, irrespective of its dependence on M_ BH.

abstract: With the robotic exploration of the moon intensifying and a new era of human exploration beginning, an increasing number of microorganisms will be transported to the lunar surface in the coming decades. While the conditions on most of the moon will rapidly deactivate most known organisms, the Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) can preserve viable bioburden for long periods of time. This arises because temperatures here are low and little ultraviolet (UV) radiation reaches these areas of the moon since the PSRs are shielded from direct sunlight. To quantify the protection offered by the PSRs, we created a microbial survival model (PSR-MSM) based on the Lunar Microbial Survival Model (LMS, Schuerger et al., 2019). This model considers the effects of vacuum, temperature and UV radiation. Calculations indicate that other lesser factors, such as galactic cosmic rays and solar wind particles may still be neglected even under these circumstances. Our model organism is b. subtilis, a typical microorganism found in space clean room environments. We applied the PSR-MSM to the environment found inside PSRs at two craters targeted for exploration by the Artemis missions, Shackleton and Faustini. The model produced rates of reduction of -0.0815 and -0.0683 logs per lunation, respectively, which implies that it would take 30.0 years for Shackleton and 30.8 years for Faustini to accumulate a single Sterility Assurance Level of -12 logs of reduction. The lunar PSRs are therefore one of the least biocidal environments in the solar system and would preserve viable terrestrial microbial contamination for decades.

abstract: Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) signpost the death of massive stars or the merger of compact objects in binaries. Their detection and localisation in the hard X-ray band represented a source of discoveries over the past 50 years. We studied the capabilities of two advanced configurations of swarms of more than eight satellites (Constellation) with improved detector performances based on the concept of the High Energy Rapid Modular Ensemble of Satellites (HERMES). The extended sensitivity of the detector down to ∼ 2-3 keV represents an assist to detect high redshift GRBs as well as the more local apparently or intrinsically population of soft and faint GRBs. Through population based model for long and short GRBs, the latter further linked to their potential detection by third generation gravitational waves detectors like the Einstein Telescope, we estimate the annual detection rate of long GRBs, high redshift GRBs, X—ray flashes and short GRBs as counterparts of GW sources produced by either binary neutron stars and black hole neutron star merger. An HERMES constellation can detect 1300-3000 yr^-1 long GRBs among which 30-75 yr^-1 at redshift z>6. Such constellations can detect 4(100) yr^-1 short GRBs as counterparts of GW events detected by Ligo-VIrgo-KAGRA during the fifth observing run (Einstein Telescope in triangle configuration with 10 Km arm length).

abstract: Supermassive black hole binaries naturally form in galaxy mergers. They can be detected as quasars with periodic variability and LSST with the millions of quasars it will detect will provide a treasure trove for quasar periodicity searches. Previous searches in time-domain surveys have revealed promising candidates, but the stochastic variability of quasars can introduce false positives and hinder the detection of genuine periodicity. I will describe the status of previously identified candidates. I will also summarize the main challenges in detecting and confirming binaries in time-domain surveys, as well as recent work to address those. Finally, I will discuss potential synergies with gravitational-wave experiments, like Pulsar Timing Arrays.

abstract: While neutron star mergers were suggested as possible sites of the r-process nucleosynthesis over half a century ago, the positive spectroscopic identification of fresh r-process elements was only made a few years ago and is still debated. The understanding of the physics of the astrophysical process depends on dissecting the element abundances in the merger ejecta. I discuss here progress over recent years in observing and decomposing the spectra of kilonovae, where the major challenges lie, and what we can expect in the coming years.

title: BNS Mergers as Sites of r-Process Nucleosynthesis: Insights from Kilonova Spectra

abstract: The astrophysical origin of the heaviest elements in the universe remains an open question, with compact binary mergers recognised as a primary site of rapid neutron-capture (r-process) nucleosynthesis. Neutron-rich outflows from the post-merger accretion disks undergo nuclear reactions that synthesise heavy elements whose radioactive decay powers observable kilonova transients. Understanding the relative contributions of dynamical ejecta and post-merger disk winds, and their dependence on central engine properties are essential for interpreting current and future multi-messenger observations. We investigate heavy-element production in post-merger disk winds using general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations performed with the HARM-EOS code, which incorporates a tabulated equation of state and neutrino-cooled microphysics. We explore a suite of 2D and 3D models spanning a range of black hole masses and spins, disk masses, and magnetic field strengths, representing both binary neutron star and black hole-neutron star post-merger configurations. Outflow trajectories are post-processed through nuclear reaction networks to obtain detailed nucleosynthesis yields. Our results reveal significant intrinsic diversity in the nucleosynthetic output across different engine configurations. The ejecta mass, velocity, electron fraction, and heavy-to-light element abundance ratios vary substantially across models. Notably, the lanthanide mass fraction spans nearly two orders of magnitude between small and massive disks, and models further differ in the spatial and chemical distributions of their ejecta. This intrinsic yield diversity, arising from a single astrophysical channel, has direct implications for kilonova modelling and contributes more broadly to our understanding of galactic chemical enrichment.

abstract: Pulsating ultraluminous X-ray (PULX) sources provide a framework to study super-Eddington accretion onto magnetized neutron stars. We present a uniform analysis of fourteen years of pointed XMM-Newton and NuSTAR observations of NGC 7793 P13, complemented by Swift monitoring. The spectra are modeled with two thermal components and one cut-off power law. At high luminosities ( 10 ** 40 erg s ** -1), the source follows a luminosity-temperature relation consistent with constant temperature rather than T ** 4 scaling expected for a standard Shakura-Sunyaev thin disc. During a two-year off-state, when the total luminosity decreases by two orders of magnitude and pulsations are not detected, the hotter thermal component shows no significant temperature evolution, while the cooler component systematically decreases. Timing analysis confirms persistent spin-up throughout the campaign. Although the cut-off power-law component is expected to trace the pulsed emission, the pulsed fraction shows no correlation with its flux fraction. Instead, beyond the known anti-correlation with total flux, the pulsed fraction is anti-correlated with the flux of all model components, indicating that the pulsations are not confined to the cut-off power-law emission. Together, these results seem to indicate that the off-state variability is driven primarily by changes in the structure and viewing angle of the super-Eddington accretion flow, rather than by intrinsic variations in the mass accretion rate. Folding the bright-state spectrum through the NewAthena/WFI response allows us to assess pulsation detectability and the prospects for phase-resolved spectroscopy, providing a direct test of whether the thermal components of NGC 7793 P13 are modulated at the neutron star spin period.

abstract: The recent discovery of 50 ultra-high-energy (UHE; E > 100 TeV) gamma-ray sources and neutrino emission along the Galactic Plane has provided compelling evidence for the existence of Galactic PeVatrons. Previous studies of TeV gamma-ray sources have demonstrated that X-ray observations play a crucial role in identifying these extreme particle accelerators by detecting synchrotron emission from primary and secondary TeV-PeV electrons. In particular, a combination of broadband spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and morphological data in the X-ray and TeV bands is a powerful tool for investigating particle acceleration, transport and energy-loss mechanisms. In this review talk, I will highlight recent X-ray observations of Galactic PeVatron candidates, including young supernova remnants, pulsar wind nebulae, microquasars, the Galactic Center and so-called dark PeVatrons. Finally, I will discuss the prospects of X-ray astrophysics in advancing our understanding of Galactic PeVatrons.

abstract: The Crab Nebula is an archetypal pulsar wind nebula and one of the most extensively studied synchrotron sources across the electromagnetic spectrum. In the X-ray band, its emission is dominated by synchrotron radiation from ultra-relativistic electrons, that defines its complex morphology, characterized by a bright equatorial torus and polar jets aligned with the pulsar spin axis, reflects the complex interplay between relativistic particle acceleration and magnetic field geometry. Because synchrotron radiation is intrinsically polarized, X-ray polarimetry provides a direct probe of the magnetic field structure in different regions of the nebula. Previous studies have revealed spatial variations in polarization degree and polarization angle between the torus and the jets (alongside spectral variations), suggesting differences in magnetic field ordering across the nebula. At the same time, the Crab exhibits an energy-dependent morphology, becoming progressively more compact at higher X-ray energies due to synchrotron enery loss. Further recent analyses indicate that polarization properties may also evolve with energy. Building on these indications, we present an energy and spatially-resolved X-ray polarization study of the Crab Nebula using multiple IXPE observations. The aim of this work is to investigate how the polarization degree and angle vary both across distinct morphological regions and as a function of energy along the source. In particular, we will present polarization maps obtained in different energy bands, allowing a direct comparison of the polarization pattern and magnetic field orientation at increasing energies. By measuring the polarization properties of the torus and jets in separate energy intervals, we explore how spatial and spectral dependencies combine, and whether the magnetic field structure inferred from polarization evolves with energy within individual regions.

abstract: Observations with the first dedicated X-ray polarimeter, IXPE, have revealed unexpectedly high polarization degrees in black hole and neutron star X-ray binaries. These measurements indicate a high degree of axial symmetry in the innermost regions of accretion flows and suggest the presence of additional mechanisms capable of enhancing the observed polarization. In this talk, I will discuss accretion disc winds as potential contributors to X-ray polarization and summarise the constraints that current polarimetric measurements place on their physical properties.

title: The IXPE view of X-ray binaries winds

abstract: Although a multitude of studies have focused on targeted observations of Galactic X-ray transients, blind surveys and population studies have been limited. We have used the ROSAT, eROSITA and Gaia source catalogs to find Galactic X-ray transients having timescales <30 years. We report the properties of 738 transients found in our search, majority of which are active stars or interacting binaries. We have also found ∼40 compact object systems among which are at least 8 newly-identified white-dwarf systems, 3 known X-ray binaries, and one known pulsar. We use eROSITA (soft X-ray) spectra of the Galactic transients to show that two distinct types of flaring systems are prevalent: one having peak around 1 keV, well fit by thermal models, and another having peak below 0.2 keV and requiring a power-law component. Our study also reveals that single star or interacting binary systems (X-ray transients) involving giant stars exhibit significantly higher X-ray luminosities than systems involving only main-sequence stars or young stellar objects. Finally, we discuss the properties of the transients in the context of their putative emission mechanisms, the fraction of transients with respect to the total population, and the rates of Galactic transients expected in blind searches of the X-ray sky.

abstract: Supermassive binary black holes are expected to be important evolutionary stages of galactic nuclei, however, they have remained elusive. While there are hints of these systems in the gravitational wave background as measured by pulsar timing arrays (PTAs), confirmation of individual sources are still years away with either PTAs or the ESA/NASA LISA mission. Through 3-d general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations, our group aims to learn how accretion may produce electromagnetic signatures with which we may search for candidates and how it may affect the orbital evolution of the binaries. In this talk, we will present recent results exploring these two aspects. We will share results of merging binaries spanning the post-Newtonian (inspiral) to dynamic GR (merger to post-merger) regimes for the first time with relaxed initial conditions for the gas. We find that the Poynting flux and thermal luminosity change over the course of merger process for different spin configurations to varying degrees. Next, we will communicate new results on long-term GRMHD simulations of the circumbinary disk using a range of radiative loss rates. We find that hotter disks lead to greater rates of increasing binary separation but no significant affect on the rate of eccentricity growth. By using a different, more realistic model of radiative losses, using the so-called "leakage" method, we will show how one models radiative losses impacts the structure of the circumbinary disk and its accretion variability.

abstract: This paper presents the strategic roadmap of Korea (KASA/KASI) for next-generation space and lunar radio astronomy, focusing on several core technologies. Key technical specifications include 300 GHz SIS receivers with 4.5 K cryogenic cooling, m-class solid-petal deployable antennas with <40 μm RMS surface accuracy, and 64 Gbps optical communication terminals. Beyond the millimeter-wave regime, a key innovation in this framework is the extension of Space VLBI to sub-GHz bands in synergy with the Square Kilometre Array (SKA). Following Korea's commitment to joining the SKAO, we propose the installation of low-frequency (sub-GHz) antennas on SVLBI platforms. This strategy enables ultra-long baselines extending beyond Earth's diameter, providing milli-arcsecond (mas) resolution in low-frequency bands. Such synergy with SKA1-Low/Mid will revolutionize studies on the Universe's "Dark Ages," pulsar timing, and exoplanetary magnetospheres. Additionally, we outline the autonomous deployment of lunar surface arrays using rovers and survival strategies for the extreme 14-day lunar night (-170^∘ C) via DTN and advanced thermal control. This comprehensive framework establishes Korea as a key technological partner in future international flagship missions.

abstract: HESS J1616-508 is one of the most prominent, unidentified gamma-ray sources in the H.E.S.S. Galactic plane survey. Extending to the TeV regime and with no clear cut-off in the HESS energy spectrum, it is a PeVatron candidate. Despite extensive multi-wavelength and interstellar medium (ISM) investigations, there has not been convincing evidence for association with known accelerators in its vicinity, such as supernova remnants or pulsar wind nebulae. High-energy gamma rays can be produced via hadronic and leptonic processes. Cosmic-ray (CR) protons interact with the ISM to produce neutral pions which decay to gamma rays, and CR electrons undergo loss processes such as inverse-Compton scattering and bremsstrahlung. Accurately modelling distributions of CR electrons and the resultant gamma-ray distributions requires numerical solutions to simulate complex processes, such as leptonic energy loss, inhomogeneous ISM fields and advection. 3D modelling considers the spatial distance between sources that cannot be achieved in 2D models and may reveal the associated accelerator to HESS J1616-508. In this contribution, we showcase our novel 3D modelling method, to simulate the CR and gamma-ray morphology around HESS J1616-508, using molecular hydrogen gas distributions from the Mopra CO survey and comparing with gamma-ray observations from HESS. We will discuss how numerical modelling is necessary for accurate CR distributions in three dimensions, how these impact modelled gamma-ray morphologies and can lead to the uncovering of the responsible accelerator.

abstract: Context. The amplitude of the detected stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) measured by pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) and the discovery of early and over-massive central black holes at high redshift by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) challenge current models of supermassive black hole (SMBH) formation. Aims. We aim to study if halos containing a significant population of primordial black holes (PBHs) would increase the amplitude of the PTA signal. PBHs add an iso-curvature component to the matter power spectrum, accelerating the formation and merger of dark-matter halos at all redshifts. Methods. We propose that black holes in the halo sink to the center via dynamical friction. The central black hole grows through hierarchical merging in addition to the gas-accretion channel. We computed the resulting GW amplitude and performed a Bayesian inference analysis using the NANOGrav 15-year dataset. Results. We show that the predicted amplitude of the gravitational-wave background agrees with the observations. Our model only requires 0.09%-0.12% of the total mass of the halo to fall to the center; this is compatible with a fraction of f<SUB>pbh</SUB> ~ 0.1 PBHs being dark matter if the in-falling PBHs in the stellar mass range represent about 1% of the total population, as was found in our previous estimation of the formation of SMBHs at z ~ 6 - 10. Conclusions. The PBH model that explains the JWST new found populations of SMBHs also explain the amplitude of the stochastic background of gravitational waves.
author: Martín-González, D.
title: Primordial black hole contribution to the stochastic background of gravitational waves

abstract: Compact objects probe physics under the most extreme conditions in the Universe, yet key questions on dense matter, strong gravity, accretion, and feedback remain unresolved. This talk will highlight how NewAthena will revolutionise studies of neutron stars and black holes through its high spectral resolution, fast timing, and sensitive wide-field imaging capabilities. I will also discuss NewAthena's role in time-domain and multi-messenger astrophysics, and its synergy with current and future facilities, illustrating how the mission will open a new era in compact-object science.
author: Degenaar, Nathalie
title: Revolutions brought by NewAthena in the study of compact objects (solicited talk)

abstract: High-energy emission from ultra-relativistic particles is present in a wide variety of astrophysical systems, providing an important link between observational multi-messenger data and fundamental physical processes that still need to be fully explored. Especially for the case of unreproducible complex systems, e.g., accretion flows around black holes or pulsar-wind nebulae, radiative signatures represent a key means of probing and understanding the extreme physics occurring in those locations. In the magnetosphere of compact objects, magnetised relativistic plasmas are ideal sites for such extreme acceleration phenomena, where relativistic magnetic reconnection is a prime candidate in powering explosive releases of magnetic energy. We investigate the outcome of nonthermal particle acceleration and synchrotron emission from particle-in-cell (PIC) numerical simulations of two reconnecting force-free flux tubes of pair plasma, initially pushed together by an external drive of a few tens of percent of the speed of light. This setup offers a novel approach to model relativistic reconnection from the onset. Indeed, in the surroundings of compact objects, magnetic structures can coalesce explosively when twisted and sheared by strongly accreting flows and relativistic frame-dragging effects. We characterise the system scaling for different magnetisation parameter values, analysing the formation of very high-energy tails in particle energy distributions and potential power-law behaviour. We reconstruct synchrotron radiation from local particle quantities and derive the temporal and spatial evolution of the total emission, with the purpose of gaining insight for interpreting and predicting observations. This work presents a primary study, with broad applicability, for modelling energetic flaring events in relativistic astrophysical plasmas and linking them to observational data.

abstract: Recent X-ray polarimetric observations with IXPE have significantly improved our understanding of weakly magnetized, Atoll-type accreting Neutron stars in Low Mass X-ray Binaries. I present the X-ray spectro-polarimetric and broadband analysis of the Atoll source 4U 1812─12 observed in the hard spectral state with IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR. A significant polarization signal is detected, consistent with Comptonization-dominated emission. I place these results in the broader context of recent IXPE observations of Atoll sources, discussing common properties and implications for the geometry of the inner accretion flow.

abstract: In the past two decades X-ray observations have established the presence of highly photoionised plasmas in the spectra of accreting neutron stars and black holes in X-ray binaries. In a few of these systems significant blueshifts have been observed, indicating outflows that carry away a substantial amount of the accreted matter. With the launch of XRISM these outflows are being characterized in unprecedented detail for the first time in X-rays, revealing the sites of line emission and the wind structure. In parallel, studies in the optical and infrared have shown a cold component, whose relation with the hot winds is still to be determined. In this talk I will review the recent advances in these topics highlighting the open questions and the key observations that can shed light on them.

title: Unveiling accretion-disc winds with multi-wavelength high-resolution spectroscopy

abstract: Compelling evidence has been presented by the North American Nanohertz Observatory for Gravitational Waves (NANOGrav) and other international pulsar timing array consortia for a stochastic gravitational wave background at nanohertz frequencies. The existence of such a stochastic gravitational wave background has been expected based on projections from mergers of galaxies and the likely occupation fraction of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in galaxies—as galaxies merge, the SMBHs in their centers should spiral together to form gravitational wave-emitting binaries. However, the amplitude of the stochastic gravitational wave background is higher than initial expectations, leading to suggestions that there may be other contributions to the stochastic gravitational wave background, such as physics beyond the Standard Model or extensions of the Hot Big Bang model. If SMBH binaries are the dominant contribution to the stochastic gravitational wave background, there should be a "local" population of SMBH binaries with sub-parsec semi-major axes. The expected angular separation of the SMBHs in a "local" binary would be a few to several hundred microarcseconds. A fraction of these may be accessible to ground-based very long baseline interferometric (VLBI) observations, but more distant or less massive binaries will require space-based VLBI observations. We report an on-going study to optimize the orbit of an orbiting radio antenna, observing in conjunction with an array of ground-based radio telescopes, for imaging of gravitational wave-emitting SMBH binaries. We describe both the optimization process and the subsequent injection and recovery imaging tests that we have conducted to illustrate the performance of the resulting ground+space VLBI array. This work was supported by Astrophysics Research & Analysis grant 80NSSC22K1747. The NANOGrav collaboration receives support from National Science Foundation (NSF) Physics Frontiers Center award Nos. 1430284 and 2020265, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, NSF AccelNet award No. 2114721, an NSERC Discovery Grant, and CIFAR. Part of this research was carried out at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, under a contract with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. Some of this material is pre-decisional information and for planning and discussion only.

abstract: In the latest years the class of the persistent Be X-ray binaries (BeXRBs) has significantly increased, with the identification of several new sources of this type. The neutron stars (NSs) in these systems are among the slowest rotators in the X-ray sky (with P_ spin of hundreds to thousands of seconds) and are in a wide (P_ orb > 30 d) and almost circular orbit around a Be star; they accrete matter directly from the wind of the companion Be star, without the formation of an accretion disk. Due to the orbit and spin properties, the matter accretion occurs at a low and almost costant rate: therefore, these sources are characterized by persistent low X-ray luminosities, with L_ X∼ 10^34-35 erg s^-1. We report how the observation of these sources with various X-ray telescopes, in particular XMM-Newton, revealed that most of them are characterized by common timing and spectral properties. While the pulsed fraction does not vary with the photon energy, contrary to other classes of X-ray binaries, the source spectrum shows a significant excess above the main power-law component: in all cases it can be described with a hot (kT = 1-2 keV) and variable blackbody spectral component which contributes for 30-40 % to the total flux. Very interestingly, this thermal component has a size of a few hundreds meters, consistent with the estimated size of the NS polar cap. As an example, here we provide the results we have recently obtained with an XMM-Newton observation of the poorly known BeXRB 4U 0728-25, which allowed us to identify it as a persistent BeXRB. We show how, for these systems, NewAthena will offer a leap in sensitivity and spectral precision that current observatories cannot match. The high count statistics provided by its large collecting area will allow us to perform high-resolution timing analysis, tracking the pulse profile evolution to see how accretion "spots" change over time; moreover, with a detailed phase-resolved spectral analysis, it will be possible to investigate the variability of the thermal component along the pulse profile. Finally, thanks to the high-resolution spectroscopy enabled by the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU), it will be possible to resolve individual emission and absorption lines from the plasma as it falls toward the neutron star, and to map the velocity, density, and ionization state of the Be star's wind.

title: The increasing family of the persistent Be X-ray binaries

abstract: The VERITAS (Very Energetic Radiation Imaging Telescope Array System) observatory continues to advance our understanding of cosmic-ray acceleration and propagation by providing TeV (E>0.1 TeV) gamma-ray observations of Galactic and extragalactic sources. With an angular resolution of < 0.1^∘ and excellent spectral sensitivity, VERITAS complements wide-field surveys such as LHAASO and HAWC, enabling detailed studies of candidate cosmic-ray accelerators in the TeV domain. Recent VERITAS results include deep observations of supernova remnants such as Tycho and Cassiopeia A, which reveal contrasting behaviors in particle acceleration efficiency, and also placing stringent limits on the TeV emission from SNR W44, bridging the gap between GeV and TeV measurements. Extended observations of the Cygnus region highlight collective particle acceleration in clusters of massive stars. Building on these studies, VERITAS has led multi-instrument follow-up campaigns targeting several PeV gamma-ray sources detected by LHAASO, including LHAASO J2108+5157 and LHAASO J0621+3755, MGRO J1908+06 and HESS J1857+026. Joint observations with HAWC, Fermi-LAT, and XMM-Newton have provided refined spectral and morphological constraints, revealing complex emission regions and, in the latter case, the first X-ray detection of PSR J0622+3749. The contribution from microquasars to the population of galactic cosmic rays will also be discussed in the context of the observed gamma-ray emission from SS 433. In coordination with LHAASO, HAWC, and Fermi, VERITAS continues to provide high-resolution TeV measurements essential to understanding the mechanisms powering the cosmic-ray accelerators in our Galaxy.
author: Errando, Manel
VERITAS Collaboration
title: Studies of Cosmic-Ray Accelerators with VERITAS

abstract: Third-generation (3G) gravitational-wave detectors will observe binary-neutron-star inspirals for nearly a day, so Earth's rotation becomes part of the signal rather than a negligible correction. This destroys the usual separation between intrinsic and extrinsic parameters and creates a major computational bottleneck for Bayesian inference. We show that the exact five-harmonic Jaranowski-Krolak-Schutz (JKS) decomposition restores the separation of the rotating antenna amplitude response from the computationally expensive intrinsic waveform calculations. By sampling the intrinsic waveform on a frequency grid set by its phase curvature and then applying error-controlled relative binning, likelihood evaluations for a 21.3-h signal are accelerated by O(10^4), making day-long 3G signal inference practical.
author: Sengupta, Anand S.
title: Fast Bayesian Inference for Long-Duration Gravitational-Wave Signals in 3G detectors

abstract: The launch of the X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM) in 2023 has marked a new era for studies of X-ray binaries and highlighted the potential of high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy to understand accretion flows around neutron stars and stellar mass black holes. These studies have also highlighted the need of a larger effective area coupled with such exquisite spectral resolution to study a variety of systems that remain unaccessible to date: from the faint galactic ultra-compact binaries, key for understanding stellar evolution and gravitational wave mergers, to the extra-galactic ultra-luminous X-ray binaries. In this talk I will present a few of the open questions in these fields and how the combination of spectral and angular resolution and effective area of NewAthena will be key to answer them.
author: Diaz Trigo, Maria
title: Unveiling accretion flows in compact objects from XRISM to NewAthena

abstract: Gamma-ray burst lightcurves begin with a bright short phase called prompt and are followed by a long-lasting, shallow decay phase called a plateau. It was discovered that the luminosity at the end of the plateau is strongly anti-correlated with the duration of the plateau. Over the years, researchers have shown a few theoretical models which explain both the shape of lightcurves and the correlation. However, often those models struggle to reproduce the brightest events. Taking inspiration from the literature, we investigate a scenario where the initial star collapses into a black hole. During the prompt phase black hole is effectively accreating matter, thus gaining mass and spin. When the initial hyperaccretion changes into accretion by a magnetically arrested disk (MAD) the high magnetic field slows the accretion and due to turbulence the disk loses angular momentum. Simultaneously, the magnetic field is high enough to launch effective jets which are powered by the rotational energy of the black hole. This causes a black hole to lose angular momentum and creates a plateau-like shaped lightcurves. We demonstrate how this model reproduces the aforementioned correlation, and explain the cosmological evolution of the burst's parameters. Furthermore, within the presented model we discuss the clustering of short and long gamma-ray bursts in the studied parameter space.

abstract: Plasma-induced propagation effects on radio waves are ubiquitous in the universe, with magnetic fields playing an especially important role. To systematically compute how different plasma environments affect radio wave propagation, we have developed EMPI—a first-principles three-dimensional numerical framework for solving radio signal propagation problems in both magnetized and non-magnetized cold plasma. This paper, the new in the EMPI code series, presents a comprehensive account of its technical architecture and computational performance. We describe the parallel implementation strategies, numerical procedures, and physical processes handled by the code, including dispersion, Faraday rotation, lensing, scintillation, and scattering. Through systematic tests on benchmark problems, we validate the convergence and reliability of EMPI in high-precision numerical computations. Parallel performance tests show that the code scales efficiently to different model conditions. With the release of massive observational datasets from radio telescopes such as "The Second CHIME/FRB Catalog", EMPI serves as a valuable tool for studying the propagation effects among the data, helping to advance the understanding of their essence and the intervening plasma environments.

abstract: The Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER), which is onboard the International Space Station enables us to closely monitor the evolution of X-tray binary outbursts of X-ray on various time scales with high sensitivity data. Using NICER observations of GX 339-4, a textbook example of a low-mass black hole X-ray binary, we studied the evolution of energy spectra in detail during state transitions in the upper and lower branches of the hardness intensity diagram. We also investigated how spectral parameters evolve in relation to the evolution of quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). We will present the results of our study and revisit the question of whether distinct spectral properties exist between observations with type-B QPOs during the upper and lower branches of the hardness intensity diagram, as determined using RXTE data. In addition, we will consider the implications of our results in relation to the accretion geometry.
author: Stiele, Holger
title: A journey through state transitions: spectral properties and QPOs

abstract: The Bayesian approach provides a robust framework for an unbiased point estimate of the polarization degree (PD) and an accurate interval estimate of the polarization angle (PA), in particular in the low signal-to-noise regime. With the prior information that PA is constrained within 0^∘ - 180^∘, the Bayesian approach will not overestimate the PA uncertainty. In scenarios where a PD upper limit of 5%-10% provides little diagnostic power, e.g., for low-magnetic-field systems, a PA uncertainty of 10^∘ - 30^∘ may offer critical physical insights. Compared with unbinned analysis which requires a pre-defined model, a fine-bin Bayesian analysis allows for the discovery of underlying physical models without assumptions a priori. We demonstrate the application of this approach to the temporal analysis of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries, highlighting its capability in extracting useful information about PA variations.
