title: When and why the Bayesian approach is needed for X-ray polarimetry

abstract: The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA detector network has propelled gravitational-wave (GW) astronomy from the landmark first detection of a binary black hole (BH) merger, GW150914, to a catalog now comprising more than two hundred events. While the population is dominated by binary BH systems, it also includes remarkable sources such as the binary neutron star (NS) merger GW170817, which was associated with gamma-ray burst GRB 170817A and ushered in the era of multi-messenger GW astronomy. Although the growing sample of GW detections has provided transformative insights into the physics of compact objects, GW-GRB associations have remained elusive since GW170817. A larger event sample and expanded, coordinated multi-messenger follow-up efforts are therefore essential to achieve a comprehensive understanding of these phenomena. In this talk, I will review the current status of multi-messenger studies of GRBs, highlight key open questions, and discuss present and future opportunities and challenges.
author: Corsi, Alessandra
title: Status and perspectives for GRB and GW detections with current detectors

abstract: The decihertz gravitational-wave band represents a crucial observational window between the millihertz regime explored by LISA and the high-frequency domain of ground-based detectors. This frequency range hosts key sources such as stellar-origin black hole binaries, binary neutron stars, intermediate-mass black holes, and compact white-dwarf systems, enabling true multiband and multi-messenger observations. In this talk, I will discuss the scientific and instrumental prospects of decihertz gravitational-wave observatories, with particular emphasis on the Lunar Gravitational-Wave Antenna (LGWA). I will highlight the synergies between decihertz detectors, space-based missions such as LISA, third-generation ground-based observatories, and electromagnetic facilities. The decihertz band acts as a bridge across frequency domains, enabling coordinated multi-band observational strategies and strengthening the scientific return of the global multi-messenger network.
author: Severgnini, Paola
title: Instrumentation plus multi-messenger astronomy with dHz GW observations

abstract: The observation of cosmic gamma rays is crucial for understanding high-energy astrophysical phenomena and cosmic-ray acceleration. Femi-LAT, launched in 2008, have observed the sub- GeV/GeV gamma-ray sky, and many new insights are obtained. Recent combined analysis using different wavelengths, gravitational waves and high-energy neutrinos makes the observation of cosmic gamma-rays even more significant. However, the results showed that the precise observation with high angular resolution is needed for making more progress in cosmic gamma-ray observation. GRAINE (Gamma-Ray Astro Imager with Nuclear Emulsion) is large-aperture-area observation project of cosmic gamma rays in the GeV/sub-GeV for precise by long balloon flights of the nuclear emulsion telescope. Nuclear emulsion is a charged particle detector with the highest spatial resolution based on the principle of silver halide photography. Due to the high spatial resolution (submicron) of the three-dimensional trajectory, the angular resolution of nuclear emulsion is close to the principle kinematical limit (0.1^∘ for 1 GeV gamma rays, 1.0^∘ for 100 MeV) and polarization information can also be provided as well. We have conducted the balloon experiments (2011, 2015, 2018) and succeeded in imaging the highest resolution of Vela Pulser during the 2018 Australian balloon experiment. As a next step, we developed a telescope with a larger aperture area (6.5 times larger than in 2018) to 2.5 m^2 and performed a balloon experiment in Australia in April 2023. Furthermore, the altitude of the flight was 35-37 km, the flight time was 23.5 hours, 1.6 times longer than in 2018, and it succeeded in covered only the Vela Pulser but also the galactic center. Through the analysis of the 2023 flight data, we confirmed that the imaging performance for the Vela pulsar with the enlarged telescope is comparable to that of the 2018 experiment. We also achieved a direct measurement of the flux within 1 degree of the Galactic Center. In this presentation, we report the latest status of the GRAINE experiment, including these results.
author: Nagahara, Shogo

title: GRAINE: Results from the Analysis of the 2023 Australian Balloon Borne Experiment for Precision GeV/Sub GeV Cosmic Gamma Ray Observations with Nuclear Emulsion

abstract: The Rashid Rover 3 is part of the Emirates Lunar Mission program of the Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Centre (MBRSC). The program includes the development and launch of the series of "Rashid" lunar rovers. MoonIS is a VIS─IR spectrometer hosted on the third rover, that will explore the lunar South Pole region. MoonIS is designed to collect hyperspectral data of the lunar surface in the range between about 0.4 and 2.3 μm. The instrument builds on the heritage of the Ma_MISS spectrometer [1] aboard ESA ExoMars Rosalind Franklin (RF) rover, but introduces notable modifications to the optical head, calibration target, thermomechanical structure, and electronics. Unlike the Ma_MISS Optical Head (OH), which is integrated into the RF rover's drill tip, the MoonIS OH will be mounted on the Rashid rover mast and connected via optical fibers to the spectrometer housed within the rover body. In its current design, MoonIS simultaneously collects three spectra from three different "spots" on the ground. By exploiting the mast movement, MoonIS can acquire more spectra scanning a broader region of interest. The primary scientific objective of the mission payload is the identification and characterization of lunar water ice. Thanks to its spectral performances and imaging capabilities enabled by mast scanning, MoonIS will acquire high quality spectral data of selected targets, allowing the detection, mapping, and analysis of water ice where present, as well as the characterization of surface mineralogy at the lunar South Pole. PSRs on the Moon and on other Solar System bodies act as cold traps where water ice and other volatiles accumulate. Lunar PSRs are expected to host significant quantities of water ice, crucial for future human lunar exploration [2─4]. However, fine scale geomorphology and ice distribution within PSRs remain poorly constrained because orbital datasets currently lack sufficient spatial resolution or signal. Moreover, it is still not clear how much water ice on the Moon is exposed, since from a morphological point of view, the regions where ice is predicted do not exhibit the expected morphological features [5]. In situ exploration of PSR to investigate water ice is therefore a primary goal of modern lunar science and a key driver of multiple ongoing and planned missions. abstract: Binary neutron stars (BNS) play a central role in various high-energy astrophysical phenomena, from short gamma-ray bursts to kilonovae. Even though the number of known systems is currently relatively small, upcoming observations are expected to drastically increase the size of both Galactic and extragalactic BNS populations. Population synthesis codes offer a powerful tool to study large BNS populations. However, the numerous physical processes involved —each governed by uncertain parameters— introduce strong degeneracies, making it challenging to interpret the resulting populations. In this talk, I will present a systematic exploration of the key parameters governing BNS formation. I will describe the methodology developed to analyze a large ensemble of synthetic populations and to identify the dominant BNS formation channels. I will then show how variations in these parameters can impact BNS formation and merger rates. Finally, I will discuss the implications for electromagnetic and gravitational-wave observations, linking specific formation channels to the transient phenomena they are expected to produce.
author: Venet, Mathieu

title: The Parameter Space of BNS Populations: Formation Channels and Merger Rates

abstract: To date, astronomical telescopes operating from radio to the UV have reached the diffraction limit, but X-ray telescopes remain four orders of magnitude away, due to shaping errors in the curved optics which greatly exceed the nm X-ray wavelengths. If this gulf in performance can be closed, the unique nature of X-rays as a probe of physical processes could be exploited, leading to revolutionary results. These include: imaging the coronae of stars tens of light years away, resolving neutron star or black hole-stellar binaries across our galaxy, and supermassive black hole binaries across most of the visible universe. An X-ray interferometer could achieve this breakthrough with simple combinations of ultra-flat mirrors to give tens of microarcseconds resolution, with an instrument that could fit on a single spacecraft. Besides ultra-precise flat optics, such a telescope requires advances in gyroscope and detector technology which are already realisable. In this talk I will describe our steps towards realising this goal in the form of technology development and a mission concept: the X-ray Interferometric space telescope (XRIstel).

abstract: GW170817 is the first binary neutron star merger detected with gravitational and electromagnetic waves, and its afterglow is still detectable 7 yr post-merger. Some previous studies of the X-ray afterglow have claimed the onset of a new afterglow component or raised concerns about the data processing techniques. Motivated thus, we present here a reanalysis of X-ray afterglow data for GW170817 and find potential sources of discrepancies between the data reduction techniques employed by various research groups. We also analyse the updated panchromatic afterglow data to find that there is no significant evidence for any new afterglow component (e.g. due to the ejecta that gave rise to the kilonova) and that the jet must be still in a mildly relativistic phase. The decline in the afterglow light curve is significantly shallower compared to that expected from the standard synchrotron afterglow jet models with sideways spreading, indicating either an additional energy injection at late times or the velocity dependence on the microphysics parameters. In this context, we discuss the implications of the late-time afterglow data on jet dynamics.
author: Katira, Aman

title: The late-time afterglow of GW170817 and implications for jet dynamics

abstract: The enhanced X-ray Timing and Polarimetry (eXTP) is a space science mission designed to study fundamental physics under extreme conditions of matter density, gravity, and magnetism. The mission carries a unique and unprecedented suite of state-of-the-art scientific instruments for the first time, enabling simultaneous spectral-timing-polarimetry studies of cosmic sources in the energy range of 0.5-10 keV. There are five themes are focused in eXTP scientific research. The mission's new white papers highlight key research themes: determining neutron star (NS) mass-radius relationships through eXTP observations; advancing understanding of black holes and strong-gravity physics; resolving longstanding questions about quantum electrodynamics (QED) effects and radiative processes in strong magnetic fields. Beyond fundamental physics, eXTP is set to become a leading facility for time-domain and multi-messenger astronomy in the 2030s, delivering unprecedented observational insights into diverse galactic and extragalactic objects.
author: Ge, Mingyu

title: The scientific research of eXTP

abstract: With an unprecedented combination of collecting area, survey capabilities and energy resolution, NewAthena will open a new window in the transient and multi-messenger domain in the 2030s and 2040s. The 2040s hold strong potential to see exciting opportunities for joint study between NewAthena and future Gravitational detector LISA to jointly probe merging supermassive black holes. The same era will likely see a global network of powerful neutrino detectors including IceCube, P-ONE, KM3Net, PLEvM-1, that can join NewAthena's study of extreme cosmic particle accelerators like blazers, Serfert galaxies, micro-quasars and pulsar wind nebula, etc. This talk will overview NewAthena's unique science cases in the synergy with near-future neutrino detectors and gravitational wave detectors.
author: Zhang, Shuo
title: NewAthena Opportunities in Transient and Multi-messenger Domain

abstract: Third-generation gravitational-wave observatories, the Einstein Telescope (ET) and Cosmic Explorer (CE), will detect thousands of binary neutron star mergers, extending the reach of multimessenger astronomy well beyond current limits. Fully exploiting this opportunity requires a comparable advance in electromagnetic sensitivity, provided in the X-ray band by NewAthena. We present realistic simulations of ET and CE detections combined with modeled gamma-ray burst afterglows as observed by NewAthena, allowing us to estimate the rate of joint gravitational-wave and X-ray detections and to build statistically significant samples. Through a joint gravitational-wave and X-ray analysis, we show how key properties of relativistic jets (such as inclination, energetics, and angular structure) can be constrained. In particular, NewAthena's sensitivity enables the study of highly inclined events, which are crucial for probing jet structure. Adopting a joint EM-GW analysis framework, we also assess the impact on cosmology, showing that combined NewAthena-ET observations can reduce parameter degeneracies and improve measurements of the Hubble constant, with the potential to solve the current Hubble tension.
author: Gianfagna, Giulia

title: The new era of multimessenger exploration with NewAthena and Einstein Telescope

abstract: Double white-dwarf (DWD) mergers are relevant astrophysical sources expected to produce massive, highly-magnetized WDs, supernovae (SNe) Ia, and neutron stars (NSs). Although they are expected to be numerous sources in the sky, their detection has evaded the most advanced transient surveys. This work characterizes the optical transient expected from DWD mergers in which the central remnant is a stable (sub-Chandrasekhar) WD. We show that the expansion and cooling of the merger's dynamical ejecta lead to an optical emission peaking at 1-10 d post-merger, with luminosities of 10^40-10^41 erg s^-1. We present simulations of the light-curves, spectra, and the color evolution of the transient. We show that these properties, together with the estimated rate of mergers, are consistent with the absence of detection, e.g., by The Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF). More importantly, we show that the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory will likely detect a few/several hundred per year, opening a new window to the physics of WDs, NSs, and SN Ia.
author: Goulart Coelho, Jaziel
title: On the optical transients from double white-dwarf mergers

abstract: Symbiotic stars are a subclass of interacting binary systems where a compact object, typically a white dwarf (WD) or a neutron star, accretes material from an evolved giant. Accretion can occur through two primary mechanisms: wind accretion or Roche lobe overflow. Wind accretion is the dominant mechanism in most symbiotic stars, but in a small fraction of symbiotic stars, Roche lobe overflow can also occur. Typical orbital periods of symbiotic stars are observed over relatively long timescales ranging from hundreds of days to decades. Shorter time-scale variability is also observed in these systems. This short- term variability in symbiotics is related to the accretion process and the formation of the accretion disk, whichis crucial for understanding the evolution of these systems. The detection of periodic modulations in the optical light curves of symbiotic binaries provides evidence for the presence of magnetic white dwarfs, which plays an important role in the accretion process by truncating the accretion disk and regulating the accretion flow. We propose to do a survey with TESS of symbiotic systems to find new candidate magnetic WD in symbiotics.

abstract: We performed a long-term study of the Z-track X-ray binary GX 17+2 using AstroSat and NICER observations between the year 2016 and 2020. The source spectra are well described by a combination of disk emission, a blackbody emission component, and a Comptonized component. As the physical factors of spectral evolution in Z-track sources remain uncertain, we investigated the variation of the spectral properties of the source across different intensity levels along the track to explore the underlying mechanisms. We find that parameters such as the covering fraction and the inner disk radius primarily drive the source evolution along the normal branch (NB). In contrast, along the flaring branch (FB), we observe a significant luminosity variation from ∼4.0 to ∼7.0 × 10^38 erg s^-1, accompanied by a corresponding change in the mass accretion rate, indicating its important role in governing the source evolution along the FB. Despite notable changes in luminosity and inner disk radius, the accretion efficiency, defined as η = L_ T/Ṁc^2, remains nearly constant at ∼ 0.18 throughout the evolution, consistent with expectations for a neutron-star accretion system.

abstract: The interaction between relativistic outflows and the surrounding medium is the fundamental mechanism powering Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) afterglow emission. We present a framework that connects GRB afterglow emission to the properties of jets produced in binary neutron star merger environments. Using three-dimensional relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) simulations of jets propagating through realistic, non-homogeneous merger ejecta, we investigate how the jet's final structure is shaped by its propagation history. Our analysis reveals that the physical interplay between the jet and the merger ejecta results in significant radial and angular stratification. We utilize these structures to generate broadband afterglow light curves, incorporating full 3D geometries and velocity profiles. We perform MCMC fits for key microphysical and observational parameters, such as the ISM density and viewing angle, and examine how their inferred values vary with different jet structures. While degeneracies remain difficult to disentangle, our results show how variations in the jet's initial injection conditions, such as luminosity and launch time, directly shape the light curve. We demonstrate that even small differences in the central engine's properties leave distinct imprints on the emission, highlighting the complexity of disentangling intrinsic jet physics from environmental properties.

abstract: Studying the chemical composition of accretion discs around compact objects, such as neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs), provides vital information about their formation and evolutionary history. This touches on a range of important topics, including key uncertainties in binary evolution such as mass transfer efficiency and common-envelope phases, that in turn impact the occurrence rates of various types of energetic transients, such as supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and gravitational wave mergers. Finally, it can improve our understanding of the demographics and connections among different classes of binaries containing (accreting) compact objects. In this talk, I will present an interesting case study to demonstrate the impact that can be made by exploiting UV and optical spectroscopy to study the composition of the transferred material in accretion discs. The LMXB UW CrB hosts a relatively small companion star, but its abundances reveal that this should be the CNO-core of a more massive, stripped companion star. Combined with its short orbital period, this suggests the system potentially underwent a common-envelope phase in its evolution. I will present UV and optical spectroscopy of UW CrB revealing the characteristics of the companion, discuss the possible formation paths, and put the system in context of the sample of accreting compact objects.

abstract: Connecting the early-time dynamics of relativistic jets from binary neutron star (BNS) mergers to late-time afterglow observations remains a significant theoretical challenge. We present a framework bridging 3D relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) simulations with sophisticated semi-analytic radiative calculations to predict quantitative afterglow light curves. By evolving jets through realistic, non-homogeneous post-merger environments up to the ballistic regime, we capture complex outflow features often missed by idealized models, including multi-shock breakout structures and angular morphology. Our analysis demonstrates that incorporating these simulation-derived insights helps a more comprehensive modeling of observational data. We find that the radial velocity profile, representing a broad distribution of Lorentz factors rather than a uniform shell, significantly broadens the rising phase of the light curve due to continuous energy injection. Furthermore, by relaxing standard assumptions of axisymmetry, we show that off-axis light curves depend strongly on the azimuthal viewing angle, introducing an additional layer of complexity to be taken into account when interpreting the results of afterglow model parameter estimation. We demonstrate this complexity by comparing our afterglow light curves with the observed GW170817 multi-wavelength data.

abstract: The connection between gravitational wave (GW) sources, short gamma-ray bursts and their X-ray afterglows in GW170817 is a cornerstone for multi-messenger cosmology, allowing for an independent measurement of the cosmic expansion. Gravitational wave signals alone cannot constrain the Hubble constant, H0, due to intrinsic degeneracies between redshift and the masses of the merging objects, and between luminosity distance and system's inclination angle relative to the observer. Electromagnetic counterparts of GW signals break these degeneracies by providing direct redshift measurements and constraints on the binary's inclination. In this presentation, I will discuss how NewAthena will play a central role in the next decade of multi-messenger astrophysics. The high-resolution offered by X-IFU will provide access to X-ray lines at the distances targeted by the third-generation gravitational waves detectors. These highly resolved spectra will deliver the missing redshift information. Meanwhile, WFI's high sensitivity is well suited to observe faint GW afterglows over long timescales, thus constraining the inclination angle of binary systems. In synergy with next-generation interferometers such as the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, NewAthena will deliver cosmological measurements that are competitive with traditional probes, further highlighting the central role of neutron stars in multi-messenger cosmology and astronomy.

abstract: We present the X-ray Doppler tomography of the Fe Kα (6.4 keV) fluorescence line of the low-mass X-ray binary 4U 1822─371 obtained with XRISM. Eleven orbits of this short period (5.57 hr) binary were covered. The Doppler shift of the line shows clear modulation with the orbital period, motivating us to apply the Doppler tomography in the X-ray band for the first time. The resulting velocity map reveals a compact feature at (v_x, v_y) ∼ (─550, +125) km s^-1. This is inconsistent with the emission originating from a symmetric accretion disk, an extended corona around the neutron star, or the surface of the neutron or companion star. Instead, it suggests that the emission originates from the accretion stream-disk overflow. Remarkably, the Fe Kα velocity map closely resembles that of the O VI 3811 Å, indicating that both X-ray and optical lines arise from the same site irradiated by the central X-ray source. These results provide the first velocity-resolved X-ray map of the fluorescent line, directly localizing the major reflector in an X-ray binary and establishing X-ray Doppler tomography as a new probe of the structures of accreting systems.

abstract: Under ordinary conditions, gravity is the weakest fundamental interaction and, in many ways, remains the least settled. It shapes everything from falling objects to galaxies, yet it also sits at the boundary of our current knowledge: it features singularities, and still resists a complete reconciliation with quantum physics. Einstein's general relativity has passed all tests so far, but for decades these have probed weak, slowly varying fields. Gravitational-wave astronomy has changed the terms of the debate. For the first time, we can listen to spacetime itself as it is driven into its most extreme dynamics: black holes and neutron stars merging and producing detectable signals. Current detectors like LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA have already observed and used such signals to test gravity at the extreme, but are limited by sensitivity and by the relatively modest signal-to-noise ratios of many events. Next-generation observatories, such as the Einstein Telescope, aim to improve sensitivity by an order of magnitude and extend observations to lower frequencies, down to 2 Hz. This will transform rare detections into precise measurements and turn the Universe into a high-precision laboratory, enabling unprecedented tests of gravity, the nature of spacetime, and strongly-interacting matter in regimes no other experiment has ever achieved before. Any persistent inconsistency would point either to new fundamental interactions or to entirely new classes of compact objects.

abstract: We present a broadband spectral study of the bright low-mass X-ray binary and Z-source GX 340+0 using AstroSat observations from May to September 2019. The source traced a complete Z-track in the hardness-intensity diagram, which we segmented into ten epochs to track spectral evolution across the horizontal (HB), normal (NB), and flaring (FB) branches. Spectral modelling was performed using two hybrid configurations incorporating thermal emission from the accretion disk and neutron star surface alongside a Comptonized component. Contrary to simple monotonic trends, we find that the mass accretion rate does not increase systematically from the HB to the FB; instead, it reaches its maximum at the hard apex and the flaring branch, with lower values observed along the normal branch. Similarly, the inner disk temperature and disk luminosity peak at the hard apex rather than increasing continuously toward the FB. The coronal electron temperature remains relatively stable throughout the Z-track. The evolution of the Comptonized flux closely traces the Z-shaped pattern in the HID, suggesting that variations in coronal geometry play a dominant role in shaping the track. Z-track evolution in GX 340+0 reflects complex, non-monotonic variation in accretion rate and coronal variations.

abstract: Ultra-Compact X-ray Binaries (UCXBs) are a subclass of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (NS-LMXBs) characterized by very short orbital periods (P < 80 min) and compact system sizes. These systems provide valuable laboratories for probing the innermost regions around compact objects. 4U 1916─05 is a UCXB observed at high inclination and is characterized by periodic X-ray dips caused by obscuration from a vertically extended, ionized absorber located in the outer accretion disk. We analyze persistent (non-dipping) X-ray spectra obtained with XRISM/Resolve to investigate the properties of the absorbing material. Preliminary results indicate the presence of at least two distinct absorbing components with different ionization states. In addition, we find tentative evidence for a blueshifted Fe XXV absorption feature in one of the components, which may indicate outflowing material. If confirmed with higher statistical significance, this feature could be consistent with a disk-wind scenario, possibly driven by magnetic processes. Overall, these results provide a more detailed characterization of the structure and ionization state of absorbers in high-inclination UCXBs and establish a foundation for future studies aimed at clarifying their dynamical properties.

abstract: Ground-based gravitational-wave (GW) observatories have transformed our view of compact-object mergers, yet their reach still limits a comprehensive reconstruction of the processes that generate these systems. Only next-generation observatories, with order-of-magnitude improvements in sensitivity and access to lower frequencies, will be capable of radically extending this detection horizon. GW observations will make it possible to detect the complete population of binary black hole (BBH) across cosmic time and enable precise reconstruction of their mass and spin distributions, while for several thousand events the signal-to-noise ratio will surpass 100, enabling precision physics of BHs and neutron stars (NSs). The access to lower frequencies will also open the intermediate-mass window, detecting systems potentially in coordination with multi-band observations from LISA. At higher redshifts, where Population III stars have so far remained beyond reach —even for the James Webb Space Telescope— GW observations by next-generation detectors will routinely provide observations of BH mergers thought to originate from these primordial stellar populations. Such measurements are expected to play a central role in clarifying the early assembly of supermassive black holes. Ultimately, the GW observations will become revolutionary for identifying the physical channels responsible for compact binary formation.

abstract: Studying the transient phenomenon of Type-I X-ray bursts in neutron star (NS) low mass X-ray binaries is a new dynamic probe into accretion disk physics, coronae and the origin of relativistic jets. Observations have shown that the accretion environment can change during these highly energetic thermonuclear bursts. I will show my results from a series of radiative GRMHD simulations in which MRI-active accretion disks dynamically react to the burst radiation. The three main dynamical effects are vertical adjustment, mass inflow and mass outflow. For optically thin accretion disks, the simulations show vertical collapse caused by rapid inverse Compton cooling. Poynting-Robertson drag causes radial inflow and radiation pressure drives radial outflow, which only perseveres for burst luminosities exceeding ∼ 0.7 L_Edd. Disks of higher optical depths require more luminous bursts for bulk outflow, although radiation scattering on the disk surface drives local mass outflow even at luminosities as low as 0.25 L_Edd. The simulations indicate that vertical adjustment and the rate of mass inflow/outflow correlate with disk optical depth and burst luminosity. Such correlations can guide future interpretations of observational data.

abstract: Our understanding of how most elements form has improved greatly in recent decades, but key questions remain. Here we focus on two issues that will remain open into the 2040s: (i) identifying all astrophysical sources of neutron-capture elements and (ii) quantifying the output of all subclasses of type Ia supernovae (SNIa). For the first topic, we know of one confirmed r-process source: neutron star mergers (NSMs). However, they are likely not the only Galactic r-process source. Large-scale chemical abundance studies of light and heavy r-process elements are needed to clarify r-process nucleosynthesis and its astrophysical origins. For the second topic, the main progenitor of SNIa is still unknown but will likely be identified by the 2040s. What will still be lacking are observational constraints to quantify the output and relative importance of each subtype in the galactic context. A fundamental breakthrough on these questions requires abundances measured to better than 0.05 dex, which is achievable only with high signal-to-noise ratio, high-resolution spectra (R ~ 40 000). Disentangling the contribution of multiple nucleosynthesis sources requires a survey of a large number of stars, formed in a range of environments at distinct epochs. Current surveys miss crucial elements (e.g. Zn and Th) needed for these science cases, many of which are only found in blue wavelengths (380─390 nm). No precision spectroscopy survey with these characteristics is planned before the 2040s.

abstract: Spinning, deformed compact objects such as neutron stars are canonical sources of continuous gravitational waves. These objects may be born with magnetic fields that can strongly influence their spin evolution and, consequently, their gravitational wave detectability. Employing a Bayesian framework, we use for the first time, the non detection of continuous gravitational waves in the LIGO Virgo KAGRA (LVK) third observing run (O3), using reported amplitude upper limits from various LVK and Einstein@Home searches, to place population level constraints on the birth magnetic field distribution of Galactic compact objects. To this end, we simulate compact object populations whose spin evolution is governed by gravitational wave emission and magnetic dipole radiation. We explore multiple ellipticity models and magnetic field decay timescales, and find that the lower limit on the birth magnetic field distribution hyperparameter $B_0$ is constrained to lie in the range $10^{9.6}\mathrm{G} \lesssim B_0\,\lesssim 10^{13.3}\mathrm{G}$. Furthermore, we reinterpret the number constraints on the total population of Galactic compact objects, reported previously by \citet{Prabhu_2024}, as upper limits on the number of compact objects with a population averaged magnetic field, presented as a function of ellipticity and gravitational wave frequency for all searches considered here.

abstract: Broadband spectroscopy and fast X-ray timing have been the primary tools for investigating the phenomenology of non-pulsating neutron stars in X-ray binaries having weak magnetic fields. However, available information was insufficient to unambiguously disentangle the relative contributions of the different emitting regions, since different geometries and physical scenarios can produce similar signatures. Nowadays, X-ray polarimetry provides information directly sensitive to understanding the nature and geometry of the emission regions. GX 13+1 is among the most peculiar systems of this class, and it was observed by the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) over four distinct epochs, enabling the first polarization measurements during dips and displaying polarization properties varying in response to intensity and spectral hardness. In particular, during dips, when the flux is lowest because the central emitting region is obscured, the measured polarization can be attributed either to an extended accretion-disk corona or to a disk-wind component. Both of these emitting regions, if partially obscured, may explain the observed changes in the polarization angle. I will present the results of the IXPE observations, focusing on the most recent one conducted in September 2025 during the source's long periodic dip. These new results confirm that polarization tracks changes in the geometric configuration, thereby validating theoretical scenarios that have long been proposed solely on the basis of dipping phenomenology.

abstract: The next generation of gravitational wave detectors will search for sources across a volume >>1000 times larger than possible today. They will discover millions of compact-object mergers, along with the first detections of gravitational waves from other sources, including nearby supernovae and rotating neutron stars. Multi-messenger signals will occur when gravitational waves arise in tandem with another messenger. Such observations offer spectacular new capabilities to answer many open questions on stellar and binary evolution, the formation and physics of compact objects, the chemical enrichment of galaxies, cosmological constants, and even have implications for where and when in the Universe complex life may be possible. The critical path enhancing the returns of multi-messenger astronomy is to increase the number of detected gravitational-wave sources. To achieve this, third-generation detectors such as the Einstein Telescope should be the field's top instrumentation priority. ESO facilities can play a crucial role in multi-messenger observations, both in the precision localisation and identification of EM counterparts with VLT-like apertures, through to detailed follow-up of signals with the E-ELT. A comprehensive ESO program focused on multi-messenger astronomy and spearheaded by a next generation gravitational wave detector could transform our understanding of astronomy, providing a direct link between GW detection and characterisation and rapid EM observations. It would enable a once-in-a-century revolution with comparable impact to the birth of multi-wavelength astronomy.

abstract: We present a detailed spectral─temporal analysis of Type-I X-ray bursts from the neutron star X-ray binary EXO 0748─676 using observations from SVOM and NuSTAR. The source, a well-known X-ray burster, exhibited a doublet Type-I burst on 1 February 2025. The first burst was detected by SVOM/ECLAIRs in the 5─20 keV band, followed by a second burst approximately 17 minutes later observed by SVOM/MXT in the 3─10 keV band. Time-resolved spectroscopy of the first burst reveals photospheric radius expansion (PRE), with the radii expanding upto ∼50 km about 20 s after the burst peak. We also present a comparative analysis of another Type-I burst from this source observed with NuSTAR in June 2024. No burst oscillations or precursor bursts are detected in any of the events. Using the peak flux of the PRE burst, we estimate a source distance of 7.96 ± 0.11 kpc. In addition, simultaneous optical observations with the VT instrument onboard SVOM reveal long-term X-ray─optical correlations, with prominent optical dips coincident with the X-ray eclipse. These results suggest that reprocessing of X-ray emission is the dominant contributor to the optical flux in this system.

abstract: I will address the scientific opportunities enabled by ultra-high resolution X-ray imaging within the broad scope of fundamental physics and cosmology. The High Angular Resolution X-ray (Hi-ReX) Imager Science Analysis Group (SAG) has been highlighting how a future NASA flagship-class instrument with ultra-high resolution X-ray imaging capabilities, achieving milliarcsecond to microarcsecond resolution, has the potential to make transformative discoveries. Indeed, X-rays are generated by matter under extreme physical conditions, such as the vicinity of compact objects or in the centers of active galaxies. Therefore, X-ray astronomy probes general relativity (GR) in the strong-field regime by analysing the emission near black holes and neutron stars, where gravity is extreme. The advent of ultra-high angular resolution instruments in the future will enable direct imaging of the region near the event horizon of black holes in X-rays. This will be analogous to the Event Horizon Telescope in the radio band. This technological advancement holds the potential to provide unprecedented insights into the testing of GR and alternative gravity theories in the vicinity of black holes, thereby offering direct evidence of spacetime warping and the mapping of accretion inflows and outflows. I will also discuss how such GR tests will complement those possible with gravitational waves.

abstract: In this paper, we present an archival search for short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs) over 13 yr (2013--2025) of Fermi/GBM (Gamma-ray Burst Monitor) data using a Poisson matched-filter pipeline that performs a fully coherent analysis across all detectors and energy channels, significantly improving sensitivity relative to the onboard triggering algorithms. A central component of the analysis is the empirical estimation of trigger significance using `timeslided' data, allowing each candidate to be assigned a probability of astrophysical origin. We also developed a new parameter-estimation framework based on the Poisson matched filter, which uses the global structure of the detected event across spectral, temporal, and spatial parameter spaces. This enables us to systematically classify bursts and distinguish between GRBs, soft gamma repeaters, terrestrial gamma-ray flashes, and solar flares. We identify 549 new GRB candidates with high confidence and thousands of magnetar bursts, significantly expanding the known short transient population in GBM data. To further strengthen the significance of the GRB candidates, we performed a targeted follow-up search in Swift/BAT rate data. Applying the follow-up to all of our triggers -- including triggers below the detection threshold yielded 1736 temporally coincident events with association probability above 90 per cent. The resulting probabilistically ranked catalogue substantially expands the population of short transients detected in GBM data and provides a statistically robust framework for multimessenger searches.

abstract: Recently, LHAASO detected γ-ray emission from the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) J1849-0001 extending up to approximately 2 PeV, providing strong evidence for petaelectronvolt (PeV) particle acceleration. To explain the origin of this ultrahigh-energy emission, we investigated three physical scenarios: a pure leptonic model, a hadronic-dominated model, and a hybrid lepto-hadronic model. We show that while both pure leptonic and hadronic-dominated models can reproduce parts of the multiwavelength spectral energy distribution, neither can simultaneously explain the entire dataset, particularly the PeV tail. The leptonic scenario requires an unrealistically high electron cutoff energy, while the hadronic model underpredicts the highest-energy emission. We therefore propose a hybrid model that combines inverse Compton emission from PWN electrons with hadronic interactions between escaped cosmic rays and a nearby molecular cloud. In this framework, a suppressed diffusion coefficient (~1% of the Galactic average) is required to confine PeV particles in the source vicinity. This model successfully reproduces the full SED, including the approximately 2 PeV emission. We further calculated the associated neutrino flux and show the sensitivity of NEON to this source. Our results support the interpretation that evolved PWNe embedded in complex environments can act as Galactic PeVatrons.

abstract: The combination of optical and X-ray polarimetry is particularly efficient in probing the geometry and emission processes of neutron star X-ray binaries. We present the results of coordinated polarimetric campaigns on two systems: Scorpius X-1 and Cygnus X-2. Scorpius X-1 displays notable behaviour across wavelengths. X-ray polarimetry hints towards an intricate geometry of the inner accretion region, while optical photometry has shown a bimodal flux distribution with a 12.5 h lag behind the X-ray state transitions, consistent with thermal reprocessing within the disk. This suggests that the optical emission traces changes in the inner flow, yet no time-resolved optical polarimetry has tested this link. We conducted an optical polarimetric campaign using the DIPol-UF instrument at the Nordic Optical Telescope and the DIPol-2 instrument at the T60 telescope. Our objectives were to constrain the system geometry better and track the evolution of polarization across optical state changes. Upon first glance, Cygnus X-2 appears to be a simpler system; its X-ray polarization angle is aligned with the radio jet, suggesting an origin in the spreading layer or an accretion-disk wind. However, historical optical polarimetry reported a polarization angle significantly offset from the jet direction. To investigate whether this discrepancy reflects a spin─orbit misalignment of the system or is due to instrumental limitations, we obtained simultaneous optical and X-ray observations, with DIPol-UF and IXPE, respectively.

abstract: Most ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are powered by super-Eddington accretion onto stellar-mass black holes and neutron stars. As ULXs are the nearest persistent super-Eddington accretors, it is critical to establish and advance further our understanding of this extreme accretion process, which most likely played an important role in the early Universe. One of the archetypal components of super-Eddington accretion is the launching of powerful, radiatively-driven outflows from the supercritical accretion disk. Such outflows were long predicted to exist in ULXs, and their observational signatures were eventually detected in the past decade in several ULXs using the XMM-Newton observatory, primarily in the soft X-rays with the RGS gratings. These outflows are of importance as they can significantly modify the inner accretion flow of ULXs, the mass accretion rate of their compact objects as well as the ULX appearance. Additionally, because of their mildly relativistic velocities of 0.1-0.3c, they carry huge kinetic power and so are strong candidates for driving the inflation of the massive bubbles in which many ULXs are located ─ possibly creating an equivalent of active galactic nucleus feedback on a much smaller scale. In my talk, I will give an overview of our current understanding of outflows from ULXs. I will discuss both the high-velocity outflows observed in the soft and hard X-ray bands, as well as the low-velocity, likely thermal winds from the outer parts of the accretion flow. Finally, I will highlight plausible future directions in this research field, especially considering the new X-ray instrumental capabilities provided at this moment by XRISM and in the future by NewAthena.

title: Winds and outflows in ultraluminous X-ray sources

abstract: Z-sources represent a class of luminous neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) in which the compact object accretes material from a low mass companion star. These systems exhibit a distinctive 'Z' shaped pattern in their X-ray hardness intensity diagram (HID) and color-color diagram (CCD), corresponding to transitions through the spectral branches: the horizontal branch (HB), normal branch (NB), flaring branch (FB) and occasionally an extended flaring branch (EFB). GX 340+0 is one of the brightest and persistent Z-sources, known to trace a complete Z-track over relatively short timescales of a few days. In this study, we present a detailed investigation of GX 340+0 using AstroSat observations, focusing on the spectral evolution along the Z-track. The track is divided into multiple segments based on the Sz values. Each segment is fitted independently with the same spectral model, allowing us to track the systematic evolution of key physical parameters with Sz . The resulting parameter trends reveal distinct variations along the Z-track, with some parameters showing pronounced turning points near the same Sz values where the HID curve changes direction. This correspondence suggests a close coupling between the spectral evolution and the physical conditions governing accretion flow geometry and radiative processes. These results can provide new insights into the mechanisms driving the motion of GX 340+0 along its characteristic Z-track.

abstract: The multi-messenger detection of the kilonova AT 2017gfo confirmed that binary neutron star mergers are a primary site of r-process nucleosynthesis. With the upcoming O5 observing run of the LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA network, we expect an increase in detection rate and horizon distance demands efficient near-infrared (NIR) follow-up strategies. We present a strategy for kilonova follow-up combining two complementary approaches. First, we conduct a systematic study of NIR detection efficiency using an extensive grid of kilonova models spanning a broad range of ejecta masses, velocities, geometries, and viewing angles, coupled with simulated O5 gravitational wave skymaps. We evaluate multiple observing strategies and quantify how detection rates depend on source distance, ejecta properties, and observation timing. We demonstrate that multi-band NIR photometry enables the independent decomposition of dynamical and wind ejecta components. Second, we develop an automated galaxy-targeted observation pipeline that, upon a gravitational wave alert, performs a three-dimensional probabilistic crossmatch between the sky localization and galaxy catalogs to identify and rank the most probable host galaxies. The pipeline optimizes telescope pointings to maximize the cumulative probability covered per observation. Applied to the PRIME telescope, a ground-based NIR facility operating in the Z, Y, J, and H bands, this framework addresses the critical 50─150 Mpc distance regime, complementing widefield optical surveys and future space-based infrared missions.
author: El Kabir, Massine
title: Hunting Kilonovae in the Near Infrared: Detection Efficiency and Automated Galaxy Targeting Follow Up

abstract: Low mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) are systems composed of a compact object (black hole or neutron star) and a low mass (<M_⊙) companion star. The compact object accretes matter from the companion, forming an accretion disk. The gas in the disk is ionized by the strong X-ray emission from the inner disk region, leading to the appearance of photoionized plasmas. Characterizing their properties (e.g. plasmas' velocity, column density, and ionization) is essential for fully understanding the accretion disk structure of LMXBs. X-ray dipping provides an excellent opportunity to study the properties of the plasmas in the accretion disk of these systems. The dipping phenomenon consists of periodic drops in X-ray flux that result from the interaction between the dense stream of colder matter accreted from the companion star and the impact region of the accretion disk. To date, this phenomenon has been observed in about two dozen high-inclination systems, however, the specifics of the structure and plasma properties in this impact region of the accretion disk are not yet understood. Building on our previous XMM-Newton study of the dipping behavior of the LMXB 4U1624-490, I will present exciting new XRISM Resolve results of this source, showcasing a newly discovered wind in the source as well as the analysis of the prominent X-ray dips, which are now studied for the first time at the highest spectral resolution available. With this study, we aim to provide insight into the dipping phenomenon, any potential connection to disk winds, as well as getting a comprehensive picture of the plasmas in the accretion disk of LMXBs.
author: Caruso, Eleonora
title: Probing accretion disk plasmas in LMXBs with XRISM

abstract: Type-I X-ray bursts in neutron star (NS) low mass X-ray binaries are highly energetic events with the power to dynamically change the accretion flow. Studying such dynamical effects is a powerful new method that could shed light on accretion disk physics, coronae and the origin of relativistic jets. Correctly modelling time resolved X-ray spectra during these bursts allows for measurements of NS radii, which can be used to constrain the NS equation of state. Observations of Type-I X-ray bursts have shown that the emission from the accretion environment often increases during thermonuclear bursts. Although previously attributed to enhanced accretion due to Poynting-Robertson drag, recent theoretical work predicts that disk heating plays a more dominant role in the increase of persistent emission. This implies that the disk component changes in spectral shape during the burst; a phenomenon often not taken into account when fitting models to observed data. Using semi-analytical calculations, I model X-ray bursts of various luminosities irradiating standard Shakura-Sunyaev disks with different persistent accretion rates. The models predict an increase in emission from the accretion flow by a factor of ∼10-100 during the burst, dominated by the heated disk rather than enhanced accretion. After the burst, a dip in emission is expected due to a carved out inner disk. Verifying these results by novel observational tests could improve spectral models of Type-I X-ray bursts.
author: van de Vosse, Simo
title: Modelling the spectral evolution of accretion disks during Type-I X-ray bursts

abstract: Compact object mergers are multi-messenger sources and known progenitors of some gamma-ray bursts, bright flashes of high-energy radiation powered by a central engine, either an accreting black hole or a neutron star. Our understanding of these events has so far been shaped primarily by observations in the gamma-ray band, leaving their prompt phase poorly constrained at lower energies. A long-lasting (≍100 s) engine-driven X-ray emission was discussed to explain rapidly fading X-ray afterglows following several (≍30%) bursts of short (≲2 s) duration. However, this prompt X-ray component was not directly observed and past candidates were not confirmed. Here we report the discovery of a minutes-long (∼560 s) flash of soft (0.5─4 keV) X-rays immediately following the short (∼0.4 s) GRB 250704B. The variability and spectral shape of this emission are inconsistent with the canonical picture of a hard, accretion-powered spike followed by a standard external-shock afterglow. Instead, the long-soft bump points to a distinct phase of prompt emission in X-rays, which would not have been detected without the soft X-ray coverage of Einstein Probe. The detection of a prompt soft X-ray counterpart in an otherwise ordinary short GRB shows that long-lasting X-ray emission is likely a common feature of merger-driven bursts and a promising electromagnetic counterpart to gravitational wave sources.

title: Minutes-long soft X-ray prompt emission from a compact object merger

abstract: Ultra-long GRB 220627A, detected by Fermi on June 27, 2022, challenges collapsar models with two bright prompt episodes separated by 600 s quiescence. We present time-resolved spectroscopy and flux variability using Fermi gamma-ray burst monitor data, showing Comptonized power-law spectra evolving hard-to-soft across episodes. Minimum variability timescales trace compact dissipation in a relativistic jet. Bayesian Blocks and HOP algorithms define adaptive time bins for precise spectral tracking. Fermi Large Area Telescope analysis confirms GeV emission exclusively during the first episode (TS = 192; maximum 15.7 GeV photon), ruling out afterglow origin. Systematic comparisons with GRB 091024A (magnetar candidate) and GRB 130925A (blue supergiant (BSG) confirmed) position GRB 220627A in the high-isotropic equivalent energy, multi-episode regime of a BSG collapsar. Transient thermal components (CPL and black-body fits, kT 22─31 keV) during peak flares indicate jet-cocoon photospheric emission at radii matching minimum variability timescales, unique to BSG progenitors with extended hydrogen envelopes. Cross-correlation function and power spectral density evolution analyses, plus absent GeV in Episode II, exclude lensing, confirming a single ultra-long event. Prolonged quiescence implies fallback accretion sustaining the jet; flares trace mass supply variations. This establishes fallback as key for ultra-long prompt emission, revealing jet dynamics and central engine longevity in BSG collapsars.

abstract: The Gamma-ray Transients Monitor (GTM) is a science payload of Formosat-8B (FS-8B) for monitoring Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) and other transients, such as magnetar bursts and solar flares, in the energy band from 50 keV to 2 MeV. GTM consists of two identical modules located on two opposite sides of FS-8B, a Taiwanese remote sensing satellite. Each module has four sensor units facing different directions to cover half of the sky. The two modules will then cover the whole sky, including the direction occulted by the Earth. Each sensor unit is composed of a GAGG scintillator array (50 mm × 50 mm × 8 mm) to be readout by SiPM with 16 pixel-channels. Based on different flux levels detected by different sensor units, the direction of the GRB event can be determined. GTM will enhance the sky coverage of contemporary missions and provide independent event localization measurement. Spectral analysis and polarization-state determination for bright GRBs can be conducted with GTM data. GTM is expected to detect about 50 GRBs per year. The GTM flight model has been integrated to FS-8B satellite bus. The launch is expected in late 2026. The Gamma-ray Polarimeter and Monitor (GPM) is a similar instrument to fly on FS-8D. Different from GTM, there are 6 sensor units in each GPM module, which form a cube to enhance polarization measurement capability by catching more Compton events. GPM flight model delivery to TASA is expected in September 2027. FS-8D is scheduled to launch in late 2028. When operating together, GTM and GPM can boost localization performance with the method of arrival time difference.

abstract: This study presents the results of a comprehensive photometric analysis of the object V725 Tau (A0535+26), which belongs to a special class of X-ray binary systems. The main objective of the research is to characterize the photometric behavior of the object during 2025─2026, to monitor its brightness variations, and to identify possible activity phases. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the brightness variability of the V725 Tau binary system in the B and V filters based on observational data obtained at the Fesenkov Astrophysical Institute (FAI). During the study, a comparative analysis was carried out using historical data and recent photometric measurements. Observations obtained between January 2025 and February 2026 show that the system's brightness level remained relatively stable, although systematic oscillations were detected. A comparison of the acquired data with archival records from the All-Sky Automated Survey for Supernovae (ASAS-SN) and the American Association of Variable Star Observers (AAVSO) indicates that the object is currently in a pre-active state, potentially preceding a new phase of enhanced activity. This assumption is associated with the evolution of the Be star disk, the strengthening of emission lines, and the interaction between the Be star and its neutron star companion. The scientific significance of this work lies in improving our understanding of mass transfer processes in X-ray binaries, accretion disk formation, and circumstellar environment dynamics. The results contribute to refining the physical parameters of X-ray binary systems and provide insight into predicting future giant outbursts. Thus, continuous photometric monitoring of the X-ray binary system V725 Tau (A0535+26) serves as an important source of information for investigating astrophysical processes in such systems.

title: Photometric Study of the Be/X-ray Binary V725 Tau

abstract: M31N 2017-01e is the second fastest recurring nova in M31, with a recurrence period of 2.5 years. It shows a remarkably low outburst amplitude of only 3 magnitudes, substantially smaller than that of typical recurrent novae. Moreover, its position coincides with a bright blue variable source exhibiting a 14.3-day photometric modulation. In this study, we combine archival datasets with recent multiwavelength follow-up to investigate the system in both quiescence and outburst. Our analysis indicates that the quiescent counterpart is consistent with a B-type star, an atypical donor for a nova system, which generally hosts low mass late-type companions. We explore the possibility that the donor star is a Be-star, a rapidly rotating B-type stars that episodically develop a circumstellar "decretion" disc driven by its near-critical rotation. While Be stars are commonly associated with neutron stars in high mass X-ray binaries, a small but growing number of Be systems hosting white dwarfs have been identified. We propose that M31N 2017-01e is a Be-white-dwarf binary containing a massive, accreting white dwarf fed by the companion's decretion disc. This scenario naturally accounts for the system's unique observational characteristics: its blue counterpart, modest eruption amplitude, and rapid recurrence. In this configuration, the interaction between the nova ejecta and the decretion disc may drive shocks capable of producing high-energy emission detectable in the X-rays and Gamma-rays. As time-domain surveys continue to discover faint and fast transients, systems like M31N 2017-01e represent a previously underexplored pathway in nova evolution, with implications for accretion physics, binary evolution, and high-energy phenomena.

abstract: Gaia has the potential to deliver several tens of new dormant black holes (BHs) with low-mass stellar companions (hereafter, Gaia BHs) in the upcoming fourth data release. Three Gaia BHs are already known, but their formation pathways remain uncertain. Here, we perform a large parametric study to explore the formation of Gaia BHs from isolated binary systems with the population-synthesis code SEVN and compare our models with the properties of the three already reported Gaia BHs. Specifically, we explore the impact of accretion efficiency, mass transfer stability, natal kicks, angular momentum transport, and core-collapse supernova prescriptions. We find that models in which stable mass transfer is highly non-conservative and angular momentum is lost as a wind from the donor surface (Jeans mode) maximize the probability of forming dormant systems that match the properties of the observed Gaia BHs in terms of both orbital period and eccentricity, because such assumptions prevent the initial orbit from shrinking too much when the BH progenitor fills its Roche lobe. If we allow for common-envelope evolution, we find that models with common-envelope ejection efficiency α < 1 predict dormant systems with orbital periods that are too short compared to the observed Gaia BHs. The eccentricity of the observed Gaia BHs, when combined with information about orbital period and BH mass, favors relatively large natal kicks, similar to those inferred from Galactic neutron stars. Finally, models in which BH natal kicks are low -- e.g. because they are modulated by fallback -- result in the formation of a large population of dormant BHs with long orbital periods (P<SUB>orb</SUB> > 10<SUP>4</SUP> days), which will be tested soon by the fourth Gaia data release.

abstract: Polarimetry offers a powerful probe of accretion flow evolution, breaking degeneracies that spectral and timing analyses alone cannot resolve. Notably, X-ray binaries exhibit unexpected polarization angle variations: rapid hour-to-day swings in several sources, remarkable constancy across QPO phases in a black hole binary, and anomalous pulse-phase dependencies in accreting X-ray pulsars. These diverse patterns encode the geometry and dynamics of evolving accretion flows. This talk reviews key observational results, discusses the accretion physics revealed by these polarization signatures, and outlines the potential of the upcoming eXTP mission.

abstract: Accreting compact objects (either a black holes or a neutron stars) in High-Mass X-ray Binaries (HMXBs) capture material from their massive stellar companions, typically an OB-type star on the main sequence or an evolved supergiant. The accretion process happens either via the formation of an accretion disk or direct capture of the stellar wind (wind accretion). As matter falls onto the compact object, gravitational energy is converted into X-ray emission, producing intense high energy X-raysthat strongly ionizes the surrounding environment. This ionization has a significant dynamical impact on the donor star's radiatively driven wind. The acceleration mechanism of the wind becomes suppressed (partially or fully), reducing the efficiency of line driving and thus wind acceleration. As a result, the wind can accumulate and form dense structures. These modified wind properties (such as enhanced density regions, photoionization wakes, etc) directly influence the observable characteristics of the system, including variability in X-ray luminosity and absorption across the orbit. X-ray Observatories (including XMM-Newton, Swift, XRISM, etc) allow us to trace these variations along the binary orbit. In particular, orbital changes in the absorbing column density (nH) provide a sensitive probe of the wind structure and its interaction with the compact object. Monitoring the evolution of nH and X-ray flux offers critical constraints on the geometry and physical conditions of the system. In this study, we construct an extensive grid of hydrodynamical simulations for well-known classical systems such as Vela X-1, as well as highly obscured systems like IGR J18027-2016. The simulations are compared directly with observational data. Our parameter grid space explores a range of wind velocities, orbital separations, and additional system properties to assess their impact on observable behavior. Moreover, we are currently developing extensions of the model to incorporate eccentric orbital configurations, enabling a more realistic description of these systems, investigating accretion dynamics and X-ray variability.

title: Wind Accretion onto Compact object in supergiant High Mass X-ray Binaries

abstract: Accurate modeling of the early X-ray emission in short GRBs is essential for probing the GRB engine, understanding jet physics, and improving electromagnetic follow-up of gravitational wave signals from binary neutron star mergers in the context of multi-messenger astronomy. Thanks to the operation of the Swift satellite over the last 20 years, we now have access to an extensive archive of GRB X-ray observations. The early X-ray light curves often exhibit a bright and steep decay phase, whose physical origin remains poorly understood. In short GRBs, this phase is particularly prominent: their fainter forward-shock emission ─ resulting from a lower energy release and a less dense circumburst environment compared to long GRBs ─ makes the steep decay easier to detect. Short GRBs therefore offer a unique opportunity to monitor this rapid decline over extended timescales, up to 15 minutes. In this talk, I will present our systematic analysis of the early X-ray emission of short GRBs detected by Swift, including both the temporal and spectral evolution. We introduce a new modeling technique that accounts for both the curvature and the intrinsic evolution of the GRB spectrum, covering the hard-to-soft X-ray band. We adopt two different spectral models: a physical synchrotron emission model and an empirical smoothly broken power-law. This approach enables us to track the evolution of spectral peak energy and the bolometric flux during the steep decay phase. Our study reveals a tight correlation between the peak energy and the isotropic equivalent luminosity. This relation enables us to infer the intrinsic properties of short GRBs and assess the detectability of their early X-ray emission with wide-field X-ray cameras. In particular, our work can help to interpret the nature of some fast X-ray transients detected by Einstein Probe and suggest observational multi-messenger strategies.

abstract: Magnetic fields are found in many astrophysical objects, ranging from galaxy clusters to the interstellar medium of galaxies and neutron stars. Strong surface magnetic fields are also observed in about 7% of OBA-type stars, and stellar mergers are the likely origin of at least some of them. We investigated magnetic-field amplification during the merger of a 9 and an 8 M<SUB>⊙</SUB> main-sequence star using 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations from our previous work. We focused on the magnetic-field amplification mechanisms, field geometry, and the structure and properties of the resulting merger, in particular its rotational configuration. The merger produces a star--torus structure in which the core of the initially less massive star is surrounded by material from the primary. The torus contains ≈3 M<SUB>⊙</SUB> and stores about 60% of the initial orbital angular momentum, and dynamic mass loss is negligible. Initially, turbulent motions driven by Kelvin--Helmholtz and magneto-rotational instabilities generate small-scale (≈0.1 R<SUB>⊙</SUB>) magnetic fields. Subsequently, large-scale ordered azimuthal flows drive a larger-scale dynamo that amplifies and redistributes the magnetic energy to larger spatial scales (≈5 R<SUB>⊙</SUB>), producing a remnant threaded by a strong large-scale magnetic field. The final magnetic configuration consists of intertwined poloidal and toroidal components, with a residual small-scale structure that resembles previously identified stable magnetic field equilibria. The amplification process is largely insensitive to the initial binary separation, numerical resolution, and seed magnetic-field strength, indicating that the final field loses memory of the initial magnetic conditions. The central regions of the merger remnant rapidly approach solid-body rotation, transitioning to a Keplerian-like profile within the surrounding torus. Our results support stellar mergers as a viable pathway for the formation of strongly magnetic massive stars and potentially highly magnetized compact remnants, such as magnetic white dwarfs and magnetars.

abstract: I will review some of IXPE's many science highlights centered on Galactic sources. IXPE has produced a rich array of highly impactful science from observing Galactic sources. For example, it has significantly impacted our understanding of black hole X-ray binary systems. Observations of the polarisation aligning with the radio jet indicate that the corona is extended in the disk plane, whereas the high values of polarisation degree that we are observing hint that our theoretical models are incomplete. Magnetars, as expected, are observed to be very highly polarised, whereas the modest polarisation of X-ray pulsars is challenging theoretical models. IXPE has also tracked light echoes from a probable tidal disruption event by Sgr A* that occurred 150 years ago.
author: Ingram, Adam
title: IXPE science highlights: Galactic sources

abstract: The Spectroscopic Time-Resolving Observatory for Broadband Energy X-rays (STROBE-X) was a proposed probe class mission aimed at high-throughput time-domain and multi-messenger astrophysics. We plan to incorporate the lessons learned from studying STROBE-X and the evolving landscape of X-ray astronomy missions into a new MIDEX concept. This would be built around two pointed instruments: a broadband telescope with NICER-like concentrating optics covering 0.2-50 keV with >5x the NICER effective area, along with an imaging telescope taking advantage of a flight-spare IXPE optic filling a role similar to the Swift XRT. In addition a wide-field monitor would be included, either derived from the STROBE-X WFM coded-aperture instrument or a lobster-eye optic. In the probe competition, STROBE-X received a Category 1 ranking and with low technical and cost risk, but was not selected. The X-ray mission that was selected (AXIS) is a high-resolution imager that does not cover any of the high-throughput, bright source, time-domain science that STROBE-X was designed for. Also, in 2025, the NICER instrument on ISS ended its science mission, removing this critical resource for high time-resolution X-ray observations, and Swift is in danger of re-entering in 2026. For some high-energy transient science other missions have recently been launched (e.g. Einstein Probe, SVOM, Insight-HXMT,) or proposed, such as THESEUS, eXTP and several smaller, more GRB-focused missions like StarBurst. A major gap will exist for a mission that can detect X-ray transients and respond with high-throughput observations that can do detailed time-resolved spectroscopy and study fast variability including pulsations and QPOs. This will enable unprecedented study of accretion processes, including disks, winds, and measurements of black hole and neutron star spins, shedding light on the formation and evolution of compact objects. We will describe the instrument advances that will be incorporated into this MIDEX and how they will enable a responsive, cost-effective mission that will serve a broad community in the era of time domain astronomy.

abstract: The origin of Galactic cosmic rays (CRs) above the PeV scale, particularly around the knee of the all-particle spectrum, remains a fundamental open question in high-energy astrophysics. It is still debated whether a single source class dominates this energy regime or whether the observed flux arises from the superposition of multiple populations. Recent precise measurements of the spectral shape and the proton-to-helium ratio favor the latter scenario, underscoring the need to quantify the contribution of individual source classes. In this context, recent detections of very-high-energy (VHE; E > 0.1) and ultra-high-energy (UHE; E>100 TeV) gamma rays from microquasars — X-ray binaries hosting a black hole or neutron star with (semi-)relativistic jets — have established them as promising PeV cosmic-ray accelerators (PeVatrons). Although only six such systems have been identified to date, even a small population of powerful accelerators could make a non-negligible contribution to the CR spectrum around the knee. The VHE─UHE detections have triggered extensive multiwavelength follow-up campaigns. The case of the microquasar SS 433 and its surrounding nebula W50 demonstrate the crucial role of X-ray observations in interpreting gamma-ray sources. The morphological correspondence between X-ray and gamma-ray emission supports a leptonic scenario. Furthermore, the identification of hard X-ray and higher-energy gamma-ray knots within the jets reveals localized particle acceleration sites. Radio continuum observations can also probe synchrotron emission from energetic electrons, while radio line observations tracing dense gas provide key diagnostics of hadronic processes. Similar multiwavelength efforts are ongoing for other gamma-ray-emitting microquasars. In this talk, I will present an overview of the six microquasars detected in the VHE─UHE regime and report recent detailed multiwavelength studies of SS 433/W50 and V4641 Sgr. These include extensive X-ray observations with Chandra, XMM-Newton, NuSTAR, XRISM, and IXPE, searches for molecular clouds with the Nobeyama 45-m telescope, and prospects for future coordinated campaigns.
author: Tsuji, Naomi
title: Multiwavelength Observation Insights into Extreme Particle Acceleration in Microquasars

abstract: In the current era of satellite mega-constellations, the prevalence of human made signals in radio observations is rapidly increasing, thereby increasing the false positive rates in transient and technosignature studies performed from the Earth. Thus, being able to perform radio observations in environments free of radio frequency interference (RFI) offers a unique opportunity to conduct transient studies without ambiguity - in other words, to perform radio astronomy from locations where virtually every detected signal is of scientific value, contributing directly to our understanding of the Universe. One such cost-effective solution to perform RFI-free observations is to do radio astronomy from the lunar farside. A radio telescope on the lunar farside elegantly overcomes two fundamental limitations of Earth-based radio telescopes: (i) the large dynamic range and spectral confusion of RFI, and (ii) the inability to observe below ∼ 30 MHz due to the ionospheric cutoff, in addition to providing an extremely stable thermal environment. However, with the advent of cost-effective access to space, simulations indicate that within the next 3─5 years, RFI from an increasing number of lunar landers and orbiters may compromise this pristine environment. We present the Lunar Farside Technosignature Transient Telescope (LFT3), a radio telescope with a suite of dual-polarized antennas from 1-2700 MHz, planned for launch by the end of this decade to exploit the unique and time-critical opportunity offered by the lunar farside. With higher sensitivity and an environment cleaner than that in which the original "Wow!" signal was detected, LFT3 will enable the most robust technosignature search in human history. Despite the fact that Breakthrough Listen Candidate 1 exhibited many of the characteristics expected of a technosignature, it could not be confidently attributed as such because the observation was performed from Earth, surrounded by pervasive RFI. Thus, conducting similar observations from an RFI-free environment such as the lunar farside would provide a decisive improvement in our ability to confirm (or refute) technosignature candidates and unambiguously detect transients with multiple temporal characteristics. In addition, LFT3 will probe previously unknown populations of low-frequency radio transients (particularly below ionospheric cutoff frequencies), perform novel low-frequency VLBI in conjunction with Earth-based facilities, conduct cosmology measurements in low radio frequencies, and provide detailed studies of outer planet emissions in the low-frequency regime.

abstract: The Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) is a NASA Small Explorer (SMEX) satellite mission in development with a planned launch into low-Earth orbit in 2027. COSI is a wide-field gamma-ray telescope designed to survey the entire sky at 0.2-5 MeV. It provides imaging, spectroscopy, and polarimetry of astrophysical sources. Science goals for COSI include studies of 0.511 MeV emission from antimatter annihilation in the Galaxy, mapping radioactive elements from nucleosynthesis, detecting and localizing multimessenger sources, and determining emission mechanisms and source geometries with polarization measurements. Compton telescopes detect multiple interactions from individual incoming photons, allowing for scattering angles to be measured. After many photons are detected from a source, the distribution of azimuthal angles provides polarization information. COSI will measure the polarization of accreting black holes, gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), and pulsars. In this talk, we will describe the COSI instrument, its polarimetry science objectives, and a status update for the mission.

abstract: HERD, the world's highest-energy, widest-field-of-view, and largest-area space-based particle physics and astrophysics facility for detecting high-energy electrons, cosmic rays, and gamma rays, is scheduled for launch and installation onto the China Space Station in 2029 to operate over an extended period. Leveraging the China Space Station—the national space science laboratory—HERD will achieve unprecedented precision and energy range in measuring the energies and spatial distributions of cosmic high-energy electrons; determine the composition and energy spectra at the "knee"—the critical feature marking the transition between galactic and extragalactic cosmic-ray origins; conduct surveys of the dynamic high-energy gamma-ray sky; search for potential signals of dark matter particle annihilation or decay; deepen our understanding of the origin and propagation of high-energy cosmic rays; and make significant contributions to the identification of high-energy neutrino astrophysical sources, observations of gamma-ray pulsars, and gravitational-wave detection.
