abstract: The latest observations by the High-Altitude Water Cherenkov Gamma-Ray Observatory (HAWC) and the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) can be used to test the assumptions on the sources of TeV-scale cosmic rays as well as the propagation assumptions of those cosmic rays within the Milky Way's interstellar medium. Including updates on the boron-to-carbon, and the beryllium isotopes cosmic-ray ratios from the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer at GeV energies, the TeV gamma-ray measurements can transform our understanding of cosmic rays at the TeV scale. I will show results where we use the LHAASO observations at 1-100 TeV gamma-ray energies as well as measurements of same energy scale neutrinos from the IcCube Neutrino Observatory. We test alternative models on the averaged properties of the Milky Way's interstellar medium conditions relying on modeling them via the GALPROP comic-ray propagation code; which also allows to calculate the diffuse gamma-ray emission at these energies. Furthermore, in our work we include the gamma-ray emission from TeV-halos associated to pulsars as those that have been detected in the HAWC observations.

abstract: X-ray binaries hosting compact objects exhibit often characteristic variability patterns in their lightcurves, which occur at high accretion rates and may be attributed to thermoviscous instabilities within their accretion disks. In particular, the limit-cycle oscillations that are believed to arise from radiation pressure instability (RPI) that operate in the inner regions of the disk. The global disk instability model, based on the alpha-viscosity prescription, was established in Janiuk et al 2002, and applied to various sources known as BHXBs. Our current work aims to investigate the effect of irradiation from the central compact source on the time-evolution of an unstable accretion disk. In recent years, the effect of irradiation as an important factor in the disk evolution has been highlighted e.g. by Dubus et al (1999). The central compact region can be a hot corona in case of black hole accretors, or a hot boundary layer, between the disk and the stellar surface, in case of accreting neutron stars. We employ the code "GLADIS" to calculate a 1-dimensional vertically averaged global hydrodynamical model of accretion disk. The energetics is modified by including the irradiating flux, which depends upon accretion rate and geometry of the system. We consider a shielding region in the inner part of the disk, to regulate variability amplitude. We probe how the irradiation affects the shape of the disk outburst pattern. We also highlight the role of disk winds in regulating the RPI instability in BHXRB sources. As a case study, we model the 'heartbeat' feature observed in the XRB 4U 1630-47, as reported by Fan et al (2025) References : Janiuk, A., Czerny, B., Siemiginowska, A. (2002). abstract: The Solar System is gifted with a diverse array of magnetospheric systems, from the familiar Dungey-cycle-driven system at Earth, to the extreme Vasyliunas-cycle-driven Gas Giants, to the unmagnetized-solar wind interactions found at Mars and Venus. Together, this diverse set of planetary magnetospheres makes it possible to probe fundamental physical processes by exploring how and under what conditions they operate in and across the Solar System. Furthermore, if we can make sense of this large parameter regime, not only will we improve our understanding of the geospace environment, we may also be able to close the gap in our understanding of plasma physics elsewhere in the cosmos, e.g., magnetospheres of pulsars and brown dwarfs. However, to reach that goal, it requires the Earth and Planetary space physics communities to give serious consideration to the physics behind the similarities and differences between these systems. Fortunately, the Geospace Environment Modeling (GEM) program—which is sponsored by the National Science Foundation (NSF)—has a focus group on Comparative planetary Magnetospheric Processes (COMP). In this presentation, we will provide a summary of the COMP efforts that have been underway since its inaugural session in 2023 as well as a list of community-solicited questions and strategies to pursue in the coming decade. Finally, we will conclude on ways for anyone interested to participate and contribute in upcoming GEM workshops.

abstract: Diamagnetic cavities (DMCs) in Earth's magnetosphere are weak─magnetic-field, high─plasma-beta regions that form around the high-altitude cusp funnel. They act as reservoirs for energetic particles and enable efficient perpendicular particle acceleration. DMCs are created by large-scale magnetic reconnection that drives the global plasma circulation known as the Dungey cycle. In addition, the DMCs are magnetically and structurally equivalent to the standard solar flare model for describing the plasma dynamics, transport and evolution during the eruption process. Thus, the investigation of the Earth's DMCs is important for the readily available in-situ spacecraft measurements. Previous studies have suggested that particles are energized up to hundreds keV when their curvature and gradient drift align with the gradient of reconnection quasi-potential. With the combination analysis from test-particle simulation and Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission, a scaling law of particle acceleration ∆∊ = α m_i V_A^2 is given, enabling the straightforward examination and prediction for energization processes in various astrophysical and even exoplanetary plasma environments, such as the solar corona, pulsars, active galactic nuclei, etc. Further, the typical plasma mass estimated contained within the DMCs is 45 times sufficient to populate the plasma sheet in the magnetotail. These emphasize the important role of Earth's DMCs in particle acceleration and transport within the global dynamics of the planetary magnetosphere.

abstract: The 2040s will be a golden era for time-domain and multi-messenger astrophysics, but many decisive phases of transient evolution are best seen at millimeter/sub-millimeter (mm/sub-mm) wavelengths, where suitably capable instruments are still lacking. mm/sub-mm uniquely probes early shock and jet emission, penetrate dust-enshrouded environments and reveal magnetic-field geometry providing key information on the physical properties of the sources. In this talk, I will describe how planned facilities such as the next-generation interferometer ALMA2040 and the wide-field single-dish telescope AtLAST could fill this gap. Wide-field monitoring and rapid tiling of large localization regions from gravitational-wave and neutrino alerts enable efficient counterpart identification. Rapid-response, broadband, full-Stokes interferometric follow-up with large sensitivity gains, simultaneous multi-frequency coverage, long baselines and VLBI compatibility can convert those detections into quantitative constraints on energetics, environments and magnetic structure. These capabilities will reshape studies of interaction-powered supernovae, novae and stellar mergers, and of engine-driven explosions such as GRBs, fast blue optical transients and tidal disruption events. They will also enable sharper view to jets from X-ray binaries and AGN, and fast coherent transients such as magnetars, pulsars and repeating FRBs. Next-generation mm facilities will make mm/sub-mm time-domain observations a core part of multi-messenger discovery and interpretation in the 2040s, and will deliver legacy datasets that map the transient millimetre sky for decades.
author: Koljonen, Karri
title: From explosions to jets: The transient millimetre Universe in the 2040s
